meta.title: Europa Strata
meta.subtitle: Cultures, empires, and genetic layers from deep time to now

ancestryKeys.label: WHG
ancestryKeys.detail: Mesolithic western/central European foragers; a substrate after farming, not a living “people” label later.

ancestryKeys.label: SHG
ancestryKeys.detail: Northern foragers of Scandinavia, often modeled as WHG with extra EHG-related affinity; important Mesolithic–Neolithic north baseline before TRB and Single Grave turnovers.

ancestryKeys.label: EHG
ancestryKeys.detail: Forest-steppe/eastern foragers with Ancient North Eurasian affinity; key ingredient of Yamnaya with CHG-related ancestry.

ancestryKeys.label: EEF
ancestryKeys.detail: Anatolian Neolithic–related farmers who spread demically into Europe from ~6500 BCE; dominant in Early Neolithic west.

ancestryKeys.label: WSH
ancestryKeys.detail: Yamnaya-related Western Steppe Herder ancestry that spreads widely after ~3000 BCE via Corded Ware and kin. Often shortened WSH or “steppe.”

ancestryKeys.label: CHG
ancestryKeys.detail: Caucasus hunter-gatherer–related ancestry; often modeled inside the steppe cline rather than as a free European component.

ancestryKeys.label: Other
ancestryKeys.detail: Catch-all for eastern Mediterranean, East Eurasian, North African, or poorly resolved medieval/modern inputs — not a deep Paleolithic cluster.

modeLegend.persistence: Substrate continues with little demographic overturn
modeLegend.replacement: Incoming ancestry largely displaces the prior gene pool
modeLegend.absorption: Incoming elite/culture absorbed into a durable local substrate
modeLegend.continuity: Deep ternary (WHG–EEF–steppe) largely stable; polity labels shift
modeLegend.cultural: Archaeological or political package spreads faster than genes

meta.linguisticDisclaimer: Languages ≠ genes. Indo-European dispersal is often correlated with steppe-related ancestry in temperate Europe, but archaeological cultures, genomes, and speech can spread independently. Confidence tags: attested (written/epigraphic), reconstructed (comparative linguistics), hypothetical (no direct evidence), mixed.
meta.mapAttribution: Base map: Natural Earth (public domain). Culture extents are schematic best-guess consensus overlays on modern borders — not precise archaeological site distributions.

glossary.name: Western Hunter-Gatherers
glossary.text: c. 14,000–5,000 BCE. Mesolithic foragers of western and central Europe; later a minority substrate in farmer and Bronze Age populations.

glossary.name: Eastern Hunter-Gatherers
glossary.text: c. 10,000–3,500 BCE. Forest-steppe foragers with Ancient North Eurasian affinity; a primary ingredient (with CHG) of Yamnaya / WSH.

glossary.name: Scandinavian Hunter-Gatherers
glossary.text: c. 9,500–4,000 BCE. Northern foragers of Scandinavia—WHG-like with elevated EHG affinity—before Funnelbeaker and Single Grave turnovers.

glossary.name: Early European Farmers
glossary.text: c. 6,500–3,000 BCE. Anatolian Neolithic–related farming populations (Cardial, LBK, and related) who spread into Europe with crops and herds.

glossary.name: Western Steppe Herders
glossary.text: c. 3,300–2,000 BCE. Yamnaya-related steppe pastoralist ancestry that remakes temperate Europe in the third millennium BCE (Corded Ware, Beaker, and related).

glossary.name: Caucasus Hunter-Gatherers
glossary.text: c. 13,000–5,000 BCE. Caucasus forager-related ancestry; usually modeled inside the steppe (WSH) cline rather than as a free European component.

periods.label: Mesolithic
periods.narrative: After the Last Glacial Maximum, Europe is resettled by genetically distinct forager populations. Western Hunter-Gatherers (WHG) dominate west and center; Eastern Hunter-Gatherers (EHG) hold the forest-steppe. Archaeological names (Azilian, Maglemosian, Narva) are tool-and-site traditions, not ethnic states. No farming, no Indo-European, no writing.
periods.culturesNote: Azilian, Sauveterrian/Tardenoisian, Maglemosian–Kongemose, Epigravettian Italy, Iron Gates, Narva/Kunda — microlithic forager facies over WHG/EHG genetics.

iberia.description: Late Upper Paleolithic to Mesolithic foragers of Iberia (Azilian and related facies). Small, mobile groups after glacial retreat. Genetically WHG-related; they become a minority substrate once Cardial farmers arrive, not a continuous “Iberian people” into history.
iberia.ancestryNote: Mesolithic Iberia ≈ WHG; local structure exists but not EEF or steppe yet.
iberia.linguisticNote: No writing. Later Iberian (non-IE) and Basque are historically attested millennia later and cannot be projected onto Azilian speech.
iberia.art: After the last cave-painting florescence, Iberian foragers favour portable marks—engraved bone, geometric microliths, and ochre on curated human remains—while still revisiting Paleolithic sanctuaries as remembered places. Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts pile shell middens that are as much seasonal calendars as rubbish dumps. Dress and weaponry stay hide, antler, and bow-and-microlith; style is regional, not imperial.
iberia.ideas: Life is organised around mobile territories of coast, estuary, and upland, not villages or chiefs. Social knowledge travels as seasonal rounds, marriage alliances between small bands, and shared hunting etiquette along the Cantabrian and Levantine façades. Contact with incoming farmers later turns these ideas into a frontier negotiation, not a blank slate.
iberia.philosophy: Cosmology is unread in words but practised in burial: ochre, flexed bodies, and occasional structured deposits imply care for the dead and for powerful places in the landscape. Rivers, caves, and shell beaches likely structured a world of spirits and seasons rather than named gods we can recover. No temples; the living map itself is the sacred architecture.
iberia.science: Foragers read tides, shellfish seasons, and deer migrations with high resolution—El Mazo–style middens even register abrupt Holocene cooling in harvest choices. Microlith geometry and composite projectiles are precision engineering in flint and mastic. Coastal navigation and inland pathfinding are the applied sciences of a drowning early Holocene shoreline.

britain.description: Post-Doggerland island foragers with microlithic technologies. Population density low. Their WHG-related ancestry is almost erased first by Neolithic farmers, then again by Beaker-age migrants — a double discontinuity unique in clarity in the aDNA record.
britain.ancestryNote: ~Pure WHG before farming; later turnovers remove most of this lineage.
britain.linguisticNote: Unknown. Not Celtic — Insular Celtic is an Iron Age/historical stage.
britain.art: Star Carr’s timber platforms and red-deer frontlets show ritualised costume as much as craft—antler headdresses for performance beside the lake. Microliths, barbed points, and rare amber or shale beads form a sparse portable art world after Doggerland’s drowning. Ireland and Britain share watery aesthetics of canoe, fish trap, and hide boat more than carved monuments.
britain.ideas: Island life after the North Sea rises forces tighter coastal and riverine schedules; Doggerland’s loss is a slow political geography rewrite, not a myth we can quote. Small bands manage seasonal rounds from upland hunting to estuary fishing. Knowledge of drowning shores and tsunami-scarred coasts (Storegga) enters living memory as caution, not cosmology we can name.
britain.philosophy: Deer-skull rites and lakeside platforms suggest transformation, hunting magic, or seasonal ceremony—practice without a recoverable creed. Burials are rare and curated; the sacred seems tied to wetlands and animals rather than stone temples. Worldview is inferred from performance gear and place reuse, not texts.
britain.science: Composite microlith weapons, dugouts, and fish weirs are precision wetland engineering. Foragers track post-glacial forest succession and shifting coasts with generation-scale environmental literacy. Star Carr’s woodworking and birch-pitch adhesives show chemical and carpentry skill in a cold early Holocene.

france.description: Mesolithic traditions of what is now France: microlithic toolkits, forest and riverine economies. WHG genetics dominate. These groups contribute ancestry back into Middle Neolithic farmers but leave no linguistic trace.
france.linguisticNote: Unattested; later Gaulish is Celtic IE and unrelated in any recoverable way.
france.ancestryNote: WHG-dominated; EEF arrives with Cardial/LBK streams later.
france.art: Tiny geometric microliths are the visual signature—almost abstract flint design—alongside bone points and rare personal ornaments. Southern rock shelters keep memory of earlier painted caves as visited places more than active ateliers. Atlantic Brittany and Mediterranean Languedoc develop distinct coastal versus inland craft dialects within one forager world.
france.ideas: Small, flexible bands stitch river valleys and plateaus into seasonal territories without villages. Knowledge of flint sources and hunting grounds is social capital exchanged through marriage and meeting. The idea of ‘frontier’ appears only when Cardial and Danubian farmers later press from south and east.
france.philosophy: Burials with ochre and curated goods imply respect for persons and places; cosmology itself stays silent in the record. Landscape memory—caves, fords, hunting stands—likely carried spirit and story. Ritual is deposition and return, not temple cult.
france.science: Microlith technology maximises cutting edge from scarce good flint—materials science in miniature. Foragers manage post-glacial oak–hazel forests and river fisheries with detailed ecological timing. Path networks across the Massif and Paris Basin are lived geodesy before roads.

central.description: Foragers of the North European Plain and Alpine foreland after reforestation. Genetically WHG with increasing EHG affinity eastward — the soft western edge of Allentoft’s later “great divide.”
central.linguisticNote: Unknown forager languages; not Germanic or Celtic.
central.ancestryNote: WHG-dominated core of the North European Plain; EHG affinity rises eastward toward the forest-steppe divide.
central.art: Bone and antler tools, microliths, and occasional amber from Baltic drift form a quiet portable art of forest and river. Rock art is rarer than in Atlantic or Alpine zones; aesthetic energy goes into projectile geometry and personal ornament. Sites such as those near the Elbe and Rhine keep forager craft distinct until LBK pottery arrives.
central.ideas: Loess belts and river corridors are hunting territories first, later the highways farmers will seize. Band mobility and flint exchange link the North European Plain to uplands without central authority. The idea of ‘empty land’ is an illusion—farmers enter a known forager geography.
central.philosophy: Ochre burials and rare structured deposits hint at afterlife care; named deities do not survive. Rivers and forest clearings likely held spirit significance in oral tradition. Worldview is practised at the grave and the kill site.
central.science: Forest hunting, plant gathering, and river fishing require fine phenological calendars. Composite tools and birch-tar adhesives are chemical crafts. Foragers’ mental maps of flint outcrops become the substrate pioneer farmers later quarry.

scandinavia.description: Coastal and inland foragers of southern and western Scandinavia (Maglemosian, Kongemose, Fosna–Hensbacka). Genetically Scandinavian Hunter-Gatherers (SHG)—WHG-related with extra EHG affinity. Later overturned first by TRB farmers, then by Single Grave / Battle Axe steppe-rich groups.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Unknown. Pre-Germanic is associated with much later Battle Axe / Nordic BA stages.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: SHG = northern foragers often modeled as WHG + elevated EHG-related affinity; Maglemosian–Kongemose world.
scandinavia.art: Bone and antler leisters, amber pendants, and later Kongemose blade elegance define a northern wetland aesthetic. Rock art begins to appear on coastal cliffs in some areas; portable amber animals and beads glow as prestige. SHG foragers carve identity from seal, fish, and forest deer rather than painted caves.
scandinavia.ideas: A watery cosmos of lakes, archipelagos, and rising Baltic/North Sea shores structures mobility and alliance. Eastern genetic affinity (EHG-related) mixes into WHG baselines—Scandinavia as a contact sea. Territorial knowledge of seal rookeries and salmon runs is political capital.
scandinavia.philosophy: Amber and animal deposits, wetland platforms, and careful burials suggest a world where water and animal persons hold power. Cosmology is maritime and forestal—no temples, many thresholds (shore, ice, forest edge). Ritual gear implies transformation and hunting covenant more than pantheon lists.
scandinavia.science: Dugout canoes, fish weirs, and leister design are marine engineering. Foragers track post-glacial rebound, changing Baltic salinity, and forest succession—an environmental science of a still-rising land. Composite tools and seal-hunting logistics sustain dense coastal living.

italy.description: Peninsula and adjacent foragers after the Late Glacial. Southern refugia matter for WHG diversity. Farming arrives by sea (Impresso/Cardial) and largely replaces this demographic layer.
italy.linguisticNote: Unknown. Historical Etruscan and Italic are not Mesolithic holdovers in any demonstrated sense.
italy.ancestryNote: WHG-related; distinctive southern diversity vs northern WHG.
italy.art: Italian foragers inherit an Epigravettian portable tradition—engraved stones, bone tools, and personal ornaments—while Alpine and Apennine rock shelters keep older image places alive as memory. Mediterranean shell ornaments and obsidian later in the sequence already hint at maritime aesthetics. Art is small-scale, mobile, and coast-aware.
italy.ideas: Peninsula geography encourages north–south and Tyrrhenian–Adriatic contrasts in foraging strategies. Obsidian and shell exchange foreshadow the sea roads Impressa farmers will intensify. Bands remain small; identity is local valley and coast.
italy.philosophy: Cave burials and ochre rites continue Paleolithic body care into the Holocene. Sacred geography likely includes caves, high passes, and shoreline shrines without recoverable god names. Continuity of place matters more than new dogma.
italy.science: Mountain and coastal foraging demands vertical seasonal scheduling—upland game, lowland plants, marine shellfish. Early obsidian recognition from Lipari and related sources is materials prospecting. Navigation along indented coasts is routine technical knowledge.

balkans.description: Danube Iron Gates and related Balkan foragers — archaeologically famous, genetically a distinctive WHG-related node used carefully in admixture models. They interact with and are partly absorbed by earliest European farmers.
balkans.ancestryNote: Iron Gates HG ≠ generic western WHG; models treat them as a separate source/proxy.
balkans.linguisticNote: Unknown. Not Greek, Thracian, or Slavic — all far later.
balkans.art: Lepenski Vir’s trapezoidal houses and sandstone fish-human sculptures are among Europe’s most striking Mesolithic art—architecture and idol fused beside the Danube. Ornaments of shell and stone, ochre, and carefully posed burials compose a riverside aesthetic of fish and ancestor. Sculpture here is monumental for foragers.
balkans.ideas: The Iron Gates gorge is a corridor of contact, not a refuge sealed from the world. Rich fisheries support denser, more sedentary forager life than northern forests allow. When Anatolian-related farmers approach, the Danube becomes a negotiation zone of genes, pots, and spouses.
balkans.philosophy: Fish-human sculptures and house burials imply a cosmology where river persons, ancestors, and the living share space. Trapezoidal houses face the water as if architecture itself prays downstream. Sacred order is riverside and bodily—no scripture, intense place cult.
balkans.science: Specialised sturgeon and migratory-fish harvesting is ecological engineering with nets, spears, and seasonal timing. Sedentary architecture and hearth management approach village science before farming. Early contact teaches foragers farmer crops and farmers gorge resources—two knowledge systems colliding.

eastern.description: EHG populations of the Volga–Don–Pontic forest-steppe with Ancient North Eurasian affinity. They are not Yamnaya yet; Yamnaya forms later when EHG-related ancestry mixes with Caucasus/Lower Volga–related groups. Linguistic IE status is not Mesolithic.
eastern.ancestryNote: EHG-dominated forest-steppe; not WHG. Later a key source for WSH/Yamnaya with CHG-related ancestry.
eastern.linguisticNote: Unknown. Proto-Indo-European is reconstructed for a much later steppe horizon.
eastern.art: Amber, animal-tooth pendants, and richly furnished burials at sites such as Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov compose a forest-steppe prestige art of the body. Bone and antler tools carry engraved designs; pottery appears in some eastern ‘Neolithic’ forager contexts without farming. Aesthetic power sits in graves and personal adornment.
eastern.ideas: EHG-related worlds keep a forager political economy east of the early farmer line—the genomic ‘great divide.’ Mobility across forest and steppe edges links Baltic, Volga, and Pontic zones. Identity is hunter-fisher with ceramics optional, ploughs absent.
eastern.philosophy: Lavish burials imply ranked persons and afterlife provisioning—tools, ornaments, animals as companions beyond death. Waterways and forest clearings structure sacred geography. Cosmology is inferred from grave theatre, not hymns.
eastern.science: Cold-forest hunting, ice-season fishing, and wide-ranging lithic procurement are survival sciences at continental scale. Early pottery among foragers shows independent or borrowed ceramic chemistry without agriculture. Path knowledge across vast low-density landscapes is the core information technology.

periods.linguistics: Speech is entirely unattested. Later farmer and Indo-European languages are not continuous with recoverable Mesolithic tongues. Treat all language labels here as placeholders for lost diversity.

mapLayers.label: Azilian
mapLayers.art: Material signature of Azilian: the objects, monuments, and dress styles that archaeologists use to draw this dominant layer on the Mesolithic map.
mapLayers.ideas: Azilian ideas of belonging are read from graves, enclosures, and exchange—who is buried with what, who shares ceramic recipes, who is kept outside the ditch.
mapLayers.philosophy: Named philosophers are anachronistic for Azilian. Treat cosmology as ritual geometry, ancestor practice, and craft taboo—reconstructed, not quoted.
mapLayers.science: Craft science of Azilian: lithic or metal chaînes opératoires, ceramic tempers, and environmental scheduling that made this horizon reproducible across sites.

ESP.name: Iberian Mesolithic bands
ESP.summary: Azilian and related forager groups along Atlantic and Mediterranean Iberia after glacial retreat.
ESP.conflicts: Local territorial foraging ranges; no states. Later replaced demographically by Cardial farmers.
ESP.literature: No written literature — meaning lived in seasonal rounds, place-names now lost, and oral lore we can only infer from ethnography and later myth residues. Think of fire-circle narrative, hunting songs, and cosmologies tied to rivers and herds rather than books. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: After the last cave-painting florescence, Iberian foragers favour portable marks—engraved bone, geometric microliths, and ochre on curated human remains—while still revisiting Paleolithic sanctuaries as remembered places. Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts pile shell middens that are as much seasonal calendars as rubbish dumps. Dress and weaponry stay hide, antler, and bow-and-microlith; style is regional, not imperial.

GBR.religion: No recoverable pantheon. Shell-midden and cave burials, ochre, and curated human bone suggest ancestor/body rites; cosmology itself stays opaque.
GBR.ideas: Island life after the North Sea rises forces tighter coastal and riverine schedules; Doggerland’s loss is a slow political geography rewrite, not a myth we can quote. Small bands manage seasonal rounds from upland hunting to estuary fishing. Knowledge of drowning shores and tsunami-scarred coasts (Storegga) enters living memory as caution, not cosmology we can name.
GBR.philosophy: Deer-skull rites and lakeside platforms suggest transformation, hunting magic, or seasonal ceremony—practice without a recoverable creed. Burials are rare and curated; the sacred seems tied to wetlands and animals rather than stone temples. Worldview is inferred from performance gear and place reuse, not texts.
GBR.science: Composite microlith weapons, dugouts, and fish weirs are precision wetland engineering. Foragers track post-glacial forest succession and shifting coasts with generation-scale environmental literacy. Star Carr’s woodworking and birch-pitch adhesives show chemical and carpentry skill in a cold early Holocene.

FRA.name: Sauveterrian / Tardenoisian groups
FRA.literature: No written literature — meaning lived in seasonal rounds, place-names now lost, and oral lore we can only infer from ethnography and later myth residues. Think of fire-circle narrative, hunting songs, and cosmologies tied to rivers and herds rather than books. French courts and vernaculars repeatedly set continental fashions of word and dress.
FRA.art: Tiny geometric microliths are the visual signature—almost abstract flint design—alongside bone points and rare personal ornaments. Southern rock shelters keep memory of earlier painted caves as visited places more than active ateliers. Atlantic Brittany and Mediterranean Languedoc develop distinct coastal versus inland craft dialects within one forager world.

FRA.religion: Forager ritual poorly named. Archaeology shows careful burials, ochre, and occasional animal deposits — practice without readable myths.
FRA.ideas: Small, flexible bands stitch river valleys and plateaus into seasonal territories without villages. Knowledge of flint sources and hunting grounds is social capital exchanged through marriage and meeting. The idea of ‘frontier’ appears only when Cardial and Danubian farmers later press from south and east.
FRA.philosophy: Burials with ochre and curated goods imply respect for persons and places; cosmology itself stays silent in the record. Landscape memory—caves, fords, hunting stands—likely carried spirit and story. Ritual is deposition and return, not temple cult.
FRA.science: Microlith technology maximises cutting edge from scarce good flint—materials science in miniature. Foragers manage post-glacial oak–hazel forests and river fisheries with detailed ecological timing. Path networks across the Massif and Paris Basin are lived geodesy before roads.

DEU.name: Central European Mesolithic
DEU.summary: Forest foragers of the North European Plain.
DEU.conflicts: No polities; later LBK farmers expand into these landscapes.
DEU.literature: No written literature — meaning lived in seasonal rounds, place-names now lost, and oral lore we can only infer from ethnography and later myth residues. Think of fire-circle narrative, hunting songs, and cosmologies tied to rivers and herds rather than books. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.
DEU.art: Bone and antler tools, microliths, and occasional amber from Baltic drift form a quiet portable art of forest and river. Rock art is rarer than in Atlantic or Alpine zones; aesthetic energy goes into projectile geometry and personal ornament. Sites such as those near the Elbe and Rhine keep forager craft distinct until LBK pottery arrives.

DEU.religion: Mesolithic belief content is lost. Scattered burials and structured faunal deposits hint at rites around death and animals, not temples or texts.
DEU.ideas: Loess belts and river corridors are hunting territories first, later the highways farmers will seize. Band mobility and flint exchange link the North European Plain to uplands without central authority. The idea of ‘empty land’ is an illusion—farmers enter a known forager geography.
DEU.philosophy: Ochre burials and rare structured deposits hint at afterlife care; named deities do not survive. Rivers and forest clearings likely held spirit significance in oral tradition. Worldview is practised at the grave and the kill site.
DEU.science: Forest hunting, plant gathering, and river fishing require fine phenological calendars. Composite tools and birch-tar adhesives are chemical crafts. Foragers’ mental maps of flint outcrops become the substrate pioneer farmers later quarry.

DNK.name: Maglemosian / Kongemose
DNK.summary: Rich coastal/lacustrine foragers of southern Scandinavia.
DNK.literature: No written literature — meaning lived in seasonal rounds, place-names now lost, and oral lore we can only infer from ethnography and later myth residues. Think of fire-circle narrative, hunting songs, and cosmologies tied to rivers and herds rather than books. Danish gatekeeping of the Baltic Sound makes culture a toll-booth as well as a stage.
DNK.art: Bone and antler leisters, amber pendants, and later Kongemose blade elegance define a northern wetland aesthetic. Rock art begins to appear on coastal cliffs in some areas; portable amber animals and beads glow as prestige. SHG foragers carve identity from seal, fish, and forest deer rather than painted caves.

DNK.religion: Maglemosian–Kongemose ritual known mainly from graves and bog finds. No named gods; body treatment and wetland deposition are the evidence.
DNK.ideas: A watery cosmos of lakes, archipelagos, and rising Baltic/North Sea shores structures mobility and alliance. Eastern genetic affinity (EHG-related) mixes into WHG baselines—Scandinavia as a contact sea. Territorial knowledge of seal rookeries and salmon runs is political capital.
DNK.philosophy: Amber and animal deposits, wetland platforms, and careful burials suggest a world where water and animal persons hold power. Cosmology is maritime and forestal—no temples, many thresholds (shore, ice, forest edge). Ritual gear implies transformation and hunting covenant more than pantheon lists.
DNK.science: Dugout canoes, fish weirs, and leister design are marine engineering. Foragers track post-glacial rebound, changing Baltic salinity, and forest succession—an environmental science of a still-rising land. Composite tools and seal-hunting logistics sustain dense coastal living.

ITA.name: Epigravettian-descended foragers
ITA.conflicts: Southern refugia matter for later WHG diversity.
ITA.literature: No written literature — meaning lived in seasonal rounds, place-names now lost, and oral lore we can only infer from ethnography and later myth residues. Think of fire-circle narrative, hunting songs, and cosmologies tied to rivers and herds rather than books. Italian cities teach prestige: from Roman monumentality to Renaissance brand management of beauty.
ITA.art: Italian foragers inherit an Epigravettian portable tradition—engraved stones, bone tools, and personal ornaments—while Alpine and Apennine rock shelters keep older image places alive as memory. Mediterranean shell ornaments and obsidian later in the sequence already hint at maritime aesthetics. Art is small-scale, mobile, and coast-aware.

ITA.religion: Epigravettian-descended foragers leave burial and ornament evidence; Mediterranean rock shelters hold ritual deposits without readable theology.
ITA.ideas: Peninsula geography encourages north–south and Tyrrhenian–Adriatic contrasts in foraging strategies. Obsidian and shell exchange foreshadow the sea roads Impressa farmers will intensify. Bands remain small; identity is local valley and coast.
ITA.philosophy: Cave burials and ochre rites continue Paleolithic body care into the Holocene. Sacred geography likely includes caves, high passes, and shoreline shrines without recoverable god names. Continuity of place matters more than new dogma.
ITA.science: Mountain and coastal foraging demands vertical seasonal scheduling—upland game, lowland plants, marine shellfish. Early obsidian recognition from Lipari and related sources is materials prospecting. Navigation along indented coasts is routine technical knowledge.

SRB.name: Iron Gates foragers
SRB.summary: Dense Danube gorge forager settlements (e.g. Lepenski-related world).
SRB.conflicts: Distinctive local identity before Starčevo farmers; contact and absorption follow.
SRB.literature: No written literature — meaning lived in seasonal rounds, place-names now lost, and oral lore we can only infer from ethnography and later myth residues. Think of fire-circle narrative, hunting songs, and cosmologies tied to rivers and herds rather than books. Serbian epic song turns defeat into repertoire; the gusle outlasts many maps.
SRB.art: Lepenski Vir’s trapezoidal houses and sandstone fish-human sculptures are among Europe’s most striking Mesolithic art—architecture and idol fused beside the Danube. Ornaments of shell and stone, ochre, and carefully posed burials compose a riverside aesthetic of fish and ancestor. Sculpture here is monumental for foragers.

SRB.religion: Iron Gates cemeteries show elaborate body treatment, sculptures, and house–burial links — unusually rich ritual archaeology for Mesolithic Europe.
SRB.ideas: The Iron Gates gorge is a corridor of contact, not a refuge sealed from the world. Rich fisheries support denser, more sedentary forager life than northern forests allow. When Anatolian-related farmers approach, the Danube becomes a negotiation zone of genes, pots, and spouses.
SRB.philosophy: Fish-human sculptures and house burials imply a cosmology where river persons, ancestors, and the living share space. Trapezoidal houses face the water as if architecture itself prays downstream. Sacred order is riverside and bodily—no scripture, intense place cult.
SRB.science: Specialised sturgeon and migratory-fish harvesting is ecological engineering with nets, spears, and seasonal timing. Sedentary architecture and hearth management approach village science before farming. Early contact teaches foragers farmer crops and farmers gorge resources—two knowledge systems colliding.

UKR.name: Ukrainian Mesolithic
UKR.conflicts: East of later Neolithic “great divide”; EHG-related.
UKR.literature: No written literature — meaning lived in seasonal rounds, place-names now lost, and oral lore we can only infer from ethnography and later myth residues. Think of fire-circle narrative, hunting songs, and cosmologies tied to rivers and herds rather than books. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: Amber, animal-tooth pendants, and richly furnished burials at sites such as Yuzhniy Oleniy Ostrov compose a forest-steppe prestige art of the body. Bone and antler tools carry engraved designs; pottery appears in some eastern ‘Neolithic’ forager contexts without farming. Aesthetic power sits in graves and personal adornment.

UKR.religion: Forest-steppe forager ritual: burials with ochre and grave goods. Named gods and afterlife doctrines are not recoverable.
UKR.ideas: EHG-related worlds keep a forager political economy east of the early farmer line—the genomic ‘great divide.’ Mobility across forest and steppe edges links Baltic, Volga, and Pontic zones. Identity is hunter-fisher with ceramics optional, ploughs absent.
UKR.philosophy: Lavish burials imply ranked persons and afterlife provisioning—tools, ornaments, animals as companions beyond death. Waterways and forest clearings structure sacred geography. Cosmology is inferred from grave theatre, not hymns.
UKR.science: Cold-forest hunting, ice-season fishing, and wide-ranging lithic procurement are survival sciences at continental scale. Early pottery among foragers shows independent or borrowed ceramic chemistry without agriculture. Path knowledge across vast low-density landscapes is the core information technology.

periods.label: Early Neolithic
periods.narrative: Farming spreads demically along Cardial/Impresso coasts and the LBK Danube corridor. Hunter-gatherer holdouts remain: Ertebølle in southern Scandinavia/south Baltic, Narva–Comb Ware in the east Baltic, and EHG forest-steppe groups east of the farmer line. Early farmer Europe is already clinal — WHG share higher toward Atlantic and northern contact zones than in LBK cores.
periods.culturesNote: Cardial, Impresso, LBK, Starčevo–Vinča + HG holdouts (Ertebølle, Narva/Comb Ware, EHG persistence).

iberia.description: Mediterranean Cardial/Impresso farming reaches Iberia by sea. Settlements, ceramics, and domesticates arrive with people who are genomically Anatolian Neolithic–related (EEF). Early farmer WHG ancestry is low; WHG rises again in later Neolithic admixture.
iberia.ancestryNote: Early Iberian farmers ≈ 85–95% EEF in published models; WHG minority.
iberia.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE farmer language(s). Not ancestral Basque or Iberian by evidence — those are later attestations.
iberia.art: Cardial pottery—rims and bodies stamped with cockle-shell edges—is the signature aesthetic of littoral pioneer farmers from Catalonia to Portugal. Polished stone axes, impressed ware, and simple clay figurines replace forager portable art as the visual language of settled households. Burial still mixes caves and open deposits; ornament stays personal (shell, stone) rather than monumental.
iberia.ideas: The big idea is the village package: cereals, sheep and goat, clay pots, and fixed houses carried by sea along the Mediterranean and Atlantic fringe. Pioneer colonisation implies planned landings and rapid coastal leaps more than slow village creep. Inland foragers remain neighbours—farming is a littoral claim, not yet a peninsula-wide law.
iberia.philosophy: Domesticated plants and animals reorder the sacred: hearths, storage pits, and household burials locate fertility and ancestry inside the settlement. Shell-stamped pots may mark group identity as much as kitchen use—a ceramic badge of belonging. Cosmology stays oral; what we see is ritual practice around food, death, and the new domestic animals.
iberia.science: Seafaring farmers move seed corn, livestock, and pottery recipes across open water—maritime logistics as technology. Early Iberian farmers manage Mediterranean crops on thin coastal soils while learning local rainfall and wild resources. Flint and polished-stone toolkits standardise woodworking and clearing for fields carved from scrub and woodland.

britain.description: Farming reaches Britain after the continental Early Neolithic. When established, Neolithic Britons are strongly EEF-derived — a first major replacement of Mesolithic WHG — until the Beaker-age collapse of this gene pool (~2500 BCE).
britain.ancestryNote: Earliest farming Britain: EEF-led; WHG higher at Atlantic edges than in pioneer cores.
britain.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE. The later Celtic languages are not this Neolithic speech.

ancestryCline.label: Core pioneer → Atlantic edge
ancestryCline.note: WHG% higher where farmers meet residual foragers; EEF highest in early pioneer packages.

britain.art: Incoming farmers bring pottery, polished axes, and eventually earthen long barrows—new media after millennia of forager portables. Carinated bowls and early chambered tombs sketch a continental-derived visual package adapted to island stone and timber. Art is still mostly functional and funerary; the great stone theatres come later.
britain.ideas: The transformative idea is demic farming: cereals, cattle, and fixed houses arrive with people who largely replace Mesolithic ancestry. Causewayed-enclosure thinking—gathering, feasting, boundary—begins to organise regional identity. Ireland’s secure house-and-cereal horizons slightly lag Britain’s earliest footprints but join the same Atlantic farmer conversation.
britain.philosophy: Ancestors move underground into long mounds and early chambers; fertility and lineage attach to monuments and herds rather than only seasonal camps. No pantheon survives in writing—ritual is deposition, animal offering, and communal gathering. The philosophical shift is from mobile forager ethics to landed, heritable place.
britain.science: Imported crop packages meet Atlantic soils and rainfall; farmers learn which cereals and animals thrive on island clay and chalk. Forest clearance, timber halls, and early quarrying for axe stone (e.g. Langdale later florescence) are applied landscape science. Seacraft still underwrites the whole colonisation—boats as the enabling technology.

france.description: Dual Neolithic streams: Mediterranean Cardial along the south/west and Danubian LBK influence toward the northeast. Both are EEF-rich demic spreads that replace most local HG ancestry, with later WHG gene flow into farmer groups.
france.linguisticNote: Unknown farmer languages; Gaulish Celtic is ~4000+ years later.
france.ancestryNote: Early farmers ~EEF; WHG admixture increases through Middle Neolithic.
france.art: Mediterranean Cardial impressed ware lights the southern and western coasts while LBK-related banded pottery and longhouses enter the northeast. Two ceramic aesthetics—shell-stamp littoral versus Danubian linear—meet in Gaul as rival visual languages of farming. Early figurines and polished axes travel with both streams.
france.ideas: France is the hinge where maritime pioneer farming and the Danube corridor almost touch. West-of-Rhine communities mix more local hunter-gatherer ancestry into farmer lives—an idea of coexistence written in genomes as much as pots. Settlement chooses loess, river terraces, and coastal enclaves rather than a uniform carpet.
france.philosophy: Household and enclosure begin to replace pure seasonal round as sacred centres. Burial rites diverge by tradition—Cardial caves and open deposits versus LBK cemetery rows—encoding different ideas of person and kin. Cosmology remains oral; archaeology catches practice at the grave and the hearth.
france.science: Farmers transplant Near Eastern crops into Atlantic and continental climates, learning frost, rainfall, and soil the hard way. Longhouse carpentry and Cardial kiln-less pottery are parallel technical schools. Early exchange of Alpine axe stone already sketches the routes later megalith builders will intensify.

central.description: The classic Central European Early Neolithic (~5500–4900 BCE): longhouses, Linearbandkeramik pottery, pioneer farming on loess. Genomes are strongly Anatolian farmer–related; initial HG admixture is limited and rises later. Not “Celtic” or “Germanic.”
central.ancestryNote: Early LBK cores often >85% EEF; WHG rises later in Mid–Late Neolithic.
central.linguisticNote: Unknown; widely assumed non-IE under steppe-IE models.

ancestryCline.label: LBK core → northern contact
ancestryCline.note: WHG higher toward northern/forest contact; EEF highest in loess LBK heartland.

central.art: Banded pottery—incised linear and spiral motifs on fine ware—and vast timber longhouses define the central European look. Clay figurines, shoe-last adzes, and Spondylus shell ornaments from the Mediterranean are prestige art inside an otherwise agrarian aesthetic. Cemeteries stage bodies with gendered tool kits as social portraiture.
central.ideas: The longhouse village invents a new social architecture: patrilocal kinship (aDNA), cattle wealth, and rapid colonisation of loess. Eastern and western LBK diverge in hunter-gatherer ancestry—same pottery brand, different genetic histories. Late LBK massacres (Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten) and Herxheim’s ritual deposits show ideas of belonging turning violently exclusive.
central.philosophy: Row-grave cemeteries and household shrines locate ancestors beside the living; fertility attaches to cattle and grain stores. Herxheim’s skull-cap rites imply a dark theology of processing the dead—or the stranger—as ritual theatre. Cosmology is communal and bodily, not textual philosophy.
central.science: LBK agronomy pairs emmer, einkorn, barley, pulses, and cattle on loess with remarkable geographic consistency. Longhouse engineering spans generations of timber joinery. Pottery kilns, flint mines, and Spondylus exchange chains are early logistical science across hundreds of kilometres.

scandinavia.description: Ertebølle foragers remain the demographic majority along Danish and south Swedish coasts while earliest Funnelbeaker farming appears in the south. Genetics: SHG/WHG holdouts beside rising EEF — the first Holocene turnover is beginning, not finished.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Ertebølle holdout still strong; earliest TRB farmers only beginning the first Holocene turnover.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Language shift likely with farming; details unknowable. Not Old Norse.

ancestryCline.label: Forager coast → earliest TRB farms
ancestryCline.note: SHG/WHG dominate Ertebølle coasts; EEF rises where earliest Funnelbeaker farming sticks.

scandinavia.art: Ertebølle pointed-base pottery—among Europe’s earliest northern ceramics—joins thick shell middens as a distinctive last-forager style. Bone combs, antler tools, and marine mammal motifs keep an aquatic aesthetic while farmers loom to the south. Art signals continuity of forager identity at the edge of the LBK world.
scandinavia.ideas: Pottery without farming: vessels for seal fat and fish, not yet a full Neolithic package. Ertebølle communities negotiate exchange and occasional violence with southern farmers while defending coastal lifeways. The idea of ‘becoming Neolithic’ is delayed, chosen, and uneven—not automatic.
scandinavia.philosophy: Shell middens double as ancestral places—refuse that is also memory. Marine animals likely remain central spirit partners even as clay pots enter ritual and daily life. Worldview resists the farmer’s grain-and-cattle sacred order until TRB centuries later.
scandinavia.science: Coastal ecology expertise peaks: oysters, seals, fish, and wild plants timed to Baltic seasons. Early ceramics require clay tempering and firing knowledge borrowed or invented at the farmer contact zone. Boat craft still underwrites economy and communication.

italy.description: Maritime Early Neolithic along Italian coasts with Impressed Ware. Strong EEF signal replaces most forager ancestry; inland uptake varies. Sets the farmer substrate later overlain by Bronze Age steppe-related ancestry and, historically, Italic/Etruscan languages.
italy.linguisticNote: Unknown Impresso-related farmer speech — not Latin, not Etruscan, and not recoverable from later Italic.
italy.ancestryNote: Early Italian Impresso farmers are EEF-dominated in published models; WHG is a minority that rises later.
italy.art: Impressed and Cardial-related wares, painted bands in some facies, and clay figurines announce the farmer aesthetic across southern and central coasts. Obsidian blades from island sources become gleaming prestige tools. Village pottery replaces forager portables as the daily visual environment.
italy.ideas: Italy is a launch corridor for Mediterranean Neolithisation—Adriatic and Tyrrhenian leapfrogs toward France and Iberia. Farming villages redefine land as fields and pastures; forager edges persist in mountains. Sea links make the peninsula a network node, not a cul-de-sac.
italy.philosophy: Domestic shrines, figurines, and burial under or near houses locate the sacred in the household and the soil. Fertility of crops and herds likely structures ritual calendars. No philosophy schools—only practised covenants with land and dead.
italy.science: Island obsidian specialised production and distribution is a measurable early industry. Farmers tune Near Eastern crops to Italian climates from Po fringe to Sicily. Boat-building and coastal pilotage are the sciences that make the Impressa expansion possible.

balkans.description: Corridor of Europe’s first farming. Starčevo–Körös–Criș and early Vinča tell settlements carry Anatolian-related farmers who mix more visibly with distinctive local HG (Iron Gates) than some early western LBK groups.
balkans.linguisticNote: Unknown Starčevo/Vinča-related languages. Ancient Greek is still far in the future and unrelated by attestation.
balkans.ancestryNote: EEF majority + elevated local HG vs early LBK extremes.
balkans.art: Painted and fine polished pottery, anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figurines, and stamp seals fill early Balkan farmer villages with a crowded visual theology of clay bodies. Starčevo and related wares are earth-toned; Vinča later darkens and sophisticates the surface. Houses on tells accumulate art as stratified memory.
balkans.ideas: The Balkans are the demic bridge from Anatolia into Europe—farming’s first European idea factory. Village life, storage, and cattle reorganise kinship and labour. From here Cardial and LBK streams will diverge, carrying Balkan-tempered farmer culture west and north.
balkans.philosophy: Figurines—often female, sometimes ambiguous—point to household cults of fertility, protection, or ancestor presence without proving a single ‘mother goddess’ church. Tell living stacks generations: the past literally underfoot. Ritual pits and house burnings suggest cyclical renewal rites.
balkans.science: Balkan farmers refine the Neolithic package for European latitudes—crop choices, animal management, and mudbrick/wattle housing. Early copper ornaments appear as metallurgical curiosity beside stone. Pottery kilns and tell drainage are settlement engineering at growing scale.

eastern.description: East of the Neolithic genomic “great divide,” many forest-steppe groups remain forager-derived while Cucuteni–Trypillia farmers expand on the western edge. Little pan-eastern EEF replacement compared with Germany or Iberia.
eastern.ancestryNote: Pre-Yamnaya: EHG + CHG-related kept separate (not yet fused as WSH). Farmer fringe only on the southwest edge.
eastern.linguisticNote: Unknown mix; not Slavic (medieval) and not yet clearly IE.

ancestryCline.label: Forest-steppe HG → farmer fringe
ancestryCline.note: EHG (+ some CHG-related) east of the Neolithic divide; EEF rises on Bug–Dniester contact — not WSH yet.

eastern.art: While true farming paints pottery farther west, eastern forager ceramics (Comb Ware, related) keep comb-and-pit decoration as a forest aesthetic. On the western fringe, early Trypillia/Precucuteni painted wares begin to appear—farmer colour advancing into the forest-steppe. Two visual systems face each other across the divide.
eastern.ideas: ‘Neolithic’ here often means pots, not crops—an idea that confuses later textbooks. Pontic and forest foragers coexist with approaching Balkan–Carpathian farmers for centuries. Exchange and occasional admixture happen without immediate lifestyle collapse.
eastern.philosophy: Forager burial richness continues; incoming farmer rites bring figurines and painted ceramics as new sacred media at the contact fringe. Worldviews pluralise along the frontier—no single conversion narrative. Ancestors and animals remain central on the forager side.
eastern.science: Forager ecological expertise persists; farmer fringe communities test crops on chernozem and forest-steppe soils. Ceramic temper and firing styles mark technical schools on both sides of the divide. River routes (Dniester, Dnieper, Bug) are the logistics backbone.

periods.linguistics: No texts. Farmer languages are unknown and usually modeled as non-Indo-European. Residual forager languages vanish or leave only undetectable substrates. Do not equate “Neolithic” with any historically named family.

DEU.name: LBK pioneer villages
DEU.conflicts: Expansion into forager landscapes; limited early conflict archaeologically visible as pioneer frontier.
DEU.literature: Still pre-literate in Europe. Story survives as ritual architecture and ceramic style: foundation deposits, house-burning rites, and the first farming songs we cannot hear — only the pots and longhouses that staged them. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.
DEU.art: Banded pottery—incised linear and spiral motifs on fine ware—and vast timber longhouses define the central European look. Clay figurines, shoe-last adzes, and Spondylus shell ornaments from the Mediterranean are prestige art inside an otherwise agrarian aesthetic. Cemeteries stage bodies with gendered tool kits as social portraiture.

DEU.religion: LBK farmers practiced domestic and enclosure ritual: foundation deposits, cattle offerings, and cemetery rows. Ancestor care and fertility rites are inferred; named gods are not.
DEU.ideas: The longhouse village invents a new social architecture: patrilocal kinship (aDNA), cattle wealth, and rapid colonisation of loess. Eastern and western LBK diverge in hunter-gatherer ancestry—same pottery brand, different genetic histories. Late LBK massacres (Talheim, Schletz, Kilianstädten) and Herxheim’s ritual deposits show ideas of belonging turning violently exclusive.
DEU.philosophy: Row-grave cemeteries and household shrines locate ancestors beside the living; fertility attaches to cattle and grain stores. Herxheim’s skull-cap rites imply a dark theology of processing the dead—or the stranger—as ritual theatre. Cosmology is communal and bodily, not textual philosophy.
DEU.science: LBK agronomy pairs emmer, einkorn, barley, pulses, and cattle on loess with remarkable geographic consistency. Longhouse engineering spans generations of timber joinery. Pottery kilns, flint mines, and Spondylus exchange chains are early logistical science across hundreds of kilometres.

ESP.name: Cardial Iberia
ESP.conflicts: Rapid coastal advance; WHG substrate remains minority.
ESP.literature: Still pre-literate in Europe. Story survives as ritual architecture and ceramic style: foundation deposits, house-burning rites, and the first farming songs we cannot hear — only the pots and longhouses that staged them. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: Cardial pottery—rims and bodies stamped with cockle-shell edges—is the signature aesthetic of littoral pioneer farmers from Catalonia to Portugal. Polished stone axes, impressed ware, and simple clay figurines replace forager portable art as the visual language of settled households. Burial still mixes caves and open deposits; ornament stays personal (shell, stone) rather than monumental.

ESP.religion: Cardial communities combine cave/open-air ritual with early megalithic experiments. Burial and ceramic deposits mark ancestor and place cults.
ESP.ideas: The big idea is the village package: cereals, sheep and goat, clay pots, and fixed houses carried by sea along the Mediterranean and Atlantic fringe. Pioneer colonisation implies planned landings and rapid coastal leaps more than slow village creep. Inland foragers remain neighbours—farming is a littoral claim, not yet a peninsula-wide law.
ESP.philosophy: Domesticated plants and animals reorder the sacred: hearths, storage pits, and household burials locate fertility and ancestry inside the settlement. Shell-stamped pots may mark group identity as much as kitchen use—a ceramic badge of belonging. Cosmology stays oral; what we see is ritual practice around food, death, and the new domestic animals.
ESP.science: Seafaring farmers move seed corn, livestock, and pottery recipes across open water—maritime logistics as technology. Early Iberian farmers manage Mediterranean crops on thin coastal soils while learning local rainfall and wild resources. Flint and polished-stone toolkits standardise woodworking and clearing for fields carved from scrub and woodland.

DNK.name: Ertebølle vs earliest TRB
DNK.conflicts: Classic contact frontier before farmer dominance.
DNK.literature: Still pre-literate in Europe. Story survives as ritual architecture and ceramic style: foundation deposits, house-burning rites, and the first farming songs we cannot hear — only the pots and longhouses that staged them. Danish gatekeeping of the Baltic Sound makes culture a toll-booth as well as a stage.
DNK.art: Ertebølle pointed-base pottery—among Europe’s earliest northern ceramics—joins thick shell middens as a distinctive last-forager style. Bone combs, antler tools, and marine mammal motifs keep an aquatic aesthetic while farmers loom to the south. Art signals continuity of forager identity at the edge of the LBK world.

DNK.religion: Ertebølle holdouts keep forager burial/wetland rites beside earliest TRB farmer ceremonies — two ritual regimes in contact, not one creed.
DNK.ideas: Pottery without farming: vessels for seal fat and fish, not yet a full Neolithic package. Ertebølle communities negotiate exchange and occasional violence with southern farmers while defending coastal lifeways. The idea of ‘becoming Neolithic’ is delayed, chosen, and uneven—not automatic.
DNK.philosophy: Shell middens double as ancestral places—refuse that is also memory. Marine animals likely remain central spirit partners even as clay pots enter ritual and daily life. Worldview resists the farmer’s grain-and-cattle sacred order until TRB centuries later.
DNK.science: Coastal ecology expertise peaks: oysters, seals, fish, and wild plants timed to Baltic seasons. Early ceramics require clay tempering and firing knowledge borrowed or invented at the farmer contact zone. Boat craft still underwrites economy and communication.

GBR.name: Earliest Neolithic arrival
GBR.conflicts: First major replacement of Mesolithic WHG.
GBR.literature: Still pre-literate in Europe. Story survives as ritual architecture and ceramic style: foundation deposits, house-burning rites, and the first farming songs we cannot hear — only the pots and longhouses that staged them. Insular voices and North Sea contact give this place a distinctive accent in the wider European chorus.
GBR.art: Incoming farmers bring pottery, polished axes, and eventually earthen long barrows—new media after millennia of forager portables. Carinated bowls and early chambered tombs sketch a continental-derived visual package adapted to island stone and timber. Art is still mostly functional and funerary; the great stone theatres come later.

GBR.religion: Earliest Neolithic Britain imports chambered-tomb and causewayed-enclosure rites: collective burial, feasting debris, and seasonal gathering places.
GBR.ideas: The transformative idea is demic farming: cereals, cattle, and fixed houses arrive with people who largely replace Mesolithic ancestry. Causewayed-enclosure thinking—gathering, feasting, boundary—begins to organise regional identity. Ireland’s secure house-and-cereal horizons slightly lag Britain’s earliest footprints but join the same Atlantic farmer conversation.
GBR.philosophy: Ancestors move underground into long mounds and early chambers; fertility and lineage attach to monuments and herds rather than only seasonal camps. No pantheon survives in writing—ritual is deposition, animal offering, and communal gathering. The philosophical shift is from mobile forager ethics to landed, heritable place.
GBR.science: Imported crop packages meet Atlantic soils and rainfall; farmers learn which cereals and animals thrive on island clay and chalk. Forest clearance, timber halls, and early quarrying for axe stone (e.g. Langdale later florescence) are applied landscape science. Seacraft still underwrites the whole colonisation—boats as the enabling technology.

periods.label: Middle–Late Neolithic
periods.narrative: Farmer Europe densifies: Atlantic megaliths, Chasséen/Michelsberg, Funnelbeaker (TRB), Cucuteni–Trypillia, early Globular Amphora. Hunter-gatherer holdouts persist beside farmers — Pitted Ware on Scandinavian coasts, Narva–Comb Ware in the east Baltic. Within TRB and other farmer packages, WHG% is clinal: higher north and west, lower in southern/central agricultural cores.
periods.culturesNote: TRB, Michelsberg, Chasséen, megalithic Atlantic, GAC, Trypillia + HG holdouts (Pitted Ware, Narva/Comb Ware).

iberia.description: Passage graves and related monuments along Atlantic and southern Iberia. Still EEF-dominated, but WHG is higher on the Atlantic façade than in inland cores — a within-culture farmer cline, not a uniform Neolithic mix. Steppe still ~0.
iberia.linguisticNote: Unknown pre-IE. Historical Iberian script languages are Copper/Iron Age attestations, not proven megalithic speech.
iberia.ancestryNote: EEF majority; WHG higher on Atlantic megalithic façades than in southern inland cores.

ancestryCline.label: Atlantic façade → inland south
ancestryCline.note: WHG% rises toward Atlantic megalithic zones; EEF higher inland/south.

iberia.art: Passage graves, tholoi, and engraved schist plaques turn the Atlantic and southern interiors into a monumental gallery. Geometric plaque ‘idols,’ engraved stones, and collective tomb architecture replace the quiet Cardial household aesthetic with public stone theatre. Amber, variscite, and exotic axes circulate as prestige display inside and beside tombs.
iberia.ideas: Collective burial and tomb reuse invent a politics of ancestry visible for kilometres—who belongs is written in stone chambers. Exchange networks for jadeitite, Iberian greenstone, and marine shell stitch coasts to hinterlands. WHG ancestry rises again inside farmer bodies even as the culture remains ‘Neolithic’—identity is practice, not purity.
iberia.philosophy: Megaliths stage a cosmology of the dead as landscape anchors: chambers aligned to horizons, offerings, and successive depositions keep ancestors present. Engraved plaques and eye motifs hint at personified powers without yielding readable pantheons. Ritual time is generational—re-entering the tomb—rather than a priestly scripture.
iberia.science: Builders master quarrying, levering, and sighting large stones into stable chambers and corridors. Agricultural intensification on Atlantic and southern soils pairs with herding; isotope and archaeobotany show mixed farming tuned to regional rainfall. Long-distance stone sourcing implies surveying of outcrops and remembered exchange routes.

britain.description: Orkney, Wessex, and related Neolithic monument societies. Genomically Anatolian farmer–related + WHG, with a north/west vs south cline in WHG share — not one uniform Neolithic percentage across Britain. This is the gene pool later replaced in the Beaker age.
britain.ancestryNote: Neolithic Britain without steppe; WHG higher in north/west monument zones than in denser southern farming.
britain.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE; later Celtic is not continuous by default.

ancestryCline.label: North/west → southern farming
ancestryCline.note: WHG% higher in northern/western Neolithic landscapes; EEF higher in denser southern farming.

britain.art: Passage tombs of the Boyne Valley, Orkney’s Maeshowe-type chambers, and stone circles culminating toward Stonehenge turn islands into ritual landscapes of carved kerbs, spiral art, and aligned passages. Grooved Ware pottery and carved stone balls add portable grammar to the monumental outdoor gallery. Skara Brae’s stone furniture shows domestic design as carefully composed as tombs.
britain.ideas: Monument clusters imply regional pilgrimage, alliance, and competitive display among farming communities. Irish Sea and northern networks share tomb forms and Grooved Ware—an Atlantic ceremonial commons. Kinship and land claims are argued in stone: who builds, who burials, who feasts at the enclosure.
britain.philosophy: Solar and lunar alignments (Newgrange’s midwinter light; circle horizons) embed a sky cosmology in architecture. Collective and successive burials keep the dead as active community members. Philosophy here is practised astronomy-and-ancestry, not named schools—time, death, and season made visible in stone.
britain.science: Megalith builders combine surveying, transport engineering, and horizon astronomy with remarkable precision for pre-literate societies. Mixed farming, manuring, and cattle feasting fuel monument labour. Flint mines and axe factories (Grimes Graves, Langdale) show specialised extraction and long-distance distribution.

france.description: Middle Neolithic cultural mosaic (Chasséen and neighbors) with megaliths in the west. Farmer–forager admixture ongoing; steppe ancestry still absent. Sets the substrate that will receive third-millennium steppe-related gene flow.
france.linguisticNote: Unknown pre-Celtic farmer languages of Chasséen/megalithic France; Gaulish appears only in the Iron Age record.
france.ancestryNote: EEF majority + WHG; WHG higher on Atlantic megalithic west than in eastern Chasséen cores.

ancestryCline.label: Atlantic west → eastern Chasséen
ancestryCline.note: WHG% higher on the megalithic Atlantic façade; EEF higher in eastern Chasséen farming.

france.art: Carnac’s alignments, Morbihan tumuli, and Barnenez-type cairns make northwest France Europe’s densest stone theatre; Chasséen pottery and enclosures organise the interior. Jadeitite ceremonial axes from Alpine sources appear broken or deposited as luminous green prestige art. Engraved stones and monumental façades turn geology into sculpture at landscape scale.
france.ideas: Competitive ritual economies—who raises the longest alignment, who buries with Alpine jade—structure Atlantic elites without kings we can name. Chasséen networks standardise pottery and flint across wide tracts, a soft political grammar. Northern France’s mixed Cardial–Danubian heritage becomes the launchpad for megalithic ideas moving toward Britain and the North Sea.
france.philosophy: Menhirs and passage graves stage a cosmology of skyline, ancestor, and processional path. Broken axe deposits suggest sacrifice of wealth to powers of place or death. Sacred time is seasonal and funerary—solstice light, tomb re-entry—not philosophical treatise.
france.science: Moving and erecting multi-tonne menhirs demands levers, ropes, ramps, and organised labour accounting. Horizon astronomy and careful siting bind monuments to solar and terrestrial landmarks. Intensive farming and herding on Armorican and Paris-Basin soils underwrite the calorie surplus behind stone spectacle.

central.description: Funnelbeaker and Michelsberg farming societies; Globular Amphora forms toward the Late Neolithic. TRB is not genetically uniform — WHG ancestry is higher in northern TRB and lower in southern/central cores. Still pre-steppe.
central.linguisticNote: Unknown. CW-linked IE comes next, not yet.
central.ancestryNote: TRB/Michelsberg farmers: WHG higher in northern TRB; EEF higher in southern/central agricultural cores. GAC forms as the farmer side later mixed into Corded Ware.

ancestryCline.label: Northern TRB → central/south core
ancestryCline.note: WHG% rises north (and toward forager contact); EEF highest in Michelsberg / southern TRB cores.

central.art: Michelsberg tulip beakers, Funnelbeaker pottery, megalithic tombs on the northern plain, and later Globular Amphora jars diversify the post-LBK visual field. Flint daggers and enclosure earthworks become status media. Monumentality is patchier than on the Atlantic but still marks ancestors in stone and earth.
central.ideas: After LBK’s crisis, regional cultures multiply—enclosures, new flint economies, and northern TRB links. WHG ancestry resurges inside farmer populations; forager blood returns without restoring forager life. Early Globular Amphora hints at cattle-centred wealth and new burial politics toward the late 4th millennium.
central.philosophy: Causewayed and ditched enclosures gather people for feasts, rites, and boundary-making—temporary sacred cities of earth. Megalithic and flat graves encode competing claims about who the dead remain. Belief stays practice-rich and name-poor.
central.science: Deep flint mining (e.g. Rijckholt tradition) and specialist axe production show industrial-scale extraction before metal. Crop–livestock systems intensify; enclosures imply organised labour and surplus. Northern TRB contact transfers farming know-how toward Scandinavia.

scandinavia.description: Southern Scandinavia hosts both Funnelbeaker farmers and Pitted Ware coastal foragers. Genetics split with that geography: EEF-led TRB inland/south vs SHG/WHG-rich Pitted Ware holdouts on the coasts — not a single Scandinavian Neolithic mix.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Unknown TRB-related speech; pre-Germanic tied to later Battle Axe models.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: TRB farmers inland/south vs Pitted Ware forager holdouts on coasts — two genetic regimes under one map period.

ancestryCline.label: Pitted Ware coasts → TRB farms
ancestryCline.note: Coastal Pitted Ware keeps high SHG/WHG; southern/inland TRB is EEF-led with residual HG.

scandinavia.art: Funnel-necked beakers, polished flint axes, and dolmens/passage graves bring farmer monumentality north. Amber and flint daggers circulate as bright prestige; megalithic art is architectural more than figurative. Beside TRB, Pitted Ware groups keep a contrasting seal-hunter ceramic style on the coasts.
scandinavia.ideas: Agriculture and megaliths arrive as a northern package, absorbing and displacing Ertebølle unevenly. Dual societies emerge in places: inland TRB farmers versus coastal Pitted Ware foragers with high HG ancestry. Cattle, clearing, and tomb building rewrite land tenure.
scandinavia.philosophy: Dolmens gather bones of many—ancestor collectives under stone caps open to the sky. Depositions of axes and pottery in wetlands continue older water rites inside a new farming religion of fertility and lineage. Cosmology fuses megalithic sky/ancestor themes with lingering maritime sacredness.
scandinavia.science: Farmers adapt cereals and livestock to short northern growing seasons and thin soils—agricultural R&D at the climatic margin. Megalith transport and flint-mine intensification (e.g. Danish mines) show organised technical labour. Pitted Ware seal hunting preserves parallel marine science beside the plough.

italy.description: Regional farmer cultures consolidating domestic economies; copper begins at the edges (toward Remedello/Gaudo). Genetics remain EEF+WHG without meaningful steppe yet.
italy.linguisticNote: Unknown; pre-Italic / pre-Etruscan deep layers unrecoverable.
italy.ancestryNote: EEF-led; steppe arrives mainly in the Bronze Age.
italy.art: Diana, Serra d’Alto, and related fine painted and polished wares push pottery toward display art; some regions raise megaliths and statue-menhir traditions. Obsidian and greenstone axes remain prestige media. Village aesthetics diversify as copper begins to glint at the period’s end in the north.
italy.ideas: Regional ceramic ‘dialects’ mark identities across a still-EEF genetic world with rising local HG admixture. Alpine jadeitite and island stone keep Italy wired into wider western exchange. Social differentiation shows in grave goods before true metal-age chiefdoms.
italy.philosophy: Figurines, structured deposits, and varied burial (caves, trenches, early megaliths) encode plural local rites. Ancestor and fertility themes dominate what we can infer; named pantheons wait for later ages. Ritual innovation tracks pottery fashion as much as theology.
italy.science: Increasingly specialised pottery firing and surface treatment show ceramic chemistry advancing. Mixed farming intensifies; early copper experiments in the Alpine foreland add metallurgical trial-and-error. Obsidian sourcing studies (modern and ancient) confirm sailors’ mental maps of island volcanoes.

balkans.description: Dense tell settlements, early copper metallurgy, Vinča and successor facies. Farmer ancestry dominant; steppe contact intensifies on the northeast Black Sea–Danube edge as Eneolithic steppe societies form.
balkans.linguisticNote: Unknown. Mycenaean Greek is still a millennium+ away.
balkans.ancestryNote: EEF+local HG; early steppe signals appear regionally toward the Copper Age.
balkans.art: Vinča dark-burnished ware, elaborate figurines, and early copper ornaments (and later tools) create a proto-metal aesthetic. House models and shrine-like rooms appear in some settlements. Visual culture is dense, repetitive, and household-centred—a clay cosmos of faces and gestures.
balkans.ideas: Tell mega-villages concentrate population and craft specialisation; some signs point toward proto-writing or symbolic inventories (Vinča symbols)—still debated, never deciphered literature. Exchange in Balkan copper and Aegean links foreshadows Eneolithic complexity. Social ranking edges upward without full urban states.
balkans.philosophy: Figurine multiplicity suggests many small powers or roles rather than one dogma. House-based ritual and possible intentional house burning encode cycles of death and renewal for buildings as well as people. Cosmology stays intimate—courtyard and oven—not temple-state.
balkans.science: Vinča-region copper mining and smelting experiments are among Europe’s earliest metallurgical sciences. Agricultural surplus on river plains supports craft specialists. Symbolic notations on pots, if communicative, would be information technology—still an open research question, not a decoded script.

eastern.description: Trypillia mega-settlements meet Eneolithic steppe groups. North Pontic aDNA tracks Caucasus–Lower Volga–related waves into Usatove and Serednii Stih — precursors of Yamnaya — while incorporating farmer and forager outsiders.
eastern.ancestryNote: Pre-Yamnaya Pontic: EHG + CHG-related as separate ingredients beside Trypillia EEF — forming steppe package, not scored as WSH yet.
eastern.linguisticNote: Unknown. Possible early IE on the steppe side only as hypothesis.

ancestryCline.label: Trypillia farms → Pontic steppe edge
ancestryCline.note: EEF higher in Trypillia; EHG/CHG-related rise toward Usatove / Serednii Stih (pre-WSH fusion).

eastern.art: Cucuteni–Trypillia painted pottery—spirals, meanders, swirling polychrome—is among prehistoric Europe’s great ceramic arts; clay figurines and house models fill settlements. Megasites arrange houses in vast concentric circuits—urban-scale design without palaces. Burned-house horizons create dramatic archaeological colour: red daub, ash, and painted sherds.
eastern.ideas: Megasites (Nebelivka, Maidanetske, Talianki) experiment with low-hierarchy mega-population living—thousands in planned circuits facing the steppe. Cattle, pulses, and manure management sustain the idea of aggregation; decline looks social as much as climatic. Neighboring steppe Eneolithic groups keep different burial politics just beyond the painted-pottery world.
eastern.philosophy: Figurines, house models, and possible deliberate house burning suggest renewal rites binding household, woman/ancestor imagery, and settlement cycle. Painted pottery may encode mythic pattern language—beautiful, undeciphered. Cosmology is village-wide and ceramic, not temple-priestly in a Near Eastern sense.
eastern.science: Isotope food-webs show sophisticated dung-manured pulse–cereal systems and fenced cattle pastures—an integrated agro-science feeding mega-populations. Settlement planning at 100–300+ ha scale requires surveying and labour coordination. Pottery firing and pigment chemistry reach artistic-technical peaks before Corded Ware–steppe transformations remake the east.

periods.linguistics: Still pre-Indo-European across most of Europe. Megalithic and Trypillia labels are not language families. Possible early IE on the steppe edge only as hypothesis.

mapLayers.label: Atlantic megalithic
mapLayers.art: Material signature of Atlantic megalithic: the objects, monuments, and dress styles that archaeologists use to draw this dominant layer on the Middle–Late Neolithic map.
mapLayers.ideas: Atlantic megalithic ideas of belonging are read from graves, enclosures, and exchange—who is buried with what, who shares ceramic recipes, who is kept outside the ditch.
mapLayers.philosophy: Named philosophers are anachronistic for Atlantic megalithic. Treat cosmology as ritual geometry, ancestor practice, and craft taboo—reconstructed, not quoted.
mapLayers.science: Craft science of Atlantic megalithic: lithic or metal chaînes opératoires, ceramic tempers, and environmental scheduling that made this horizon reproducible across sites.

GBR.name: British megalith builders
GBR.summary: Orkney, Wessex, and related Neolithic societies.
GBR.conflicts: Regional monument competition; gene pool later collapses in Beaker age.
GBR.literature: Megalithic Europe speaks in stone alignments and passage-grave orientations — a literature of astronomy and ancestry without alphabet. Later folklore about giants and stone tables is a distant echo, not a primary source. Insular voices and North Sea contact give this place a distinctive accent in the wider European chorus.

Later folklore about giants and stone tables is a distant echo, not a primary source. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: Cucuteni–Trypillia painted pottery—spirals, meanders, swirling polychrome—is among prehistoric Europe’s great ceramic arts; clay figurines and house models fill settlements. Megasites arrange houses in vast concentric circuits—urban-scale design without palaces. Burned-house horizons create dramatic archaeological colour: red daub, ash, and painted sherds.

UKR.religion: Cucuteni–Trypillia: house figurines, intentional house burning, and cemetery rites — domestic and settlement-scale cult practice at huge agrarian sites.
UKR.ideas: Megasites (Nebelivka, Maidanetske, Talianki) experiment with low-hierarchy mega-population living—thousands in planned circuits facing the steppe. Cattle, pulses, and manure management sustain the idea of aggregation; decline looks social as much as climatic. Neighboring steppe Eneolithic groups keep different burial politics just beyond the painted-pottery world.
UKR.philosophy: Figurines, house models, and possible deliberate house burning suggest renewal rites binding household, woman/ancestor imagery, and settlement cycle. Painted pottery may encode mythic pattern language—beautiful, undeciphered. Cosmology is village-wide and ceramic, not temple-priestly in a Near Eastern sense.
UKR.science: Isotope food-webs show sophisticated dung-manured pulse–cereal systems and fenced cattle pastures—an integrated agro-science feeding mega-populations. Settlement planning at 100–300+ ha scale requires surveying and labour coordination. Pottery firing and pigment chemistry reach artistic-technical peaks before Corded Ware–steppe transformations remake the east.

DNK.name: TRB Scandinavia
DNK.conflicts: Residual forager (Pitted Ware) coexistence on coasts.
DNK.literature: Megalithic Europe speaks in stone alignments and passage-grave orientations — a literature of astronomy and ancestry without alphabet. Later folklore about giants and stone tables is a distant echo, not a primary source. Danish gatekeeping of the Baltic Sound makes culture a toll-booth as well as a stage.
DNK.art: Funnel-necked beakers, polished flint axes, and dolmens/passage graves bring farmer monumentality north. Amber and flint daggers circulate as bright prestige; megalithic art is architectural more than figurative. Beside TRB, Pitted Ware groups keep a contrasting seal-hunter ceramic style on the coasts.

DNK.religion: TRB Scandinavia: megalithic tombs, amber offerings, and wetland deposits. Ancestor burial architecture is the clearest ritual signature.
DNK.ideas: Agriculture and megaliths arrive as a northern package, absorbing and displacing Ertebølle unevenly. Dual societies emerge in places: inland TRB farmers versus coastal Pitted Ware foragers with high HG ancestry. Cattle, clearing, and tomb building rewrite land tenure.
DNK.philosophy: Dolmens gather bones of many—ancestor collectives under stone caps open to the sky. Depositions of axes and pottery in wetlands continue older water rites inside a new farming religion of fertility and lineage. Cosmology fuses megalithic sky/ancestor themes with lingering maritime sacredness.
DNK.science: Farmers adapt cereals and livestock to short northern growing seasons and thin soils—agricultural R&D at the climatic margin. Megalith transport and flint-mine intensification (e.g. Danish mines) show organised technical labour. Pitted Ware seal hunting preserves parallel marine science beside the plough.

SWE.name: TRB & Pitted Ware
SWE.summary: Farmer inland/south vs coastal Pitted Ware.
SWE.conflicts: Dual economies; steppe pulse still ahead.
SWE.literature: Megalithic Europe speaks in stone alignments and passage-grave orientations — a literature of astronomy and ancestry without alphabet. Later folklore about giants and stone tables is a distant echo, not a primary source. Swedish culture often exports northern clarity — from rock art to modern design temperaments.
SWE.art: Funnel-necked beakers, polished flint axes, and dolmens/passage graves bring farmer monumentality north. Amber and flint daggers circulate as bright prestige; megalithic art is architectural more than figurative. Beside TRB, Pitted Ware groups keep a contrasting seal-hunter ceramic style on the coasts.

POL.name: TRB / early GAC Poland
POL.literature: Megalithic Europe speaks in stone alignments and passage-grave orientations — a literature of astronomy and ancestry without alphabet. Later folklore about giants and stone tables is a distant echo, not a primary source. Polish–Lithuanian and later Polish culture specializes in noble liberty myths and romantic survival art.
POL.art: Michelsberg tulip beakers, Funnelbeaker pottery, megalithic tombs on the northern plain, and later Globular Amphora jars diversify the post-LBK visual field. Flint daggers and enclosure earthworks become status media. Monumentality is patchier than on the Atlantic but still marks ancestors in stone and earth.
