POL.religion: TRB / early GAC: megalithic and flat cemeteries, animal offerings, and enclosure rites. GAC cattle-and-amber ritual intensifies toward the steppe contact zone.
POL.ideas: After LBK’s crisis, regional cultures multiply—enclosures, new flint economies, and northern TRB links. WHG ancestry resurges inside farmer populations; forager blood returns without restoring forager life. Early Globular Amphora hints at cattle-centred wealth and new burial politics toward the late 4th millennium.
POL.philosophy: Causewayed and ditched enclosures gather people for feasts, rites, and boundary-making—temporary sacred cities of earth. Megalithic and flat graves encode competing claims about who the dead remain. Belief stays practice-rich and name-poor.
POL.science: Deep flint mining (e.g. Rijckholt tradition) and specialist axe production show industrial-scale extraction before metal. Crop–livestock systems intensify; enclosures imply organised labour and surplus. Northern TRB contact transfers farming know-how toward Scandinavia.

periods.label: Copper / Yamnaya
periods.narrative: Yamnaya pastoralists expand on the Pontic–Caspian steppe while Late Neolithic farmer Europe (TRB, GAC, Iberian Copper Age, British Late Neolithic) continues west of the steppe. Scandinavian/Baltic forager holdouts (Pitted Ware, late Narva–Comb) still mark the map. Steppe ancestry is high on the core steppe and falls off west/north — a gradient, not an instant uniform coat.
periods.culturesNote: Yamnaya/Yamna, Afanasievo (eastward), late Trypillia, Usatove contacts, Remedello/Gaudo in Italy, late TRB/Pitted Ware in the north.

iberia.description: Fortified Copper Age centers (e.g. Los Millares tradition) and related communities. Metallurgy and social hierarchy intensify, but steppe-related ancestry is still minimal. Bell Beaker pottery will spread as a cultural package before/with later, more gradual steppe gene flow — unlike Britain’s cliff-edge replacement.
iberia.linguisticNote: Unknown pre-IE. Do not equate Copper Age cultures with Celtic.
iberia.ancestryNote: Still largely EEF+WHG; steppe ≈ 0–few percent at Copper Age start.
iberia.art: Fortified hilltop centres such as Los Millares frame tholos tombs, copper tools, and schematic idols in a visual language of walls and collective chambers. Beaker pottery is still only a whisper; prestige is stone architecture, ivory, and early metal blades. Dress stays wool and linen with personal ornaments—status written in settlement fortification more than in steppe kurgans.
iberia.ideas: Hierarchy intensifies through metallurgy and defended villages while ancestry remains almost entirely EEF+WHG—steppe ideas have not yet remade the gene pool. Collective tombs and craft specialisation argue for ancestral corporations controlling copper and exotic exchange. Iberia’s Copper Age is a farmer world organising itself for metal, not a Yamnaya outpost.
iberia.philosophy: No named schools; cosmology is tomb and idol. Tholoi and engraved plaques keep the dead as corporate ancestors, while schematic ‘eye’ idols hint at personified powers without a readable pantheon. Sacred order is architectural—who may enter the chamber, who owns the copper—rather than doctrinal text.
iberia.science: Copper smelting, casting, and arsenical alloys are the period’s hard science, paired with fortification surveying on arid southeastern hills. Farmers manage Mediterranean crops under increasing aridity while sourcing ivory and ostrich-egg shell through long Atlantic–Mediterranean chains. Ceramic and lithic chaînes opératoires standardise household production beside the new metal workshops.

britain.description: Final centuries of the Neolithic farmer society before the Beaker demographic break (~2500 BCE). Monumental landscapes continue; genetically still the EEF+WHG island population about to be replaced.
britain.linguisticNote: Unknown non-IE Neolithic speech about to be marginalized/replaced in IE-shift models.
britain.ancestryNote: Still Neolithic Britain — steppe negligible until Beaker.

ancestryCline.label: North/west → south
ancestryCline.note: Residual WHG cline within Late Neolithic Britain; steppe still ~0–few %.

britain.art: Stonehenge’s later Neolithic phases, timber circles, Grooved Ware, and carved chalk objects keep a monumental island aesthetic untouched by steppe kurgan art. Collective and cremation rites, carved stone, and ceremonial landscapes dominate; metal is still scarce. Dress and ornament remain Neolithic—jet, amber, and stone—before Beaker gold arrives.
britain.ideas: Island ceremonial commons and ancestral monuments organise politics without Yamnaya pastoral kings. Gene pools stay EEF+WHG; the ‘steppe story’ is still a continental rumour. Labour and pilgrimage around henges imply large-scale cooperation among farming communities who do not yet know they are about to be replaced.
britain.philosophy: Solar alignments, processional avenues, and successive monument rebuilds encode a sky-and-ancestor cosmology in stone and timber. The dead and the solstice structure time; no pantheon is named. Sacred knowledge is architectural and calendrical—how to stand stones to catch the sun—not philosophical prose.
britain.science: Megalithic and timber engineering, horizon astronomy, and quarry logistics (bluestones, sarsens) are peak Neolithic applied science. Mixed farming on chalk and clay fuels seasonal gatherings. Trackways and boat craft stitch coasts and rivers into a pre-metal transport web.

france.culture: Late Neolithic France — first steppe pulses
france.description: Northern French Late Neolithic burials capture steppe-related ancestry arriving in real time (~3000–2600 BCE admixture pulses; Science Advances 2024). Not yet a uniform Corded Ware map — patchy early contact into a Neolithic substrate.
france.ancestryNote: Site-variable early steppe (order ~10–20% in some modeled groups); not Britain-level replacement.
france.linguisticNote: Possible early IE speech with steppe gene flow — contested; no texts.
france.art: Late Neolithic collective tombs, Chasséen and Artenacoid ceramics, and Armorican megalithic afterlives still look farmer-European while early steppe ancestry trickles in. Art is chamber, plaque, and polished axe—not yet Corded battle-axe fashion everywhere. Paris Basin and Atlantic façades keep distinct visual dialects.
france.ideas: Bréviandes-type burials capture steppe ancestry arriving inside Neolithic families—admixture in real time, not a finished Corded Ware map. Ideas of kinship stretch to include eastern-connected men without instantly rewriting pottery brands. France is a hinge of pulses (~3000/2900 BC) before Beaker standardisation.
france.philosophy: Collective tombs continue ancestor corporations even as new bloodlines enter; cosmology is still megalithic and household. Ritual deposits and chamber reuse matter more than any steppe stela cult. Philosophy is practice at the tomb door—who may lie inside—during a genetic hinge.
france.science: Farmers keep Atlantic and loess agrosystems while copper knowledge spreads unevenly from south and east. Tomb carpentry, stone transport, and flint networks remain the technical backbone. Early pastoral signals appear in isotopes and ancestry before full steppe material packages dominate.

central.description: Central Europe at the hinge: GAC farmers meet expanding steppe-admixed groups. Corded Ware emerges as a new cultural-genetic formation (Yamnaya-related + GAC-like), the engine of much temperate European Indo-Europeanization in standard models.
central.linguisticNote: Leading archaeological correlate of early IE expansion into the European plain.
central.ancestryNote: Late TRB/GAC still farmer-led; early steppe signals uneven — higher toward the east.

ancestryCline.label: West GAC/TRB → eastern contact
ancestryCline.note: Steppe% rises east toward Pontic contact; western Late Neolithic stays more EEF+WHG.

central.art: Globular Amphora jars, cattle burials, and flint axes define late farmer display before Corded Ware’s cord-impressed amphorae and battle-axes take over. Art is ceramic body and animal deposit more than figurative stone. The visual hinge is amphora → cord beaker within a few centuries.
central.ideas: GAC cattle wealth and Yamnaya-related incomers collide to midwife Corded Ware—admixture as ethnogenesis. Social ideas pivot from collective Neolithic claims toward single-grave politics. Central Europe becomes the factory floor of temperate Indo-Europeanization in standard models.
central.philosophy: Cattle offerings and amphora graves imply a pastoral sacred economy; Corded dawn adds gendered weapon burial. Cosmology is read from animals, pots, and posture—practice without named teachers or schools. Ancestor and herd are the moral pair.
central.science: Wheel and wagon knowledge filters west with steppe contact; GAC and early CW communities manage mixed farming with rising pastoral mobility. Flint and early metal chaînes opératoires intensify. Ceramic temper recipes and cord decoration are reproducible craft science across the plain.

scandinavia.description: Farmer TRB coexists with coastal Pitted Ware (more HG-leaning genetically). The Single Grave Culture (Corded Ware) takeover — Denmark’s second near-total turnover — follows in the next centuries.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Pre-IE/transitional; pre-Germanic linked to ensuing Battle Axe/SGC.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Mostly pre–Single Grave; Pitted Ware coasts keep HG-rich profiles beside TRB farms.

ancestryCline.label: Pitted Ware → late TRB
ancestryCline.note: Coastal holdouts stay HG-rich; southern TRB is EEF-led with only slight early steppe.

scandinavia.art: Funnelbeaker megaliths and pottery coexist with Pitted Ware seal-hunter aesthetics—bone harpoons, marine mammal art, and coastal camps. Visual Scandinavia is split: farmer stone tombs inland/south versus forager maritime kits on the coasts. Steppe battle-axe fashion is still approaching.
scandinavia.ideas: Dual economies—TRB farms and Pitted Ware seas—encode two ideas of the good life in one peninsula. Early steppe signals are slight; the coming Single Grave turnover is not yet destiny. Identity is diet and burial as much as pottery brand.
scandinavia.philosophy: Megalithic ancestor chambers versus coastal forager rites offer rival sacred geographies. Seals, pigs, and cattle likely carried different ritual charges. Cosmology is place-and-prey, not scripture.
scandinavia.science: TRB agronomy on northern soils meets Pitted Ware marine mammal hunting and sealing technology—two applied ecologies. Megalith engineering continues; coastal navigation is forager science. Pottery tempers diverge with lifestyle.

italy.description: Northern and peninsular Copper Age cultures with distinctive burial rites and early metal. Steppe ancestry appears later and more moderately than in the Corded Ware north — Italy’s BA path is not a clone of Poland or Denmark.
italy.linguisticNote: Unknown. Historical Italic and Etruscan are still ahead.
italy.ancestryNote: Mostly EEF+WHG; limited early steppe vs CW heartland.
italy.art: Remedello weapon graves and Gaudo chamber tombs define Copper Age Italy with tanged daggers, halberds, and distinctive pottery—an aesthetic of metal and rock-cut tomb. Stele statues in the Alpine fringe hint at anthropomorphic display. Steppe kurgan art is still foreign.
italy.ideas: Peninsular and Po communities intensify metallurgy and hierarchy on largely EEF+WHG bases; steppe ancestry is limited versus the Corded north. Copper Age Italy is a Mediterranean farmer–metal world, not a Yamnaya province. Regional tomb rites encode local belonging.
italy.philosophy: Chamber tombs and weapon deposits locate honour and ancestry underground. Alpine stelae may personify ancestors or powers without yielding readable myths. Cosmology is funerary and martial-practical.
italy.science: Early copper daggers and arsenical alloys show specialised smithing. Rock-cut tomb engineering and Mediterranean crop systems continue Neolithic agronomy with metal tools. Alpine greenstone and metal routes sketch north–south technical exchange.

balkans.description: Lower Danube and Black Sea–adjacent communities enter contact with expanding Yamnaya horizons. Early steppe-related ancestry is patchy; Aegean farmer substrates remain important further south.
balkans.linguisticNote: Contact zone; Greek ancestor speech not yet Mycenaean-attested.
balkans.ancestryNote: Variable steppe on EEF-rich bases; not uniform Yamnaya replacement.
balkans.art: Danube–Black Sea contact zones show kurgan-style burials beside older tell and cemetery traditions; ochre, weapons, and pastoral kits appear on farmer edges. Figurines and fine pottery of Balkan Eneolithic traditions persist inland. Art is a contact collage—stela and tell.
balkans.ideas: Yamnaya horizons push into the Lower Danube while Aegean farmer substrates hold farther south. Patchy steppe ancestry means diplomacy, marriage, and raiding—not uniform replacement. The Balkans are a corridor of packages, not a single people.
balkans.philosophy: Kurgan rites import steppe afterlife theatre; tell communities keep household and cemetery cults. Competing sacred geographies meet along the rivers. Cosmology is plural and contact-shaped.
balkans.science: Wheel/wagon and pastoral mobility meet Balkan metallurgy (already ancient here). Riverine exchange and early horse presence are logistical sciences. Farmers and herders hybridise crop–livestock calendars on steppe edges.

eastern.description: Mobile pastoralists of the Pontic–Caspian steppe (~3300–2600 BCE), kurgan burial rite, wagon/horse pastoral economy. Formed from Eneolithic steppe mixtures (Serednii Stih–related; CLV contributions). Expanding Yamnaya-related ancestry is the source labeled “steppe” across European BA aDNA. Archaeological Yamnaya ≠ identical genomes in every kurgan.
eastern.ancestryNote: Yamnaya = WSH package (EHG+CHG already fused). Shown as WSH, not re-split into EHG and CHG.
eastern.linguisticNote: Best archaeological match for late Proto-Indo-European (or a sister) in the steppe hypothesis — reconstructed lexicon, not Yamnaya inscriptions.

ancestryCline.label: Yamnaya core → farmer edge
ancestryCline.note: WSH% highest on Yamnaya core steppe; EEF rises toward late Trypillia / western contact.

eastern.art: Kurgans with ochre-covered flexed burials, stone stelae, cord-decorated pots, and wagon fittings define the steppe look. Animal offerings and early metal daggers stage pastoral wealth in death. Dress is wool, leather, and status pins—mobile prestige, not city walls.
eastern.ideas: CLV and Serednii Stih fusions (Lazaridis & Nikitin 2025) create WSH ancestry that will remake Europe; Afanasievo carries the package to the Altai. Social ideas centre on herd, kurgan lineage, and mobility. Language candidates (late PIE) are reconstructed from later tongues, not Yamnaya texts.
eastern.philosophy: Kurgan cosmology: ochre, wagon, animal, and sky over the mound—practice without scripture. Stelae may mark persons or powers; dairying and herd fertility likely charged the sacred. No named philosophers; the grave is the treatise.
eastern.science: Wilkin et al. 2021: ubiquitous ruminant dairying (and some horse milk) underwrites expansion—proteomic proof of secondary-products science. Wagon/wheel carpentry, pastoral scheduling, and early metallurgy are the measurable technologies of WSH success.

periods.linguistics: Steppe speech is reconstructed only via Indo-European comparative method. Yamnaya ≈ late PIE (or a close sister) is mainstream but unprovable from inscriptions. Western Europe still largely non-IE.

mapLayers.label: Yamnaya core steppe
mapLayers.art: Material signature of Yamnaya core steppe: the objects, monuments, and dress styles that archaeologists use to draw this incoming layer on the Copper / Yamnaya map.
mapLayers.ideas: Yamnaya core steppe ideas of belonging are read from graves, enclosures, and exchange—who is buried with what, who shares ceramic recipes, who is kept outside the ditch.
mapLayers.philosophy: Named philosophers are anachronistic for Yamnaya core steppe. Treat cosmology as ritual geometry, ancestor practice, and craft taboo—reconstructed, not quoted.
mapLayers.science: Craft science of Yamnaya core steppe: lithic or metal chaînes opératoires, ceramic tempers, and environmental scheduling that made this horizon reproducible across sites.

mapLayers.science: Craft science of Final Trypillia: lithic or metal chaînes opératoires, ceramic tempers, and environmental scheduling that made this horizon reproducible across sites.

UKR.name: Yamnaya pastoralists
UKR.summary: Kurgan steppe societies of the Pontic–Caspian zone.
UKR.conflicts: Expansion into Danube/Carpathian Basin; pressure on Trypillia and GAC worlds.
UKR.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Comparative Indo-European poetics later reconstructs a world of sky gods, cattle wealth, and praise of patrons — a hypothetical echo chamber, not a recovered library. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: Kurgans with ochre-covered flexed burials, stone stelae, cord-decorated pots, and wagon fittings define the steppe look. Animal offerings and early metal daggers stage pastoral wealth in death. Dress is wool, leather, and status pins—mobile prestige, not city walls.

UKR.religion: Yamnaya steppe religion is read from kurgans: ochre-covered flexed burials, wagons/animal offerings, and stelae. Sky/ancestor pastoral cult inferred; no native texts.
UKR.ideas: CLV and Serednii Stih fusions (Lazaridis & Nikitin 2025) create WSH ancestry that will remake Europe; Afanasievo carries the package to the Altai. Social ideas centre on herd, kurgan lineage, and mobility. Language candidates (late PIE) are reconstructed from later tongues, not Yamnaya texts.
UKR.philosophy: Kurgan cosmology: ochre, wagon, animal, and sky over the mound—practice without scripture. Stelae may mark persons or powers; dairying and herd fertility likely charged the sacred. No named philosophers; the grave is the treatise.
UKR.science: Wilkin et al. 2021: ubiquitous ruminant dairying (and some horse milk) underwrites expansion—proteomic proof of secondary-products science. Wagon/wheel carpentry, pastoral scheduling, and early metallurgy are the measurable technologies of WSH success.

RUS.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. Russian and wider Rus’ cultures translate Byzantine inheritance into forest and empire scales.

RUS.ideas: CLV and Serednii Stih fusions (Lazaridis & Nikitin 2025) create WSH ancestry that will remake Europe; Afanasievo carries the package to the Altai. HUN.name: Yamnaya in the Carpathian Basin
HUN.conflicts: Contact/conflict with local Late Neolithic/Copper communities.
HUN.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Comparative Indo-European poetics later reconstructs a world of sky gods, cattle wealth, and praise of patrons — a hypothetical echo chamber, not a recovered library. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. Hungarian culture keeps a steppe-origin memory inside a Latin-Christian and later Habsburg frame.
HUN.art: Globular Amphora jars, cattle burials, and flint axes define late farmer display before Corded Ware’s cord-impressed amphorae and battle-axes take over. Art is ceramic body and animal deposit more than figurative stone. The visual hinge is amphora → cord beaker within a few centuries.

HUN.religion: Yamnaya-related Carpathian Basin graves import kurgan burial grammar (ochre, mounds, pastoral goods) into farmer Europe’s ritual map.
HUN.ideas: GAC cattle wealth and Yamnaya-related incomers collide to midwife Corded Ware—admixture as ethnogenesis. Social ideas pivot from collective Neolithic claims toward single-grave politics. Central Europe becomes the factory floor of temperate Indo-Europeanization in standard models.
HUN.philosophy: Cattle offerings and amphora graves imply a pastoral sacred economy; Corded dawn adds gendered weapon burial. Cosmology is read from animals, pots, and posture—practice without named teachers or schools. Ancestor and herd are the moral pair.
HUN.science: Wheel and wagon knowledge filters west with steppe contact; GAC and early CW communities manage mixed farming with rising pastoral mobility. Flint and early metal chaînes opératoires intensify. Ceramic temper recipes and cord decoration are reproducible craft science across the plain.

ESP.name: Los Millares & Copper Age Iberia
ESP.conflicts: Internal hierarchy; Beaker package arrives before major steppe ancestry.
ESP.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Comparative Indo-European poetics later reconstructs a world of sky gods, cattle wealth, and praise of patrons — a hypothetical echo chamber, not a recovered library. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: Fortified hilltop centres such as Los Millares frame tholos tombs, copper tools, and schematic idols in a visual language of walls and collective chambers. Beaker pottery is still only a whisper; prestige is stone architecture, ivory, and early metal blades. Dress stays wool and linen with personal ornaments—status written in settlement fortification more than in steppe kurgans.

ESP.religion: Los Millares / Copper Age Iberia: fortified ritual centers, collective and emerging individual tombs, idol plaques — not Yamnaya kurgans, but parallel sacral intensification.
ESP.ideas: Hierarchy intensifies through metallurgy and defended villages while ancestry remains almost entirely EEF+WHG—steppe ideas have not yet remade the gene pool. Collective tombs and craft specialisation argue for ancestral corporations controlling copper and exotic exchange. Iberia’s Copper Age is a farmer world organising itself for metal, not a Yamnaya outpost.
ESP.philosophy: No named schools; cosmology is tomb and idol. Tholoi and engraved plaques keep the dead as corporate ancestors, while schematic ‘eye’ idols hint at personified powers without a readable pantheon. Sacred order is architectural—who may enter the chamber, who owns the copper—rather than doctrinal text.
ESP.science: Copper smelting, casting, and arsenical alloys are the period’s hard science, paired with fortification surveying on arid southeastern hills. Farmers manage Mediterranean crops under increasing aridity while sourcing ivory and ostrich-egg shell through long Atlantic–Mediterranean chains. Ceramic and lithic chaînes opératoires standardise household production beside the new metal workshops.

GBR.name: Late Neolithic Britain
GBR.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Comparative Indo-European poetics later reconstructs a world of sky gods, cattle wealth, and praise of patrons — a hypothetical echo chamber, not a recovered library. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. Insular voices and North Sea contact give this place a distinctive accent in the wider European chorus.
GBR.art: Stonehenge’s later Neolithic phases, timber circles, Grooved Ware, and carved chalk objects keep a monumental island aesthetic untouched by steppe kurgan art. Collective and cremation rites, carved stone, and ceremonial landscapes dominate; metal is still scarce. Dress and ornament remain Neolithic—jet, amber, and stone—before Beaker gold arrives.

GBR.religion: Late Neolithic Britain: continuing megalithic and henge rites (Stonehenge landscape) before Beaker individual graves rewrite burial fashion.
GBR.ideas: Island ceremonial commons and ancestral monuments organise politics without Yamnaya pastoral kings. Gene pools stay EEF+WHG; the ‘steppe story’ is still a continental rumour. Labour and pilgrimage around henges imply large-scale cooperation among farming communities who do not yet know they are about to be replaced.
GBR.philosophy: Solar alignments, processional avenues, and successive monument rebuilds encode a sky-and-ancestor cosmology in stone and timber. The dead and the solstice structure time; no pantheon is named. Sacred knowledge is architectural and calendrical—how to stand stones to catch the sun—not philosophical prose.
GBR.science: Megalithic and timber engineering, horizon astronomy, and quarry logistics (bluestones, sarsens) are peak Neolithic applied science. Mixed farming on chalk and clay fuels seasonal gatherings. Trackways and boat craft stitch coasts and rivers into a pre-metal transport web.

ITA.name: Remedello / Gaudo
ITA.conflicts: Limited early steppe vs CW north.
ITA.literature: No Yamnaya texts. Comparative Indo-European poetics later reconstructs a world of sky gods, cattle wealth, and praise of patrons — a hypothetical echo chamber, not a recovered library. Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. Italian cities teach prestige: from Roman monumentality to Renaissance brand management of beauty.
ITA.art: Remedello weapon graves and Gaudo chamber tombs define Copper Age Italy with tanged daggers, halberds, and distinctive pottery—an aesthetic of metal and rock-cut tomb. Stele statues in the Alpine fringe hint at anthropomorphic display. Steppe kurgan art is still foreign.

ITA.religion: Remedello / Gaudo: Copper Age cemeteries with weapon graves and formal rite — Italian paths to status burial without steppe kurgans.
ITA.ideas: Peninsular and Po communities intensify metallurgy and hierarchy on largely EEF+WHG bases; steppe ancestry is limited versus the Corded north. Copper Age Italy is a Mediterranean farmer–metal world, not a Yamnaya province. Regional tomb rites encode local belonging.
ITA.philosophy: Chamber tombs and weapon deposits locate honour and ancestry underground. Alpine stelae may personify ancestors or powers without yielding readable myths. Cosmology is funerary and martial-practical.
ITA.science: Early copper daggers and arsenical alloys show specialised smithing. Rock-cut tomb engineering and Mediterranean crop systems continue Neolithic agronomy with metal tools. Alpine greenstone and metal routes sketch north–south technical exchange.

Treat reconstructed hymns as models, not quotations from the steppe. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.

DEU.philosophy: Cattle offerings and amphora graves imply a pastoral sacred economy; Corded dawn adds gendered weapon burial. Cosmology is read from animals, pots, and posture—practice without named teachers or schools. Ancestor and herd are the moral pair.

periods.label: Corded Ware & Bell Beaker
periods.narrative: Corded Ware and Bell Beaker remake temperate Europe with Yamnaya-related steppe ancestry — but not uniformly. Steppe% is typically higher in northern/central Corded Ware and Single Grave Denmark than in Iberian Beaker; British Beaker shows near-total turnover of the prior Neolithic pool. Residual farmer/HG clines persist under the new packages.
periods.culturesNote: Corded Ware, Single Grave, Battle Axe, Bell Beaker (Britain high-turnover; Iberia more gradual) — steppe gradients, not one %.

iberia.description: Bell Beaker Iberia keeps a strong EEF base. Steppe ancestry enters more gradually (and often male-biased) than in Britain — a west Mediterranean cline of lower steppe%, not a copy of the British turnover.
iberia.ancestryNote: Beaker Iberia: more gradual, often male-biased steppe intake — lower steppe% than Britain/SGC.
iberia.languages: Pre-IE Iberian substrates; early IE uncertain
iberia.linguisticNote: Culture≠language. IE (later Celtic/Italic-related?) is not automatic with Beaker pots; non-IE Iberian is attested in the Iron Age.

ancestryCline.label: Beaker steppe intake → EEF base
ancestryCline.note: Steppe rises with Beaker-associated lineages but usually stays below British/Danish levels; EEF remains the base.

iberia.art: Maritime Bell Beakers, palmela points, wristguards, and gold ornaments redefine display—an archery-and-drink package that looks pan-European yet sits on local Copper Age bodies. Tomb reuse and Beaker deposits restyle older megalithic stages without erasing them. Art is portable prestige: pots, daggers, and archery kits more than new megamonuments.
iberia.ideas: The Beaker idea travels farther than steppe genes here: cultural fashion and often male-biased ancestry intake, not Britain’s near-total replacement. Communities negotiate belonging through Beaker rites inside a still-strong farmer substrate. Atlantic and interior networks compete—same pottery brand, different demographic bargains.
iberia.philosophy: Ritual centres on individualising Beaker graves and drinking sets that stage personhood and alliance. Cosmology stays oral; what archaeology recovers is gendered kits and ancestral tomb re-entry, not theology. Worldview is a prestige ethic of archery, metal, and hospitality performed at the grave.
iberia.science: Copper and early bronze recipes refine casting and sheet-gold work; archery gear implies measured craft of bow, point, and wristguard. Farmers and herders keep Mediterranean agrosystems while plugging into Beaker exchange for metal and exotics. Navigation and coastal logistics still underwrite the Atlantic Beaker face.

britain.description: Bell Beaker Britain: genomic turnover of the Neolithic population. The new mix is steppe + EEF + WHG, with steppe typically highest in the early Beaker pulse and a bit more farmer/HG in some later local profiles — not a single flat percentage.
britain.ancestryNote: ~90% turnover of prior Neolithic ancestry; resulting ternary still varies site-to-site.
britain.linguisticNote: Often paired with IE language shift models (early Celtic or pre-Celtic IE). Exact branch and timing remain debated; no contemporary texts.

ancestryCline.label: Early Beaker pulse → later mix
ancestryCline.note: Steppe-rich Beaker immigrants vs slightly more EEF/WHG in some later/local mixes — Britain stays high-steppe overall.

britain.art: Beaker pots, copper daggers, wristguards, and gold lunulae/discs arrive with a new funerary fashion of single graves under round barrows. The Amesbury Archer’s kit is portraiture in metal and stone. Older stone theatres stay standing while the people who gather there genetically transform—continuity of place, rupture of flesh.
britain.ideas: Olalde et al.’s ~90% turnover makes Britain the textbook of demic Beaker transformation: steppe-rich continental ancestry and R1b lineages replace Neolithic pools within centuries. Round-barrow individualism and archery prestige rewrite social ideals. Monuments are reused by newcomers who inherit landscapes they did not build.
britain.philosophy: Single-grave ideology personalises the afterlife—weapons, beakers, and gendered kits for a journey—contrasting collective Neolithic chambers. Cosmology remains wordless; practice says the person, armed and provisioned, matters at death. No named sages; ritual drinking and barrow skyline are the doctrine.
britain.science: Early metallurgy (copper then bronze), barrow surveying, and continental navigation are the enabling sciences of the takeover. Isotope studies show mobile individuals; craft recipes for Beaker ceramics and goldworking spread with people. Farming continues, but smithing and archery tech mark the new skill elite.

france.culture: Bell Beaker & late Corded Ware France
france.description: Northern France shows admixture pulses tying steppe ancestry to CW/Beaker-era dynamics (~3000/2900 and ~2600 BCE). Paris Basin collective burials capture Neolithic substrates meeting incoming steppe-related ancestry in “real time.”
france.linguisticNote: Early IE dialects hypothesized with CW/Beaker gene flow; Gaulish attested only much later.
france.ancestryNote: Beaker/CW France intermediate — higher steppe northeast, more EEF southwest.

ancestryCline.label: Northeast → southwest
ancestryCline.note: Steppe% higher toward Rhine/CW contact; southwest keeps more Neolithic EEF+WHG.

france.art: Corded Ware reaches the northeast with single graves and battle-axes; Bell Beaker colours the west and south with maritime pots, archery kits, and gold. Megalithic stages host Beaker inserts—old stone theatres restyled. Visual France becomes a patchwork of CW male packages and Beaker drinking sets.
france.ideas: Two demographic pulses—CW-linked then Beaker-linked—mix with lasting Neolithic substrates more gently than in Britain. Regional identities form along Rhine, Atlantic, and Mediterranean corridors. Prestige goods and marriage networks, not a single empire, remake belonging.
france.philosophy: Gendered single graves and Beaker kits personalise death beside older collective rites still in memory. Cosmology is inferred from posture, ochre, weapons, and tomb reuse—thick practice, thin doctrine. No schools; an ethic of alliance through drink, gift, and armed burial.
france.science: Copper–bronze metallurgy, archery craft, and ceramic standardisation spread with mobility. Farmers adapt herds and cereals to a more pastoral-influenced economy in the north. River and Atlantic routes become measured exchange sciences linking Bohemia to Brittany.

central.description: Corded Ware across Germany–Bohemia–Poland with Globular Amphora farmer admixture. Steppe ancestry is clinal: higher in early/eastern CW, lower where GAC-like farmer ancestry persists in the west — not one Corded Ware percentage.
central.ancestryNote: Corded Ware steppe% higher early/east; more GAC-like farmer ancestry persists west/south.
central.linguisticNote: Core correlate of temperate European Indo-Europeanization in steppe models.

ancestryCline.label: Early/east CW → west farmer mix
ancestryCline.note: Steppe highest in early Corded Ware; western/southern profiles keep more Globular Amphora–like EEF.

central.art: Cord-impressed pottery, faceted battle-axes, hammer-headed pins, and single graves under mounds are the classic look. Bohemian cemeteries show early diversity then Y-lineage narrowing—art kits standardise as lineages bottleneck. Male weapon packages and female ornament sets stage a gendered gallery of the dead.
central.ideas: Papac et al. show CW as Yamnaya-related plus farmer mix, not pure steppe clones; social selection reshapes Y-diversity by ~2600 BC. Corded Ware expands as a marriage-and-migration system across the North European Plain. Belonging is amphora, axe, and mound alignment.
central.philosophy: Single-grave ideology personalises destiny—flexed bodies, ochre, gendered gifts for an afterlife journey. Ancestral mound lines create ritual geographies of lineage. Doctrine is funerary geometry; named philosophers do not exist.
central.science: Pastoral–agrarian scheduling, early bronze uptake, and ceramic standardisation scale across hundreds of kilometres. Mobility (isotopes, aDNA) is itself a researched ancient practice of seasonal and marital movement. Battle-axe stone grinding and cord-paddle pottery are precision crafts.

scandinavia.description: Scandinavian Corded Ware: Single Grave Culture in Jutland and Battle Axe in Sweden. Denmark aDNA shows ~60–85% steppe-related ancestry and limited local TRB farmer contribution — a second near-complete Holocene turnover after the farmer pulse (Allentoft et al. 2024).
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Single Grave / Battle Axe: often ~60–85% steppe-related; southern SGC higher steppe than some inland mixes.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Standard archaeological correlate of pre-Germanic on the northern arc.

ancestryCline.label: Single Grave south → inland mix
ancestryCline.note: Danish Single Grave often at the high end of steppe%; some inland/northern mixes keep more farmer/HG.

scandinavia.art: Danish Single Grave barrows with corded beakers and Swedish boat-shaped battle-axes remake the north’s funerary gallery. Polished stone axes become sculptural status; Pitted Ware art fades. Gendered kits and mound skylines replace collective TRB chambers as the dominant aesthetic.
scandinavia.ideas: Allentoft et al. 2024: a second near-total Danish turnover—steppe-rich SGC replaces Funnelbeaker pools, aligning ancestry toward later Danes. Battle Axe Sweden joins the Corded Ware horizon with local farmer admixture (Malmström 2019). The idea of the person-under-the-barrow conquers the megalith commons.
scandinavia.philosophy: Weapon burial and single graves preach an ethic of individual martial destiny and patrilineal mound lines. Older megaliths become landscape memory, not the main afterlife technology. No runes yet; cosmology is axe, ochre, and barrow.
scandinavia.science: Incoming pastoral–agrarian mixes, early metal trickle, and barrow construction organise northern landscapes. Isotopes show diet shifts with the cultural break. Stone battle-axe manufacture is standardised prestige engineering.

italy.description: Beaker and early Bronze influences enter a Copper Age peninsula. Steppe-related ancestry appears but generally at lower/later intensity than in the CW heartland; Italy keeps more Neolithic substrate into the BA.
italy.linguisticNote: IE (toward Italic) and non-IE (toward Etruscan) lineages both still ahead historically.
italy.ancestryNote: Moderate steppe on EEF+WHG base; not Danish SGC extremes.
italy.art: Bell Beaker pots and archery kits appear in the north and along contact zones, then Early Bronze facies diversify. Polada lake-dwellings and related settlements add timber architecture to the Beaker portable package. Art mixes Beaker prestige with local tomb traditions.
italy.ideas: Beaker fashion and moderate steppe ancestry enter without cloning British replacement levels. Italy remains a mosaic—EEF-heavy, regionally stubborn. Ideas of warrior archery and drinking alliance graft onto Copper Age hierarchies.
italy.philosophy: Beaker single-grave gestures coexist with older collective habits; cosmology stays archaeological. Lake and tomb rites structure community without texts. Worldview is craft, feast, and burial posture.
italy.science: Bronze recipes spread; pile-dwelling carpentry in wet northern basins is environmental engineering. Caprine–cereal economies adapt to Apennine and Po ecologies. Metal and amber trickle through Alpine passes as measured trade.

balkans.description: Patchwork of steppe-admixed and more farmer-persistent communities along the Danube and toward the Aegean. Sets divergent paths: Mycenaean Greece will show moderate steppe on an Aegean base; northern Balkans track Carpathian–steppe networks.
balkans.linguisticNote: Early IE dialects + substrates; Greek becomes visible with Linear B later.
balkans.ancestryNote: Steppe present but typically lower than CW Poland/Germany averages.
balkans.art: Early Bronze facies diversify—Ezero-related, Cetina, and regional metal styles—with tumuli and weapon graves in places. Aegean links foreshadow later shaft-grave glitter. Art is regional metal and pottery, not a single Beaker carpet.
balkans.ideas: Steppe-related ancestry consolidates unevenly; southern Balkans keep stronger farmer bases. Exchange toward the Aegean and Carpathians structures prestige. Cultural labels multiply quickly on a still-forming ternary ancestry.
balkans.philosophy: Tumulus and cemetery rites encode local ancestor politics. Aegean contact brings new prestige theologies of metal and import. No Linear B yet—worldview remains archaeological.
balkans.science: Bronze casting spreads through Danube–Aegean corridors. Mining and metallurgy in the Carpathian–Balkan arc feed wider Europe. Agricultural terraces and herding adapt to broken terrain.

eastern.description: Post-Yamnaya steppe sequence (Catacomb and related). While CW carries steppe ancestry into Europe, the steppe itself continues pastoralist cultural change. Still the reservoir of steppe-related genetic profiles.
eastern.linguisticNote: Continuing steppe IE continuum (details of dialect geography unknown).
eastern.ancestryNote: Catacomb / steppe-contact as WSH package + farmer remainder — no separate EHG/CHG slices.

ancestryCline.label: Steppe/Catacomb → western contact
ancestryCline.note: WSH highest on Catacomb/steppe; EEF rises toward western Corded Ware contact.

eastern.art: Catacomb graves under kurgans, distinctive pottery, and continued weapon–ornament kits evolve the Yamnaya visual order. Corded Ware to the west is the temperate sibling package; on the steppe, catacomb architecture restyles the mound world. Stelae and ochre traditions persist.
eastern.ideas: Steppe societies diversify after Yamnaya’s peak while feeding CW and Beaker west with ancestry and ideas. Catacomb horizons organise regional pastoral polities without cities. East–west clines of exchange keep metal, animals, and people moving.
eastern.philosophy: Catacomb burial redesigns the journey of the dead—side chambers, new postures—within kurgan sacred geography. Herd and ancestor remain the moral poles. Cosmology stays funerary and pastoral.
eastern.science: Pastoral mobility, bronze uptake, and kurgan engineering continue. Horse management intensifies toward later chariot horizons. Ceramic and metal recipes mark regional technical schools across the Pontic–Caspian.

periods.linguistics: Primary window hypothesized for Indo-Europeanization of temperate Europe. Pre-Germanic and other early IE lineages are often tied to CW/Battle Axe; Celtic/Italic pathways more debated. Iberian Beaker material culture does not imply IE speech.

mapLayers.ideas: Corded Ware (Germany–Bohemia) ideas of belonging are read from graves, enclosures, and exchange—who is buried with what, who shares ceramic recipes, who is kept outside the ditch.
mapLayers.philosophy: Named philosophers are anachronistic for Corded Ware (Germany–Bohemia). Treat cosmology as ritual geometry, ancestor practice, and craft taboo—reconstructed, not quoted.
mapLayers.science: Craft science of Corded Ware (Germany–Bohemia): lithic or metal chaînes opératoires, ceramic tempers, and environmental scheduling that made this horizon reproducible across sites.

mapLayers.philosophy: Named philosophers are anachronistic for Corded Ware (Poland). Treat cosmology as ritual geometry, ancestor practice, and craft taboo—reconstructed, not quoted.

DEU.name: Corded Ware Germany
DEU.conflicts: Overlaps and succession with Bell Beaker in the west; GAC substrate absorbed.
DEU.literature: Corded Ware’s central European heartland speaks through single-grave choreography and cord decoration — a ceramic dialect. Later Germanic verse is a distant cousin at best; do not put Beowulf in a Corded Ware mouth. Praise of patrons and cattle may be older Indo-European habits, but here they are archaeological silence surrounding loud pots.
DEU.art: Cord-impressed pottery, faceted battle-axes, hammer-headed pins, and single graves under mounds are the classic look. Bohemian cemeteries show early diversity then Y-lineage narrowing—art kits standardise as lineages bottleneck. Male weapon packages and female ornament sets stage a gendered gallery of the dead.

DEU.religion: Corded Ware: gendered single graves (battle-axe male package), amphora/beaker offerings, and ancestral mound reuse. Steppe-linked burial ideology over older megalithic collectivity.
DEU.ideas: Papac et al. show CW as Yamnaya-related plus farmer mix, not pure steppe clones; social selection reshapes Y-diversity by ~2600 BC. Corded Ware expands as a marriage-and-migration system across the North European Plain. Belonging is amphora, axe, and mound alignment.
DEU.philosophy: Single-grave ideology personalises destiny—flexed bodies, ochre, gendered gifts for an afterlife journey. Ancestral mound lines create ritual geographies of lineage. Doctrine is funerary geometry; named philosophers do not exist.
DEU.science: Pastoral–agrarian scheduling, early bronze uptake, and ceramic standardisation scale across hundreds of kilometres. Mobility (isotopes, aDNA) is itself a researched ancient practice of seasonal and marital movement. Battle-axe stone grinding and cord-paddle pottery are precision crafts.

DNK.science: Incoming pastoral–agrarian mixes, early metal trickle, and barrow construction organise northern landscapes. Isotopes show diet shifts with the cultural break. Stone battle-axe manufacture is standardised prestige engineering.

GBR.name: Bell Beaker Britain
GBR.literature: Britain’s Beaker age leaves no texts, but it leaves a funerary grammar: beakers by the face, archer wrist-guards, copper knives. Later British poetry of barrows and ‘ancient Britons’ is Victorian dreamwork laid over this genomic rupture — read it as reception, not reportage. The real ‘literature’ is the grave as staged sentence: who drinks, who owns metal, who lies crouched.
GBR.art: Beaker pots, copper daggers, wristguards, and gold lunulae/discs arrive with a new funerary fashion of single graves under round barrows. The Amesbury Archer’s kit is portraiture in metal and stone. Older stone theatres stay standing while the people who gather there genetically transform—continuity of place, rupture of flesh.

GBR.religion: Bell Beaker Britain: individual graves with beaker, copper/bronze, and archer kits; henge landscapes still used. Beaker rite overlays older monumental religion.
GBR.ideas: Olalde et al.’s ~90% turnover makes Britain the textbook of demic Beaker transformation: steppe-rich continental ancestry and R1b lineages replace Neolithic pools within centuries. Round-barrow individualism and archery prestige rewrite social ideals. Monuments are reused by newcomers who inherit landscapes they did not build.
GBR.philosophy: Single-grave ideology personalises the afterlife—weapons, beakers, and gendered kits for a journey—contrasting collective Neolithic chambers. Cosmology remains wordless; practice says the person, armed and provisioned, matters at death. No named sages; ritual drinking and barrow skyline are the doctrine.
GBR.science: Early metallurgy (copper then bronze), barrow surveying, and continental navigation are the enabling sciences of the takeover. Isotope studies show mobile individuals; craft recipes for Beaker ceramics and goldworking spread with people. Farming continues, but smithing and archery tech mark the new skill elite.

ESP.name: Bell Beaker Iberia
ESP.summary: Beaker package on Neolithic-like genomes early on.
ESP.conflicts: Gradual steppe influx (often male-biased) vs Britain’s cliff replacement.
ESP.literature: Still pre-literate. Meaning travels in burial theatre: single graves, gendered grave goods, drinking vessels. Later IE epic genres are centuries downstream — useful analogies, not Corded Ware novels. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: Maritime Bell Beakers, palmela points, wristguards, and gold ornaments redefine display—an archery-and-drink package that looks pan-European yet sits on local Copper Age bodies. Tomb reuse and Beaker deposits restyle older megalithic stages without erasing them. Art is portable prestige: pots, daggers, and archery kits more than new megamonuments.

ESP.ideas: The Beaker idea travels farther than steppe genes here: cultural fashion and often male-biased ancestry intake, not Britain’s near-total replacement. Communities negotiate belonging through Beaker rites inside a still-strong farmer substrate. Atlantic and interior networks compete—same pottery brand, different demographic bargains.
ESP.philosophy: Ritual centres on individualising Beaker graves and drinking sets that stage personhood and alliance. Cosmology stays oral; what archaeology recovers is gendered kits and ancestral tomb re-entry, not theology. Worldview is a prestige ethic of archery, metal, and hospitality performed at the grave.
ESP.science: Copper and early bronze recipes refine casting and sheet-gold work; archery gear implies measured craft of bow, point, and wristguard. Farmers and herders keep Mediterranean agrosystems while plugging into Beaker exchange for metal and exotics. Navigation and coastal logistics still underwrite the Atlantic Beaker face.

periods.label: Nordic & European Bronze
periods.narrative: The Nordic Bronze Age (c. 1700–500 BCE) is a Scandinavian cultural climax — rock art, prestige bronzes, amber routes — on a gene pool already reset by Single Grave/Battle Axe. Southward: Tumulus then Urnfield, Atlantic Bronze, El Argar, Terramare, Mycenaean Greece (Linear B = early Greek). Deep ancestry is the WHG–EEF–steppe ternary in regional proportions; culture names proliferate faster than genetic turnovers.
periods.culturesNote: Nordic Bronze Age, Wessex, El Argar, Tumulus, Urnfield, Terramare/Apennine, Mycenaean, Srubnaya — BA facies on post-3000 BCE mixes.

iberia.description: El Argar (southeast) is an early complex Bronze Age society with fortified settlements; Atlantic Bronze networks link the west. Steppe-related ancestry is established but the Neolithic substrate remains substantial compared with post-Beaker Britain — continuity-with-admixture, not a second island-style replacement.
iberia.linguisticNote: Likely mosaic of early IE and non-IE; Iberian (non-IE) and Celtic appear in later written record.
iberia.ancestryNote: Ternary mix with higher EEF retention than Britain; rough schematic ~50/20/30 EEF/WHG/steppe varies by site.
iberia.art: El Argar’s hillforts, intramural urn burials, and stark silver diadems create a severe court style in the southeast; Atlantic Bronze hoards and warrior gear shine farther west. Pottery and metal diverge by province—argaric goblets versus Atlantic carp’s-tongue swords. Visual politics is fortress, grave under the floor, and hoarded bronze.
iberia.ideas: Southeast Iberia experiments with early complex society—controlled metal, marked inequality, fortified centres—while Atlantic façades join wider European bronze circuits. Steppe ancestry is present but diluted beside a durable Neolithic substrate; culture change outruns genetic revolution. Regional kingdoms of craft and coercion precede Celtic names by centuries.
iberia.philosophy: Intramural burial under houses binds the dead to domestic space—an ancestor theology of the threshold. Atlantic hoards in wet places suggest offerings to water powers or sworn destruction of wealth. No philosophers; ethics of honour and metal debt are inferred from weapons, diadems, and deliberate deposition.
iberia.science: Argolic metallurgy, silver working, and fortification engineering mark specialised technical classes. Atlantic smiths participate in pan-European sword and scrap-bronze economies—recycling as industrial practice. Dryland farming and storage inside defended sites are survival science under hierarchical provisioning.

britain.description: Post-Beaker Bronze Age Britain (Wessex culture and successors). Rich barrow burial and continental metal links. Ancestry remains the Beaker-set WHG–EEF–steppe ternary; archaeological facies change without another 90% turnover.
britain.linguisticNote: On the path hypothesized toward Insular Celtic; absolute Celtic chronology debated.
britain.ancestryNote: Continuous with Beaker Britain; steppe typically near ~half in many models.
britain.art: Wessex rich graves—gold lozenges, amber, bronze daggers—and later Deverel–Rimbury urnfields stage a barrow aristocracy in metal and cloth. Stonehenge’s Bronze Age reworkings keep the old sky theatre in elite service. Rock art is scarcer than in Scandinavia; prestige is portable gold and continental-style weaponry.
britain.ideas: Post-Beaker Britain consolidates a WHG–EEF–steppe ternary under named archaeological facies (Wessex, etc.) without another island-wide replacement. Chiefly exchange with Brittany, the Rhine, and Nordic zones advertises belonging to a European bronze club. Land, herds, and barrow cemeteries fix lineage claims in chalk country.
britain.philosophy: Barrow cemeteries and hoards in watery places suggest ancestors and offerings structuring obligation. Solar and martial symbolism travels with continental metal styles more than with local scripture. Worldview is elite funerary theatre—gold, dagger, and mound—plus older henge memory still charged with power.
britain.science: Tin from southwest Britain makes the islands a strategic node in bronze recipes across Europe. Smiths alloy, cast, and recycle; field systems and roundhouses organise agrarian production. Seagoing exchange of metal and amber is applied geography at continental scale.

france.description: Bronze Age cultural provinces over the third-millennium genetic settlement. Tumulus burial traditions and Atlantic exchange; ancestry stable relative to CW/Beaker formation.
france.linguisticNote: Toward early Celtic; Gaulish attested only in the Iron Age.
france.ancestryNote: Established ternary; no Denmark-scale new pulse.
france.art: Tumulus barrows, Atlantic bronze hoards, and later Urnfield cremation urns diversify funerary art. Swords, spears, and ornamented bronze advertise warrior fashion shared with Central Europe. Monumentality shifts from megalith to mound and hoard—metal as the sculptural medium.
france.ideas: Bronze Age provinces overlie the third-millennium genetic settlement; culture names change faster than ancestry. Atlantic and Tumulus networks pull elites into pan-European exchange. Toward Urnfield, cremation communities reimagine the dead as ash collectives—an idea of belonging through fire.
france.philosophy: Hoards in rivers and bogs look like gifts to watery powers or ritual destruction of weapons. Cremation reorients the body–soul problem without texts to explain it. Sacred life is depositional and funerary—sun, metal, and mound—not academy philosophy.
france.science: Bronze casting, sheet-working, and long-distance scrap economies are industrial knowledge. Field systems and hilltop occupations organise production and defence. Tin, copper, and amber routes make France a corridor science of weights, alloys, and seasonal trade.

central.description: Central European Middle–Late Bronze Age sequence: Tumulus Culture into Urnfield cremation complexes. Likely connected (debated) to later Celtic ethnolinguistic formations. Genetics largely stabilize the Corded Ware–derived mix.
central.linguisticNote: Pre-Celtic / early Celtic hypotheses for Urnfield–Hallstatt arc — debated.
central.ancestryNote: CW-descended ternary; cultural change ≫ genetic replacement.
central.art: Middle Bronze Tumulus weapon graves yield to Late Bronze Urnfield cremation cemeteries—urns, bronze swords, and situla art on the southern edge. Visual culture shifts from body-under-mound to ash-in-urn. Hillforts and hoards add landscape punctuation.
central.ideas: Genetic continuity with CW-descended mixes under rapid cultural renaming. Urnfield networks may seed later Celtic linguistic zones—debated, but the idea of wide cremation communities is clear. Warrior fashion and bronze scrap economies integrate the Carpathian–Alpine arc.
central.philosophy: Cremation reframes the person as fire-transformed; urnfields are cities of the dead without biographies. Hoards suggest vows, trophies, or offerings to powers of water and earth. Worldview is ritual technology of fire and metal, not written ethics.
central.science: Advanced bronze casting (including early lost-wax flourishes), mining in the eastern Alps, and recycling economies are industrial science. Urnfield agronomy and fortification engineering organise surplus and defence. Weight systems and ingot trade imply quantitative exchange literacy.

scandinavia.description: c. 1700–500 BCE cultural fluorescence: figurative rock art, longhouse farms, ostentatious bronzes, amber export. Genetically continuous with Late Neolithic/Battle Axe steppe-rich ancestry — a cultural peak, not a third total population replacement after TRB and SGC.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Post–Single Grave ternary; WHG residual higher than in some southern BA zones.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Mainstream view: pre-Germanic speakers in a Nordic BA cultural frame — reconstructed, not attested.
scandinavia.art: Figurative rock art (Tanum, Bohuslän, Østfold), the Trundholm sun chariot, oak-coffin costumes, lurs, and Viksø helmets make Scandinavia Bronze Age Europe’s great image culture. Ships, sun discs, warriors, and ploughs cover coastal bedrock. Denmark’s dressed dead are prehistoric couture.
scandinavia.ideas: Imported metal founds a prestige economy—amber out, bronze in—binding chiefs to Únětice, Carpathian, then Italian copper routes (Nørgaard et al. 2021). Genetically continuous with Battle Axe/SGC; this is cultural climax, not third replacement. Rock-art fleets advertise maritime ideology and meeting places for exchange.
scandinavia.philosophy: Sun-cult imagery (Trundholm; rock-art discs) and watery hoards stage a cosmology of light, voyage, and offering. Processions and twin myths are guessed from paired figures and horns—reconstructed ritual, not named theology. Sacred knowledge is metal, ship, and sun performed on rock and in bog.
scandinavia.science: Scandinavia’s science is network metallurgy: sourcing, alloying, and recycling foreign copper with local tin strategies, plus ship carpentry inferred from rock art and later boat finds. Longhouse farms and barrow labour organise surplus. Amber grading and route knowledge are commercial geography.

italy.description: Po Valley Terramare pile-dwelling/settlement systems and Apennine cultures further south. Ancestry mixes Italian Neolithic substrate with moderate BA steppe-related input — foundation for later Iron Age Italic/Etruscan genetic landscape.
italy.linguisticNote: Toward Proto-Italic and non-IE (Etruscan) lines — historical split still ahead.
italy.ancestryNote: EEF-heavier than CW north; steppe present but moderate.
italy.art: Terramare embanked villages of the Po plain—planned ditches, banks, and dense housing—are civic art in earth and timber; Apennine pottery and pastoral sites mark the mountains. Cremation and inhumation rites vary by facies. Visual identity is settlement geometry more than rock-art fleets.
italy.ideas: Organised Po settlements imply collective labour and perhaps proto-urban control of floodplain wealth. Apennine mobility links coasts to uplands. Ancestry keeps Italian EEF weight with moderate BA steppe—foundation for later Italic/Etruscan genetic landscapes.
italy.philosophy: Settlement rituals, structured deposits, and cemeteries suggest civic-sacral order without Nordic sun chariots. Water, ditch, and bank may themselves be charged boundaries. No philosophy schools; ethics of communal embankment and pastoral seasonality.
italy.science: Hydraulic and embankment engineering, bronze workshops, and floodplain agronomy are Terramare sciences. Apennine herding calendars manage vertical mobility. Northern Italian copper later feeds Nordic networks—Italy as ore science for the north.

balkans.description: Mycenaean palace societies (Linear B tablets = early Greek). Genetically, Mycenaeans show steppe-related ancestry on an Aegean/Anatolian-farmer-rich base — typically less steppe than Corded Ware north. Northern Balkans participate in Carpathian–Danube BA networks.
balkans.ancestryNote: Mycenaean steppe fraction model-dependent, generally moderate (<< CW Denmark).
balkans.linguisticNote: Mycenaean Greek is attested. Other Balkan IE (later Thracian/Illyrian) poorly documented.
balkans.art: Mycenaean palaces, shaft and tholos tombs, gold masks, frescoes, and chamber tombs create Europe’s first palace visual regime; northern Balkans join Carpathian metal fashions. Linear B tablets are administrative marks, not epic manuscripts. Art is gold, megarons, and painted plaster.
balkans.ideas: Palace centres redistribute goods, sponsor warriors, and write early Greek—political theology of wanax and sanctuary. Genomes show moderate steppe on Aegean farmer bases—language attested, demography not CW-Denmark. Northern Balkan BA networks parallel Mycenaean without sharing palaces.
balkans.philosophy: Linear B records offerings to named gods (e.g. di-we / Zeus forms, Poseidon, female deities)—a real pantheon in accounting, not philosophy seminars. Sanctuary deposits and funerary gold stage honour and divine reciprocity. Thought is ritual and administrative; Homer is still ahead as epic memory.
balkans.science: Palace metrology, seal administration, chariot workshops, and Mediterranean shipping are bureaucratic sciences. Bronze armour, fresco chemistry, and ashlar masonry are specialised crafts. Northern Balkan metallurgy and amber routes link Aegean demand to Carpathian supply.

eastern.description: Late Bronze Age steppe/forest-steppe pastoralist cultures (Srubnaya and kin). Maintain steppe-rich ancestry and sit on hypothesized pathways toward Indo-Iranian — parallel to European BA diversification further west.
eastern.linguisticNote: Often linked toward early Indo-Iranian; details contested.
eastern.art: Timber-grave (Srubnaya) kurgans, bone and bronze weapon sets, and settlement traces keep a pastoral-steppe aesthetic; forest-steppe edges mix farmer motifs. Chariot-related imagery and horse gear echo Sintashta innovations farther east. Art is grave timber, weapon, and herd wealth.
eastern.ideas: Srubnaya and kin maintain steppe-rich ancestry on pathways often linked toward early Indo-Iranian—parallel to European BA diversification west. Fortified Sintashta-type experiments (Urals) show war-tech and metallurgy intensifying. Identity is pastoral confederacy more than Mycenaean palace.
eastern.philosophy: Kurgan and timber-grave rites continue ancestor–herd cosmologies; chariot burials farther east sacralise speed and war. Fire, horse, and sky motifs are reconstructed from Indo-Iranian comparisons with caution—not quoted steppe scripture. Ethics of guest, raid, and offering are inferred, not authored.
eastern.science: Sintashta–Petrovka chariots (spoked wheels, horse teams) and bronze arsenals are peak steppe engineering of the early 2nd millennium BC. Timber-grave communities manage herds, metallurgy, and forest-steppe farming edges. Long-distance horse and metal knowledge feeds both European and Asian Bronze Ages.

periods.linguistics: Indo-European branches diversifying. Mycenaean Greek is attested (Linear B). Pre-Germanic in the north and Celtic-adjacent IE in the west are reconstructed. Non-IE substrates (later Iberian/Basque lines, Etruscan line) persist as hypotheses or later attestations.

mapLayers.label: Nordic Bronze Age
mapLayers.art: Material signature of Nordic Bronze Age: the objects, monuments, and dress styles that archaeologists use to draw this dominant layer on the Nordic & European Bronze map.
mapLayers.ideas: Nordic Bronze Age ideas of belonging are read from graves, enclosures, and exchange—who is buried with what, who shares ceramic recipes, who is kept outside the ditch.
mapLayers.philosophy: Named philosophers are anachronistic for Nordic Bronze Age. Treat cosmology as ritual geometry, ancestor practice, and craft taboo—reconstructed, not quoted.
mapLayers.science: Craft science of Nordic Bronze Age: lithic or metal chaînes opératoires, ceramic tempers, and environmental scheduling that made this horizon reproducible across sites.

DNK.name: Nordic Bronze Age Denmark
DNK.conflicts: Rival chiefly networks across south Scandinavia; links to Tumulus Europe.
DNK.literature: The Trundholm chariot is a one-object poem: a gilded sun pulled by a bronze horse on a ritual wagon. Oak-coffin burials with textiles preserve bodies as soft sculpture. No runes yet — meaning is metal and cloth.
DNK.art: Figurative rock art (Tanum, Bohuslän, Østfold), the Trundholm sun chariot, oak-coffin costumes, lurs, and Viksø helmets make Scandinavia Bronze Age Europe’s great image culture. Ships, sun discs, warriors, and ploughs cover coastal bedrock. Denmark’s dressed dead are prehistoric couture.

GBR.philosophy: Barrow cemeteries and hoards in watery places suggest ancestors and offerings structuring obligation. Solar and martial symbolism travels with continental metal styles more than with local scripture. Worldview is elite funerary theatre—gold, dagger, and mound—plus older henge memory still charged with power.
GBR.science: Tin from southwest Britain makes the islands a strategic node in bronze recipes across Europe. Smiths alloy, cast, and recycle; field systems and roundhouses organise agrarian production. Seagoing exchange of metal and amber is applied geography at continental scale.

ESP.name: El Argar
ESP.conflicts: Fortified centers; rivalry with Atlantic Bronze networks.
ESP.literature: No native scripts in the Nordic zone; meaning is cut into rock and cast in bronze. Later Eddic myth is a distant Iron/Viking-Age reframing — handle as comparative poetry, not Bronze Age reportage. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: El Argar’s hillforts, intramural urn burials, and stark silver diadems create a severe court style in the southeast; Atlantic Bronze hoards and warrior gear shine farther west. Pottery and metal diverge by province—argaric goblets versus Atlantic carp’s-tongue swords. Visual politics is fortress, grave under the floor, and hoarded bronze.

ESP.religion: El Argar: intramural and cemetery burials with sharp status grading; Argaric ritual is household/tomb-focused rather than Nordic sun-chariot religion.
ESP.ideas: Southeast Iberia experiments with early complex society—controlled metal, marked inequality, fortified centres—while Atlantic façades join wider European bronze circuits. Steppe ancestry is present but diluted beside a durable Neolithic substrate; culture change outruns genetic revolution. Regional kingdoms of craft and coercion precede Celtic names by centuries.
ESP.philosophy: Intramural burial under houses binds the dead to domestic space—an ancestor theology of the threshold. Atlantic hoards in wet places suggest offerings to water powers or sworn destruction of wealth. No philosophers; ethics of honour and metal debt are inferred from weapons, diadems, and deliberate deposition.
ESP.science: Argolic metallurgy, silver working, and fortification engineering mark specialised technical classes. Atlantic smiths participate in pan-European sword and scrap-bronze economies—recycling as industrial practice. Dryland farming and storage inside defended sites are survival science under hierarchical provisioning.

DEU.name: Tumulus Culture
DEU.literature: No native scripts in the Nordic zone; meaning is cut into rock and cast in bronze. Later Eddic myth is a distant Iron/Viking-Age reframing — handle as comparative poetry, not Bronze Age reportage. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.
DEU.art: Middle Bronze Tumulus weapon graves yield to Late Bronze Urnfield cremation cemeteries—urns, bronze swords, and situla art on the southern edge. Visual culture shifts from body-under-mound to ash-in-urn. Hillforts and hoards add landscape punctuation.

DEU.religion: Tumulus Culture: barrow cemeteries, weapon graves, and bronze hoards. Central European BA religion visible mainly as funerary and deposition rites.
DEU.ideas: Genetic continuity with CW-descended mixes under rapid cultural renaming. Urnfield networks may seed later Celtic linguistic zones—debated, but the idea of wide cremation communities is clear. Warrior fashion and bronze scrap economies integrate the Carpathian–Alpine arc.
DEU.philosophy: Cremation reframes the person as fire-transformed; urnfields are cities of the dead without biographies. Hoards suggest vows, trophies, or offerings to powers of water and earth. Worldview is ritual technology of fire and metal, not written ethics.
DEU.science: Advanced bronze casting (including early lost-wax flourishes), mining in the eastern Alps, and recycling economies are industrial science. Urnfield agronomy and fortification engineering organise surplus and defence. Weight systems and ingot trade imply quantitative exchange literacy.

ITA.name: Terramare
ITA.conflicts: Internal collapse debates; Apennine neighbors south.
ITA.literature: No native scripts in the Nordic zone; meaning is cut into rock and cast in bronze. Later Eddic myth is a distant Iron/Viking-Age reframing — handle as comparative poetry, not Bronze Age reportage. Italian cities teach prestige: from Roman monumentality to Renaissance brand management of beauty.
ITA.art: Terramare embanked villages of the Po plain—planned ditches, banks, and dense housing—are civic art in earth and timber; Apennine pottery and pastoral sites mark the mountains. Cremation and inhumation rites vary by facies. Visual identity is settlement geometry more than rock-art fleets.

ITA.religion: Terramare: settlement rituals, structured deposits, and cemetery practice in embanked villages — Po-plain civic-sacral order without Nordic rock-art cosmology.
ITA.ideas: Organised Po settlements imply collective labour and perhaps proto-urban control of floodplain wealth. Apennine mobility links coasts to uplands. Ancestry keeps Italian EEF weight with moderate BA steppe—foundation for later Italic/Etruscan genetic landscapes.
ITA.philosophy: Settlement rituals, structured deposits, and cemeteries suggest civic-sacral order without Nordic sun chariots. Water, ditch, and bank may themselves be charged boundaries. No philosophy schools; ethics of communal embankment and pastoral seasonality.
ITA.science: Hydraulic and embankment engineering, bronze workshops, and floodplain agronomy are Terramare sciences. Apennine herding calendars manage vertical mobility. Northern Italian copper later feeds Nordic networks—Italy as ore science for the north.

GRC.name: Mycenaean palaces
GRC.summary: Palace states with Linear B Greek.
GRC.conflicts: Rivalry among palaces; Aegean–Anatolian conflicts culminating in LBA crises.
GRC.literature: No native scripts in the Nordic zone; meaning is cut into rock and cast in bronze. Later Eddic myth is a distant Iron/Viking-Age reframing — handle as comparative poetry, not Bronze Age reportage. Greek language and forms remain a reusable antiquity — quarried by every later age for prestige.
GRC.art: Mycenaean palaces, shaft and tholos tombs, gold masks, frescoes, and chamber tombs create Europe’s first palace visual regime; northern Balkans join Carpathian metal fashions. Linear B tablets are administrative marks, not epic manuscripts. Art is gold, megarons, and painted plaster.

GRC.religion: Mycenaean palaces: named gods appear in Linear B (e.g. Poseidon, Potnia); palace sacrifice, libation, and tholos/chamber tombs. First European written pantheon fragments.
GRC.ideas: Palace centres redistribute goods, sponsor warriors, and write early Greek—political theology of wanax and sanctuary. Genomes show moderate steppe on Aegean farmer bases—language attested, demography not CW-Denmark. Northern Balkan BA networks parallel Mycenaean without sharing palaces.
GRC.philosophy: Linear B records offerings to named gods (e.g. di-we / Zeus forms, Poseidon, female deities)—a real pantheon in accounting, not philosophy seminars. Sanctuary deposits and funerary gold stage honour and divine reciprocity. Thought is ritual and administrative; Homer is still ahead as epic memory.
GRC.science: Palace metrology, seal administration, chariot workshops, and Mediterranean shipping are bureaucratic sciences. Bronze armour, fresco chemistry, and ashlar masonry are specialised crafts. Northern Balkan metallurgy and amber routes link Aegean demand to Carpathian supply.

UKR.name: Srubnaya
UKR.literature: No native scripts in the Nordic zone; meaning is cut into rock and cast in bronze. Later Eddic myth is a distant Iron/Viking-Age reframing — handle as comparative poetry, not Bronze Age reportage. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: Timber-grave (Srubnaya) kurgans, bone and bronze weapon sets, and settlement traces keep a pastoral-steppe aesthetic; forest-steppe edges mix farmer motifs. Chariot-related imagery and horse gear echo Sintashta innovations farther east. Art is grave timber, weapon, and herd wealth.
