UKR.religion: Srubnaya: timber-grave steppe rite under kurgans with weapons and animal offerings — continuing Pontic funerary religion into the Late Bronze Age.
UKR.ideas: Srubnaya and kin maintain steppe-rich ancestry on pathways often linked toward early Indo-Iranian—parallel to European BA diversification west. Fortified Sintashta-type experiments (Urals) show war-tech and metallurgy intensifying. Identity is pastoral confederacy more than Mycenaean palace.
UKR.philosophy: Kurgan and timber-grave rites continue ancestor–herd cosmologies; chariot burials farther east sacralise speed and war. Fire, horse, and sky motifs are reconstructed from Indo-Iranian comparisons with caution—not quoted steppe scripture. Ethics of guest, raid, and offering are inferred, not authored.
UKR.science: Sintashta–Petrovka chariots (spoked wheels, horse teams) and bronze arsenals are peak steppe engineering of the early 2nd millennium BC. Timber-grave communities manage herds, metallurgy, and forest-steppe farming edges. Long-distance horse and metal knowledge feeds both European and Asian Bronze Ages.

periods.label: Iron Age
periods.narrative: Iron metallurgy and oppida/city-states. Hallstatt then La Tène define Celtic material Europe; Jastorf-related groups mark Germanic ethnogenesis; Classical Greece and early Rome/Etruria write history; Scythian Iranian-speakers hold the steppe; Iberia mixes non-IE Iberian with Celtiberian. Genetics mostly continue Bronze Age mixes — “Celtic” and “Germanic” are linguistic-cultural, not new deep ancestry components.
periods.culturesNote: Hallstatt, La Tène, Jastorf, Classical Greek poleis, Etruscan/early Rome, Iberian/Celtiberian, Scythian — first dense linguistic attestation.

iberia.description: Iron Age Iberia splits linguistically and culturally: non-Indo-European Iberian societies on the Mediterranean/east (with scripts) versus Celtic-speaking Celtiberians and related IE groups inland/west, plus the Aquitanian/Basque line in the north. Deep ancestry remains the BA ternary; polity names are not new genetic components.
iberia.ancestryNote: Schematic continuity with BA Iberia (~EEF-rich ternary). No separate “Iberian race” component in aDNA terms.
iberia.linguisticNote: Among Europe’s clearest Iron Age language mosaics: written Iberian alongside Celtic IE; Basque/Aquitanian is the long-lived non-IE western outlier.

britain.description: Hillfort-dominated later Iron Age Britain with La Tène–influenced material culture. Speakers of Brittonic Celtic. No Beaker-scale genetic replacement; ancestry continuous with Bronze Age Britain until early medieval North Sea influxes.
britain.linguisticNote: Insular Celtic stage; Latin arrives only with Rome.
britain.ancestryNote: BA ternary continuity; steppe typically substantial; “Celtic” ≠ new ancestry component.

france.description: Celtic-speaking Gaul of oppida, coinage, and La Tène art before and during early Roman contact. Tribal polities (Aedui, Arverni, etc. in historical sources). Genetic continuity from BA with mobility; ethnolinguistic “Celtic” is not a WHG/EEF/steppe relabel.
france.linguisticNote: Gaulish is attested in inscriptions; later replaced by Latin→French.
france.ancestryNote: BA-derived ternary; urban/military Roman gene flow still limited pre-conquest.

central.description: Hallstatt elite centers (early Iron Age) develop into the La Tène cultural expansion often treated as the archaeological face of Continental Celtic Europe. Ancestry remains BA-derived; the shift is cultural-linguistic organization, not a Yamnaya-scale migration visible as a new deep component.
central.linguisticNote: Core zone of attested/continental Celtic before Romanization.
central.ancestryNote: Urnfield/BA continuity; Celtic label is linguistic-cultural.

scandinavia.description: Post–Nordic Bronze Age societies with simpler visible elites at first, then renewed complexity. Jastorf-related Germanic ethnogenesis is clearer archaeologically to the south; Scandinavia remains in the North Germanic trajectory. Ancestry continuous with BA.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Reconstructed stage before Elder Futhark Proto-Norse inscriptions.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Nordic BA ternary persists; no new continental replacement pulse.

italy.description: Literate Iron Age Italy: Etruscan cities (non-IE language isolate/family), Latin and other Italic IE speakers, Greek colonies in the south. Rome rises among Latin speakers. Antonio et al. (2019): Iron Age central Italians already a West Eurasian mix — distinct from later Imperial Rome’s eastern Mediterranean pulse.
italy.ancestryNote: IA Italy ≈ local BA + Mediterranean contacts; Imperial eastern Med influx comes later.
italy.languages: Latin/other Italic; Etruscan; Greek in Magna Graecia
italy.linguisticNote: Best-documented early Italian multilingualism; Etruscan proves non-IE survival beside IE.

balkans.description: City-state Greece produces the classical literary corpus; Thracian and Illyrian societies to the north/west are IE but poorly attested. Genetic profiles continue BA Aegean/Balkan patterns — classical glory is cultural, not a genomic reset.
balkans.linguisticNote: Greek richly attested; Thracian/Illyrian known mainly from names/glosses.
balkans.ancestryNote: BA Aegean/Balkan continuity + local structure; “Classical” is not a genetic cluster.

eastern.description: Iranian-speaking steppe confederations (Scythians and kin) across the Pontic steppe. Mounted nomadism, kurgan elites. Genetically steppe-rich with variable East Eurasian admixture — important regionally, not a pan-European replacement.
eastern.ancestryNote: West–east cline; eastern groups often higher East Eurasian (“other” in UI).
eastern.linguisticNote: Iranian steppe languages attested indirectly (names, Greek ethnography) and by comparative IE.

periods.linguistics: Attested map: Gaulish and other Celtic; Italic (Latin emerging); Greek; early Germanic (runes begin later); Iberian (non-IE) and Aquitanian/Basque line; Thracian/Illyrian fragmentary; Scythian Iranian.

mapLayers.label: Hallstatt West
mapLayers.art: Western Hallstatt elites stage power in wagon graves, gold neck-rings, and Mediterranean banqueting gear—bronze situlae, Attic cups, and the Vix krater’s monumental wine theatre at Mont Lassois. Hillfort Fürstensitze (Heuneburg’s mudbrick bastions) borrow southern architectural glamour. Dress signals rank with fibulae, coral, and amber rather than coin portraits.
mapLayers.ideas: Prestige flows up the Rhône–Saône from Massalia: wine, olive oil, and status feasting knit Alpine foreland chiefs into a Mediterranean periphery. Princely seats concentrate tribute and craft; their later abandonment (c. 480–430 BC) reopens the political map toward La Tène warrior networks. Belonging is shown by who drinks from imported vessels and who is buried under a monumental tumulus.
mapLayers.philosophy: No written philosophy. Worldview is reconstructed from chamber tombs, feasting kits, and sanctuary deposits—an ethic of elite hospitality, ancestor display, and southern luxury as sacred capital. Cosmology sits in the banquet and the grave, not in treatises.
mapLayers.science: Iron smelting and forging overtake bronze for weapons while salt, wagon carpentry, and long-distance amber routes remain technical pillars. Dendrochronology of elite timber and Mediterranean import dating show chiefs scheduling trade seasons with precision. Hillfort engineering—ramparts, gates, planned terraces—is applied geometry of power.

mapLayers.label: Hallstatt East
mapLayers.art: Eastern Hallstatt (Austria–Bohemia–western Hungary–Slovenia) keeps tumulus burials, bronze defensive gear, and Kalenderberg ceramics while situla art along the Adriatic–Alpine edge narrates processions and contests in embossed bronze. The Hallstatt salt-mining complex itself is an industrial landscape of tools, textiles, and preserved organic craft. Warrior kits and horse gear mark a more martial eastern visual grammar than the western wine-chief floruit.
mapLayers.ideas: Control of alpine passes and salt underwrites political weight between Italy, the Danube, and the north. Eastern zones adopt La Tène packages more gradually than the western Fürstensitze collapse narrative. Identity is regional chiefdom and mining community more than a single ‘Celtic empire.’
mapLayers.philosophy: Funerary display and situla scenes imply ideals of feast, contest, and ranked companionship without named doctrines. Sacred practice likely tied salt, mountain routes, and ancestral tumuli into one landscape religion—oral, local, and non-scribal.
mapLayers.science: Deep-shaft salt mining at Hallstatt demands timbering, haulage, and underground logistics among Europe’s earliest industrial sciences. Bronze and early iron weapon production, horse tack, and Adriatic exchange require metrology of weight and alloy. Eastern workshops keep parallel technical schools to the Rhône corridor.

mapLayers.label: La Tène Gaul
mapLayers.art: La Tène Gaul invents Europe’s great Iron Age design language: curvilinear vegetal ornament on scabbards, torcs, the Agris helmet’s gold vinework, painted pottery, and later oppida coin portraits. Checked woolens, trousers, and massive neck-rings dress a warrior-farmer elite. Sanctuary deposits of bent weapons (Gournay, Ribemont traditions) turn metalwork into ritual sculpture.
mapLayers.ideas: Tribal polities (Aedui, Arverni, and peers in later sources) negotiate through clientage, coinage, and oppida markets before Caesar. Druids, bards, and vates—known through Greek and Roman ethnography—organize law, memory, and cult without books as a matter of principle. Pan-Gallic assemblies and shared art styles create a soft cultural commons short of unitary statehood.
mapLayers.philosophy: Caesar and Poseidonius attribute to druids teachings on soul immortality and cosmic cycles—secondhand, but the strongest named intellectual claim for Celtic Gaul. Ethics of guest-friendship, feud, and sanctuary asylum structure daily obligation. No surviving native philosophical dialogues; thought is oral and juridical.
mapLayers.science: Oppida planning, rotary querns, iron ploughshares, and coin die-engraving are Gaulish applied sciences. Medical and astronomical lore later credited to druids cannot be recovered as textbooks, but agricultural calendars and metallurgical chaînes opératoires are archaeologically robust. Riverine and Atlantic boat carpentry ties inland Gaul to Massaliote and British waters.

mapLayers.label: British / Irish Celtic IA
mapLayers.art: Insular La Tène translates continental curves onto mirrors, sword scabbards, horse gear, and gold torcs (Snettisham). Hillfort earthworks and roundhouse settlements dominate the visual landscape; chariot burials in the east add a funerary theatre. Irish royal sites (Tara, Navan/Emain) and bog deposits create a parallel ceremonial aesthetic without classical temples.
mapLayers.ideas: Tribal territories and hillfort communities manage land, cattle, and alliance without Roman urban templates. Continental contact brings style and some goods; ancestry stays largely Bronze Age British/Irish. Later mythic cycles must be used cautiously as Iron Age evidence—they remember, but after Christian filters.
mapLayers.philosophy: No native philosophical schools. Ritual deposits in rivers, bogs, and shafts imply a sacred economy of offering and kingship tied to landscape. Cosmology is practised at enclosure and watery place, not written as metaphysics.
mapLayers.science: Hillfort rampart engineering, quern technology, salt production, and Atlantic/North Sea seafaring are core skills. Fine bronze casting and sheet-work show specialist smiths. Agricultural mixed farming on heavy soils underwrites the calorie base of tribal politics.

mapLayers.label: La Tène Central Europe
mapLayers.art: From the Marne–Moselle and Middle Rhine outward, Early Style La Tène (Glauberg, Dürrnberg flagons) pioneers mask motifs, vegetal scrolls, and chariot burials that redefine Celtic art after Hallstatt. Later oppida (Manching and peers) add minting, glass bracelets, and dense craft quarters. Weapon sets and fibula typologies become the region’s chronological art history.
mapLayers.ideas: Central Europe is the workshop of Continental Celtic expansion and contraction—pressure toward Italy and the Balkans, then Roman and Germanic reordering. Elite mobility and shared art packages matter more than fixed ethnic borders. Coin legends and oppida markets sketch proto-urban political economies.
mapLayers.philosophy: Learned classes analogous to western druids are poorly attested here in texts; worldview is read from sanctuary weapon deposits, chariot graves, and later interpretatio Romana of Celtic gods. Honour, hospitality, and martial display structure an oral ethic.
mapLayers.science: High-grade ironworking, coin metallurgy, glassmaking, and oppida water/road logistics show specialised craft science. Contact with Italian and Greek metrology arrives via trade and mercenary service. Agricultural surplus on loess and river terraces funds artisan quarters.

mapLayers.label: Celtiberian
mapLayers.art: Celtiberian workshops fuse La Tène weapon aesthetics with Iberian ceramic and sculptural habits: painted pottery, warrior stelae, and distinctive fibulae. Hillforts (castros) and later Roman-facing oppida frame a meseta visual world of stone, iron, and horse gear. Coinage arrives as both art and political badge.
mapLayers.ideas: Indo-European Celtic speech inland meets non-IE Iberian coasts—identity is bilingual frontier politics. Tribal confederations resist and negotiate Carthaginian then Roman power. Hospitality, cattle wealth, and warrior reputation organize social capital before provincial law.
mapLayers.philosophy: No named schools. Funerary warrior imagery and sanctuary deposits imply ideals of courage and ancestral continuity. Later Roman writers project ethnography onto Celtiberians; native thought survives as practice, not treatise.
mapLayers.science: Iron weapon manufacture, highland pastoral scheduling, and castro masonry are regional technical strengths. Script contact (Iberian and later Latin) brings literacy to elites without displacing oral law overnight. Mining zones of the interior feed Mediterranean metal hunger.

mapLayers.label: Iberian (non-IE)
mapLayers.art: Iberian culture (Mediterranean east/south) produces the Lady of Elche’s limestone polychromy, sculpted warriors, painted geometric pottery, and sanctuary terracottas. Urbanising oppida and Greek/Punic coastal contact shape a visual language distinct from La Tène curves. Writing appears on lead plaques and ceramics—art and script intertwined.
mapLayers.ideas: Non-Indo-European Iberian languages mark a deep western European outlier beside Celtic and later Latin. City and sanctuary politics along the coast negotiate Greek Emporion, Carthaginian, and Roman pressure. Elite display uses southern Mediterranean templates without full Hellenisation.
mapLayers.philosophy: No philosophical corpus. Funerary sculpture and votive deposits imply personhood, divine patrons, and afterlife care. Cosmology is local and polytheistic, later syncretised under Rome—recoverable as cult practice, not dialectic.
mapLayers.science: Iberian script literacy, wheel-made finewares, silver metallurgy, and coastal navigation are applied sciences of a trading façade. Agricultural terraces and irrigation knowledge intensify under Mediterranean crop packages. Urban fortification adapts Hellenistic siege awareness.

mapLayers.label: Lusitanian zone
mapLayers.art: Northwestern Iberian castros combine circular stone houses, warrior statues, and Atlantic La Tène–influenced metalwork. Gold torcs and localized ceramics mark a hillfort aesthetic facing the ocean more than the meseta. Rock sanctuaries and inscribed dedications (later) braid indigenous and Roman forms.
mapLayers.ideas: Lusitanian and related western groups become famous in Roman war narratives for mobility and resistance (Viriathus in memory). Cattle, raid, and hillfort autonomy structure politics before provincial absorption. Atlantic exchange links Galicia–Portugal to wider Celtic material spheres without erasing local speech.
mapLayers.philosophy: Worldview inferred from warrior imagery, castro layout, and later Lusitanian theonyms under Roman epigraphy. No native philosophical literature; ethics of guerrilla honour appear only through enemy ethnography.
mapLayers.science: Castro masonry, goldworking, and Atlantic seafaring/fishing calendars are core knowledges. Mining and pastoral transhumance tune technology to rugged terrain. Military adaptation against Roman legions shows tactical learning recorded by opponents.

mapLayers.label: Jastorf
mapLayers.art: Jastorf cemeteries favour cremation urnfields with restrained grave goods—fibulae, pins, pottery—rather than Hallstatt princely theatre. Material culture looks northern and sober beside La Tène bling, though contact goods appear at the southern fringe. Dress archaeology, not monumental sculpture, carries style.
mapLayers.ideas: Often treated as the archaeological backdrop to early Germanic ethnolinguistic formation north of the Celtic world. Social ideas emphasise cemetery community and regional groups over oppida kingship. Southern contact with Hallstatt/La Tène zones is selective, not wholesale adoption.
mapLayers.philosophy: No texts. Cosmology is urnfield practice—fire, vessel, and cemetery continuity as statements about person and kin. Named gods appear only much later in Roman and medieval sources; for this horizon, avoid invented pantheons.
mapLayers.science: Ironworking spreads into northern Germany and Jutland with a chronological lag behind the south. Cremation pyrotechnology, ceramic temper recipes, and agrarian clearance of sandy soils are the measurable sciences. Amber and metal exchange keep northern routes in the European technical network.

mapLayers.label: Pre-Roman Iron Age Scandinavia
mapLayers.art: After Nordic Bronze Age splendour, early Iron Age Scandinavia looks quieter: simpler graves, bog offerings, and gradual iron tools. Weapon deposits and later richly furnished graves renew display; rock-art traditions fade as bronze razors and lurs exit the prestige economy. Textile and wooden craft dominate a forest–fjord aesthetic.
mapLayers.ideas: Communities recalibrate after bronze-network disruption—local iron and bog sacrifice replace some long-distance bronze politics. Clan and farmstead autonomy precede the later Roman Iron Age chieftains who trade south. Identity is regional Scandinavian, not yet ‘Viking.’
mapLayers.philosophy: Bog deposits of people, weapons, and animals imply sacred negotiation with waters and powers of place. No runic philosophy yet; worldview is sacrificial and seasonal. Later Norse myth must not be back-projected wholesale onto this horizon.
mapLayers.science: Bog-iron extraction, boatbuilding continuity, and cold-climate farming/herding are survival sciences. Dendro and pollen records show farmers managing forest regeneration and field systems. Knowledge of southern metal styles arrives through limited contact before Roman-period boom.

mapLayers.label: Etruscan
mapLayers.art: Etruscan art speaks in painted tombs (Tarquinia), terracotta temple sculpture, bronze mirrors engraved with myth, and gold granulation jewellery. Banqueting couples on sarcophagus lids and urban temple podia invent an Italian visual luxury that teaches early Rome. Bucchero pottery and engraved cistae export taste across the peninsula.
mapLayers.ideas: City-leagues, aristocratic clans, and haruspicy as statecraft organize Etruscan politics facing Greek Campania and rising Rome. Literacy in a non-IE language records names, gifts, and cult—not epic philosophy. Elite women appear with unusual public visibility in funerary art relative to later Roman norms.
mapLayers.philosophy: The disciplina Etrusca—divination from entrails, lightning, and prodigies—is a systematic sacred science later respected (and archived) by Romans. Ethical life is aristocratic and cultic rather than Socratic dialogue. Cosmology is readable in ritual books’ reputation, though few texts survive.
mapLayers.science: Hydraulic engineering, arch and podium architecture, mining (Elba iron), and surveying underwrite Etruscan cities. Medical and divinatory observation share a culture of reading signs in nature. Shipbuilding and Tyrrhenian trade make them technical peers of Greek colonists.

mapLayers.label: Latin / early Rome
mapLayers.art: Early Rome’s art is still Italic and Etruscan-leaning: terracotta temple sculpture, warrior gear, and emerging urban monumentalism on the Capitoline and Forum. Coinage and triumph imagery come later; the Republic’s early centuries prefer severe civic stone and borrowed Greek forms over a unique ‘Roman style.’ Dress and arms already broadcast citizen-soldier status.
mapLayers.ideas: Mos maiorum, consular collegiality (in tradition), and expansion through alliance and colony frame Republican political thought before philosophy schools arrive. Conflict with Etruscans, Samnites, and Gauls forges a militarised civic identity. Law and auspices bind politics to the gods.
mapLayers.philosophy: Named Greek-style philosophy is not yet Roman; intellectual life is priestly law, augury, and exemplary history. The Twelve Tables (mid-5th c. tradition) encode civic ethics as statute. Stoic and Epicurean import waits for the later Republic.
mapLayers.science: Road-building beginnings, centuriation instincts, military camp discipline, and borrowed Etruscan engineering are Rome’s early applied sciences. Calendar reform and pontifical timekeeping are sacred metrology. Agricultural writers come later; practice precedes literature.

mapLayers.label: Classical Greek poleis
mapLayers.art: Classical Greek poleis invent the visual canon Europe never forgets: marble temple architecture (Parthenon), contrapposto sculpture, red- and black-figure pottery, and theatre as civic art. Panhellenic sanctuaries (Olympia, Delphi) stage statues and treasuries as interstate competition. Dress, armour, and symposium ware make daily life an aesthetic system.
mapLayers.ideas: The polis—citizen body, assembly, and law—is the master political idea, with Athenian democracy, Spartan mixed constitution, and countless variants. Colonies from Massalia to the Black Sea export Hellenic urban form. Panhellenic identity coexists with ruthless interstate war.
mapLayers.philosophy: Historically grounded schools and thinkers: Presocratics (Ionian natural philosophy), Socrates, Plato’s Academy, Aristotle’s Lyceum, then Hellenistic Stoics, Epicureans, and Skeptics. Political theory (politeia), ethics, and metaphysics become teachable disciplines. Tragedy and historiography (Aeschylus, Herodotus, Thucydides) are parallel inquiries into justice and chance.
mapLayers.science: Euclidean geometry’s later codification rests on Classical mathematical practice; Hippocrates founds a medical tradition; Aristotle’s biology and mechanics organise observation. Astronomy (Eudoxus) and engineering (Archimedes in the early Hellenistic sequel) extend polis science. Surveying, ship design, and battlefield tactics are everyday technical literacy.

mapLayers.label: Thracian
mapLayers.art: Thracian elite art dazzles in gold and silver rhyta, parade greaves, and tomb paintings (Kazanlak, Sveshtari) that fuse local taste with Greek workshop skill. Warrior and horse imagery dominate; Orphic-adjacent mystery aesthetics later colour Greek imagination of Thrace. Fortified residences and mound burials mark kings more than classical agoras.
mapLayers.ideas: Kingdoms and tribal confederations (Odrysian power among them) mediate between Greek colonies and interior Europe. Royal gift economies and mercenary service in foreign armies export Thracian military reputation. Identity is aristocratic and regional under Greek ethnographic labels.
mapLayers.philosophy: Greeks associate Thrace with Orpheus and Dionysiac religion—mythic philosophy projected from outside. Native thought appears as royal cult, tomb cosmology, and later interpretatio under Macedonian and Roman rule, not as Academy-style schools.
mapLayers.science: Toreutics (metal vessel chasing), horsemanship, and mining in the Rhodope/Balkan zones are technical strengths. Greek colonial contact transmits coinage, writing for elites, and architectural forms. Military light-armed tactics become a Mediterranean export skill.

mapLayers.label: Illyrian
mapLayers.art: Illyrian coastal and hinterland elites display helmets, greaves, amber, and hillfort material culture under Adriatic Greek and Italian contact. Monumental art is thinner than in Greece; status rides on weapon burial, fibulae, and imported symposium gear. Later royal centres (before full Roman conquest) intensify Mediterranean display.
mapLayers.ideas: Tribal kingdoms and piracy narratives in Greek sources frame Illyrians as Adriatic rivals and partners. Political life is dynastic and maritime-facing, squeezed between Macedon, Rome, and Celtic movements. Belonging is regional and kin-based under a catch-all Greek ethnonym.
mapLayers.philosophy: No native philosophical literature. Cult and burial imply polytheistic practice later syncretised with Greek and Roman gods. Ethics of raid, alliance, and guest relations appear only through external historians.
mapLayers.science: Shipbuilding, coastal navigation, iron weapon craft, and hillfort engineering are core skills. Greek colonial neighbours transmit literacy and coin use selectively. Pastoral–agricultural scheduling in karst landscapes is local environmental science.

mapLayers.label: Scythian
mapLayers.art: Scythian animal-style gold—stags, panthers, swirling predators—defines steppe prestige art in kurgan burials from the Black Sea hinterland. Greek–Scythian workshops on the Bosporus blend Hellenic toreutics with nomad iconography (Kul-Oba and peers). Scale armour, akinakes swords, and horse gear are wearable sculpture.
mapLayers.ideas: Iranian-speaking nomad confederations dominate Pontic grasslands while trading grain and slaves with Greek poleis (Olbia and others). Royal tombs advertise mobile sovereignty; Herodotus’s ethnography, however filtered, makes them Europe’s first richly described steppe society. Political power is confederation and royal kindred, not city walls.
mapLayers.philosophy: Herodotus reports Scythian customs, oaths, and cult (including Ares-associated rites)—ethnography, not a Scythian philosophical school. Worldview centres on horse, bow, royal burial, and steppe mobility. Avoid treating Greek mythic projections as native doctrine.
mapLayers.science: Composite bow technology, horse breeding, kurgan engineering, and felt/leather craft are steppe sciences of high sophistication. Gold alloying and Greek collaborative workshops show selective urban technical adoption. Seasonal migration schedules encode ecological literacy across vast distances.

mapLayers.label: Sauromatian / early Sarmatian
mapLayers.art: Sauromatian and early Sarmatian horizons east of the Don carry animal-style metalwork, weapon graves, and—in some cemeteries—prominently equipped female burials that fed Greek Amazon stories. Portable prestige (horse gear, mirrors, jewellery) replaces sedentary monumental art. Styles foreshadow later Sarmatian polychrome taste.
mapLayers.ideas: Mobile pastoral politics on the steppe fringe negotiate with Scythians, Greeks, and forest-steppe neighbours. Gendered warrior ideals in burial (debated in detail) become a Greek ethnographic obsession. Identity is confederative and mobile.
mapLayers.philosophy: No texts. Kurgan ritual and weapon deposition sketch honour, ancestry, and perhaps gendered spiritual roles without recoverable theology. Cosmology is funerary and equine.
mapLayers.science: Mounted archery, wagon/tent logistics, and metalworking on the move are the technical core. Ecological management of grassland herds is the primary applied science. Southern trade brings selective Greek goods without urbanisation.

FRA.name: Gallic tribes (La Tène)
FRA.literature: Gaul’s learned men kept law and lore unwritten by principle, says Caesar — so we meet them through his war diary and Greek ethnography. Bardic praise and druidic cosmology are real institutions glimpsed in hostile paraphrase. The land later grows troubadours; their ancestors here still sing in the air only.
FRA.art: Gaulish La Tène art peaks in torcs, the Agris helmet, painted ceramics, and sanctuary heaps of ritually killed weapons. Oppida mint coin portraits that turn chiefs into miniature icons. Trousers, checked weaves, and gold neck-rings make the body the primary gallery.

FRA.religion: La Tène Gallic religion: polytheism later named by Romans (e.g. syncretized Mercury/Teutates types); rituals include sanctuary deposits, weapon offerings, and funerary feasting. Druids as learned ritual specialists in classical reports.
FRA.ideas: Tribal clientage, druidic oral law, and oppida markets organise Gaul before Caesar’s conquest narrative. Massalia’s long Greek presence on the coast supplies wine ideology and urban contrast. Pan-Gallic sacred sites and shared style create cultural unity without a single capital.
FRA.philosophy: Druidic teachings on the soul and cosmos appear in Caesar and Poseidonius—use as filtered report, not recovered scripture. Everyday ethics are hospitality, feud limit, and sanctuary. No Academy; memory specialists carry thought.
FRA.science: Iron agriculture, oppida craft zoning, coin metallurgy, and river transport are Gaul’s practical sciences. Calendrical and medical lore attributed to druids remains archaeologically mute but metallurgical chaînes opératoires do not.

GBR.name: British Iron Age tribes
GBR.conflicts: Tribal warfare; Belgic contacts; Rome imminent.
GBR.literature: Celts enter Greek and Roman ethnography (Poseidonius, Caesar) while keeping their own oral learned classes — druids, bards, vates. Epic and law live in memory; we overhear them through hostile or fascinated classical prose. Further east, steppe peoples appear in Herodotus’s glittering hearsay. Insular voices and North Sea contact give this place a distinctive accent in the wider European chorus.
GBR.art: Insular La Tène mirrors, scabbards, and torc hoards (Snettisham) define British Iron Age beauty. Hillfort skylines and roundhouse settlements are the architecture; chariot burials add eastern funerary flair. Art is metal and earthwork more than stone temple.

GBR.religion: British Iron Age: shrine deposits, bog/river offerings, chariot burials in the east, and hillfort ceremonial spaces. Local gods later equated with Roman deities after conquest.
GBR.ideas: Tribal territories negotiate alliance and raid without Roman towns. Continental style arrives without Beaker-scale population replacement. Later Roman conquest will overlay, not erase, this political geography.
GBR.philosophy: Watery deposits and shrine sites imply sacred landscape ethics. No named philosophers; cosmology is offering and kingship rite. Druidic presence is reported for Britain in Roman war propaganda—handle critically.
GBR.science: Hillfort engineering, salt and quern technology, and Channel/North Sea boats are core knowledges. Fine bronze sheet-work shows specialist smiths serving regional elites.

IRL.name: Irish Iron Age
IRL.literature: Celts enter Greek and Roman ethnography (Poseidonius, Caesar) while keeping their own oral learned classes — druids, bards, vates. Epic and law live in memory; we overhear them through hostile or fascinated classical prose. Further east, steppe peoples appear in Herodotus’s glittering hearsay. Irish monastic and later Gaelic learned traditions punch above demographic weight in Europe’s imagination.
IRL.art: Irish Iron Age display concentrates on fine metalwork, bog deposits, and ceremonial landscapes around royal sites (Tara, Emain Macha) more than dense hillfort carpets. La Tène curves arrive selectively; later Early Christian art will transform the same curvilinear inheritance. Gold and bronze speak louder than stone cities.

IRL.religion: Irish Iron Age ritual: royal sites (Tara, Emain), bog deposits, and later mythic cycles that must be used cautiously as Iron Age evidence. Sovereignty and otherworld themes dominate later texts.
IRL.ideas: Regional kingship and assembly places structure politics on an island outside Roman conquest. Cattle wealth and clientship (later law tracts remember related forms) organise power. Contact with Britain carries style and goods without imperial administration.
IRL.philosophy: Ritual deposition and royal-site ceremonial imply sacral kingship ideologies later echoed—and rewritten—in medieval literature. No contemporary philosophical texts; treat mythic cycles as distant mirrors, not Iron Age transcripts.
IRL.science: Bog-iron, fine metal casting, trackways across wetlands, and Atlantic seafaring are applied sciences. Agricultural mixed farming underwrites assembly feasts and craft specialists.

DEU.name: Jastorf / La Tène frontier
DEU.conflicts: Cultural frontier; later Roman wars in Germania.
DEU.literature: Celts enter Greek and Roman ethnography (Poseidonius, Caesar) while keeping their own oral learned classes — druids, bards, vates. Epic and law live in memory; we overhear them through hostile or fascinated classical prose. Further east, steppe peoples appear in Herodotus’s glittering hearsay. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.
DEU.art: German lands sit on a style frontier: southern zones show La Tène ornament and oppida edges; northern Jastorf urnfields keep restrained cremation aesthetics. Fibulae typologies and weapon sets map the cultural gradient better than any single ‘Germanic art.’ Contact goods from Celtic south appear as prestige accents.

DEU.religion: Jastorf / La Tène frontier: weapon and bog offerings, cremation cemeteries, and sacred enclosures. Germanic and Celtic ritual zones meet without a single pantheon list.
DEU.ideas: Ethnogenesis labels (Celtic vs early Germanic) are linguistic-cultural, not new deep ancestry components. Frontier exchange and selective adoption define belonging. Political units are regional groups, not empires.
DEU.philosophy: No schools. Southern sanctuary deposit habits and northern urnfield rites offer two ritual philosophies of death and offering. Named Germanic gods are later; do not invent Iron Age pantheons here.
DEU.science: Iron spreads north with a lag; Jastorf pyrotechnology and southern La Tène metallurgy form adjacent technical schools. Amber routes and river corridors are the information network.

ESP.name: Iberians & Celtiberians
ESP.conflicts: Iberian–Celtiberian rivalry; Carthaginian then Roman wars.
ESP.literature: Celts enter Greek and Roman ethnography (Poseidonius, Caesar) while keeping their own oral learned classes — druids, bards, vates. Epic and law live in memory; we overhear them through hostile or fascinated classical prose. Further east, steppe peoples appear in Herodotus’s glittering hearsay. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: Iberia’s Iron Age visual split is sharp: Mediterranean Iberian sculpture (Lady of Elche) and scripts versus inland Celtiberian warrior gear and La Tène-influenced weapons. Castro northwest adds circular stone settlements and warrior statues. Greek and Punic coastal art filter into indigenous workshops.

ESP.religion: Iberian & Celtiberian cults: sanctuaries, inscribed deity names in places, warrior/funerary stelae, and cave or high-place rites — local pantheons, not a uniform Celtic church.
ESP.ideas: Non-IE Iberian, Celtic, and Lusitanian zones make the peninsula a language mosaic. Urbanising coasts and meseta confederations face Carthage then Rome with different toolkits. Identity is plural—never a single ‘Spanish’ Iron Age culture.
ESP.philosophy: No named schools. Funerary sculpture, warrior stelae, and sanctuary votives encode honour and divine patronage. Later Roman syncretism overlays without documenting a prior philosophical literature.
ESP.science: Iberian literacy, silver mining, castro masonry, and Mediterranean navigation are regional sciences. Agricultural intensification on coast and plateau underwrites oppida and mercenary export.

ITA.name: Rome vs Etruscans / Samnites
ITA.conflicts: Roman expansion wars across the peninsula.
ITA.literature: Celts enter Greek and Roman ethnography (Poseidonius, Caesar) while keeping their own oral learned classes — druids, bards, vates. Epic and law live in memory; we overhear them through hostile or fascinated classical prose. Further east, steppe peoples appear in Herodotus’s glittering hearsay. Italian cities teach prestige: from Roman monumentality to Renaissance brand management of beauty.
ITA.art: Italy’s Iron Age gallery is multi-ethnic: Etruscan painted tombs and temple terracottas, Latin civic beginnings, Greek colonial temples in Magna Graecia, and Italic warrior belts. Banquet and symposium imagery teach Rome how elites should look. Early Republican severity still leans on Etruscan and Greek forms.

ITA.religion: Rome vs Etruscans/Samnites: Roman state cult (Jupiter, Mars, Vesta) with augury and sacrifice; Etruscan haruspicy and tomb ritual; Italian peoples keep distinct sanctuary traditions.
ITA.ideas: Competition among Etruscan cities, Latin communities, Samnite highland leagues, and Greek colonies invents Italian geopolitics. Rome’s alliance-and-colony method emerges from this cage match. Citizenship and treaty law become weapons as sharp as swords.
ITA.philosophy: Etruscan disciplina (divination) and Greek colonial philosophy (Eleatics in the south; Pythagorean traditions in Magna Graecia) are the grounded intellectual streams. Early Rome contributes priestly law and exempla, not yet Lucretius or Cicero.
ITA.science: Etruscan hydraulics and arches, Greek colonial geometry and medicine, and Roman military road instincts coexist. Mining, surveying, and shipbuilding make the peninsula a technical crossroads.

GRC.name: Greek poleis
GRC.conflicts: Persian Wars; Peloponnesian War; Macedonian rise.
GRC.literature: Celts enter Greek and Roman ethnography (Poseidonius, Caesar) while keeping their own oral learned classes — druids, bards, vates. Epic and law live in memory; we overhear them through hostile or fascinated classical prose. Further east, steppe peoples appear in Herodotus’s glittering hearsay. Greek language and forms remain a reusable antiquity — quarried by every later age for prestige.
GRC.art: Classical Greece: Parthenon Doric perfection, Polykleitos’s canon of proportion, vase painting’s narrative intelligence, and theatre festivals as mass art. Sanctuary dedications turn bronze and marble into interstate soft power. Everyday kylixes make philosophy’s symposium setting a designed object.

GRC.religion: Greek poleis: Olympian pantheon, civic temples, blood sacrifice, festivals (Panathenaia, Dionysia), oracles, and mystery cults (Eleusis). Religion is public liturgy as much as private piety.
GRC.ideas: Citizenship, law, and contested constitutions are the political software of the polis. Colonisation and Persian Wars forge Panhellenic self-consciousness beside lethal rivalry. Rhetoric becomes a teachable civic technology.
GRC.philosophy: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle; Presocratic nature philosophy; then Stoa, Garden, and Academy traditions. This is the one Iron Age European zone where ‘philosophy’ is an emic institutional word. Ethical and political argument become portable exports.
GRC.science: Hippocratic medicine, mathematical proof culture, Aristotelian biology, and astronomical modelling. Engineering and navigation support naval empires. Science and philosophy are often one conversation.

BGR.name: Thracian kingdoms
BGR.conflicts: Conflict with Macedon, Greeks, later Rome.
BGR.literature: Celts enter Greek and Roman ethnography (Poseidonius, Caesar) while keeping their own oral learned classes — druids, bards, vates. Epic and law live in memory; we overhear them through hostile or fascinated classical prose. Further east, steppe peoples appear in Herodotus’s glittering hearsay. Bulgarian letters pioneer Slavic Christian literacy — a soft empire of books south of the Danube.
BGR.art: Thracian gold rhyta, tomb frescoes, and parade armour stage kings between Greek naturalism and local animal-ornament taste. Burial mounds are the museums. Greek colonial pottery and coins circulate as prestige accents inland.

BGR.religion: Thracian kingdoms: royal burials with rich grave goods, rock sanctuaries, and later Greek reports of Zalmoxis/immortality ideas — elite funerary religion at the core.
BGR.ideas: Odrysian and peer kingdoms mediate Greek coastal trade and interior tribal power. Mercenary service abroad exports Thracian military identity. Kingship and gift are the political ideas, not citizen assemblies.
BGR.philosophy: Orphic and Dionysiac associations are largely Greek projections onto Thrace. Native intellectual life is royal cult and tomb cosmology—no Academy. Later Hellenistic and Roman rule add interpretatio without recovering earlier treatises.
BGR.science: Metal toreutics, horsemanship, and mining are Thracian technical signatures. Greek contact brings literacy for some elites and architectural models for residences.

UKR.name: Scythian nomads
UKR.conflicts: Raids and alliances with Greek colonies; Sarmatian pressure.
UKR.literature: Celts enter Greek and Roman ethnography (Poseidonius, Caesar) while keeping their own oral learned classes — druids, bards, vates. Epic and law live in memory; we overhear them through hostile or fascinated classical prose. Further east, steppe peoples appear in Herodotus’s glittering hearsay. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: Pontic Scythian kurgans yield animal-style gold, Greek collaborative vessels, and horse gear that define steppe prestige aesthetics. Scale armour and akinakes swords are art you wear to ride. Settled Greek coasts supply a contrasting marble-and-pottery visual world at the edge.

UKR.religion: Scythian nomads: kurgan elites, horse sacrifice, cannabis/vapor rites in Herodotus, and golden ritual gear. Ancestor and sky/animal cult inferred from graves and art.
UKR.ideas: Nomad royal confederations control grain hinterlands feeding Greek poleis—symbiosis and tension. Herodotus makes Scythians thinkable to Europe; archaeology corrects his marvels without erasing mobile sovereignty. Political ideas travel with the horse, not the agora.
UKR.philosophy: Custom, oath, and royal burial rite—not school philosophy. Herodotus’s reports are ethnographic philosophy-of-the-other. Treat kurgan cosmology as practice: weapons, horses, and precious metal for the dead.
UKR.science: Composite bows, horse breeding, kurgan construction, and seasonal steppe logistics. Greek workshop collaboration advances goldsmithing without sedentarising the elite core.

AUT.name: Hallstatt / early La Tène elites
AUT.conflicts: Trade and rivalry across Celtic Europe.
AUT.literature: Celts enter Greek and Roman ethnography (Poseidonius, Caesar) while keeping their own oral learned classes — druids, bards, vates. Epic and law live in memory; we overhear them through hostile or fascinated classical prose. Further east, steppe peoples appear in Herodotus’s glittering hearsay. Habsburg capitals stage empire as opera — multilingual, ceremonial, slightly melancholic.
AUT.art: Hallstatt’s salt-zone cemeteries and eastern Alpine tumuli invent early Iron Age elite display: swords, wagons, bronze vessels, and textile preservation unique to the mines. Early La Tène then overlays Dürrnberg-style flagons and new art on the same corridors. Situla art narrates feast and contest in embossed bronze.

AUT.religion: Hallstatt / early La Tène elites: princely graves, banqueting ritual, and sanctuary deposits in the Alpine foreland — status afterlife and feasting ideology.
AUT.ideas: Salt, pass control, and Mediterranean imports make the eastern Alps a hinge of European prestige economies. Princely burial advertises ranked society before La Tène reorganises warrior networks. ‘Celtic’ labels here are archaeological-linguistic shorthand, not a passport ethnicity.
AUT.philosophy: Feasting ideology and ancestor tumuli carry worldview. No named philosophers in the Hallstatt core—cosmology is grave and banquet. Later Celtic learned classes are better attested farther west in Classical ethnography.
AUT.science: Salt-mining engineering at Hallstatt is flagship European industrial science of the age. Iron adoption, wagon technology, and alpine route logistics complete the toolkit.

periods.label: Classical / Roman Republic–early Empire
periods.narrative: Rome conquers the Mediterranean and much of Western Europe (Republic into early Principate). Greek remains the eastern prestige language; Celtic and Germanic societies press the frontiers. Empires redraw politics and urban demography faster than they erase provincial BA ancestry — though Imperial Rome itself shows a clear eastern Mediterranean genetic pulse (Antonio et al. 2019).
periods.culturesNote: Roman Empire (west/east), residual Gallic tribes, Britannia, Germanic societies beyond the limes, Sarmatians, Greek East.

iberia.description: Rome organizes Iberia into provinces after centuries of conquest. Urbanism, law, and Latin spread over Iberian, Celtic, and Basque-line populations. Genetic change is mainly Mediterranean urban admixture into a durable local BA/IA substrate — absorption/romanization, not settler replacement of the whole peninsula.
iberia.ancestryNote: Local IA continuity + urban Mediterranean gene flow; no precise single “Roman %.”
iberia.linguisticNote: Latin → Hispano-Romance; Basque survives Romanization — key non-IE continuity.

britain.description: Claudian conquest (43 CE) creates a frontier province. Towns, army, and administration are cosmopolitan; rural majority remains Brittonic-speaking longer. Genetically, rural continuity with Iron Age Britain dominates until early medieval North Sea migrations — Roman rule ≠ Italian settler replacement.
britain.languages: Brittonic; Latin in army, towns, inscriptions
britain.linguisticNote: Bilingual province; Latin does not fully replace Celtic as in Gaul.
britain.ancestryNote: Mostly IA British ternary; military/urban samples can look more cosmopolitan.

france.description: From Caesar to the Principate, Gaul becomes Roman provinces. Intensive cultural Latinization produces Gallo-Romance. Demographically an absorption pattern: Roman institutions and settlers mix into a Celtic IA majority rather than erasing it genetically.
france.languages: Vulgar Latin (spreading); residual Gaulish; Greek in ports
france.linguisticNote: One of history’s clearest elite/administrative language shifts ending in Romance.
france.ancestryNote: Gallic IA substrate + Mediterranean/Roman mobility; not a blank-slate colony.

central.description: Roman provinces south of the Danube/Rhine face Germanic societies beyond. The frontier is military, commercial, and bilingual. Ancestry on both sides continues Iron Age profiles with army mobility — “Roman” and “Germanic” are political-linguistic identities on shared deep BA foundations.
central.languages: Latin; early Germanic dialects; residual Celtic in places
central.linguisticNote: Limes as a language frontier, not a genetic species boundary.
central.ancestryNote: IA continuity; castra towns enrich Mediterranean links.

scandinavia.description: Outside the Empire but tied by trade: Roman goods in elite graves, political awareness of the south. Ancestry continuous with Nordic Iron Age; linguistically early North Germanic.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Early North Germanic continuum outside the Empire; Proto-Norse runes follow in the later Roman Iron Age / Migration Period.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Local continuity; exotic grave goods ≠ mass Roman migration.

italy.description: Italy as imperial core. Antonio et al. (2019): Rome’s Imperial-period populations show elevated eastern Mediterranean / Near Eastern–related ancestry versus Iron Age — a real urban demographic pull — with later medieval samples shifting westward again. Rural Italy remains more local.
italy.ancestryNote: Urban imperial “other” can reach tens of percent; not uniform across the peninsula.
italy.linguisticNote: Latin standard of empire; Greek prestige in the East and among elites.

balkans.description: Heavily provincialized Balkans and Greek-speaking East under Rome. Latin in the military/Danube provinces; Greek dominates the Aegean cultural sphere. Ancestry = BA Balkan/Aegean base + imperial Mediterranean mobility.
balkans.linguisticNote: Foundation of later Byzantine Greek continuity in the south.
balkans.ancestryNote: Elevated eastern Med/imperial admixture in cities vs hinterlands.

eastern.description: Iranian-speaking Sarmatian confederations on the steppe; Greek cities and Roman clients on the Black Sea littoral. Steppe ancestry with eastern admixture persists. Rome touches the edge; it does not Romanize the open steppe.
eastern.linguisticNote: Multilingual Pontic rim; Iranian nomads ≠ Slavic yet.
eastern.ancestryNote: Steppe + East Eurasian variable; coastal towns more Mediterranean.

periods.linguistics: Latin and Greek dominate administration and literature. Vulgar Latin begins Romance. Celtic and Germanic persist outside/at edges; Basque/Aquitanian survives; Iranian on the steppe; bilingualism is normal in cities.

mapLayers.label: Italia
mapLayers.art: Imperial Italy sets the template: Augustan marble ideology (Prima Porta), Pompeian frescoes and mosaic floors, concrete architecture (dome, vault, bath). Portrait realism and historical relief (Ara Pacis) make politics visible. Legionary kit—lorica, scutum, gladius—becomes modular military design.
mapLayers.ideas: Citizenship expansion, legal culture, and the Principate’s restoration rhetoric reorganise Italian belonging after civil war. Latin literature (Virgil, Livy, Ovid, Horace) scripts imperial destiny and private desire. Urban patronage and collegia structure daily civic life.
mapLayers.philosophy: Grounded schools in Italy: Ciceronian Academic skepticism and political philosophy; Lucretius’s Epicurean physics-poem; Roman Stoicism (later Seneca, Musonius; roots in mid-Republic imports). Philosophy is moral training for elites under empire as much as metaphysics.
mapLayers.science: Vitruvius on architecture; Roman surveying (gromatici), aqueduct hydraulics, road metrology, and military medicine. Agricultural writers (Varro, Columella soon after) systematise farming. Concrete chemistry and crane logistics are world-class engineering.

mapLayers.label: Gallia
mapLayers.art: Gallo-Roman art mixes classical temples, theatres, and mosaics with Celtic decorative survival in bronze and stone. Imperial cult centres (Lugdunum) and urban fora broadcast Roman style; rural sanctuaries keep hybrid gods. Dress codes mark citizen toga against trousered ‘barbarian’ memory.
mapLayers.ideas: Latinisation and city status (colonia, municipium) remake Gallic elites as Roman provincials. Interpretatio Romana renames Celtic gods without always erasing them. Road and river fisc knit Gaul into Italian markets.
mapLayers.philosophy: Elite education imports Greek and Latin rhetoric and Stoic/academic moral philosophy through schools in cities like Massalia and Lugdunum. Native druidic intellectual life is suppressed or marginalised under Roman policy (reported bans). Thought becomes Greco-Roman curriculum plus local cult practice.
mapLayers.science: Cadastre, road building, viticulture intensification, and urban water systems transplant Italian engineering. Medical and surveying knowledge travels with army and administrators. Pottery industrialisation (samian/terra sigillata spheres) is applied materials science.

mapLayers.label: Hispania
mapLayers.art: Hispania’s Roman art includes theatre and amphitheatre programmes, imperial sculpture, mosaics, and lingering Iberian votive habits in rural shrines. Emerita Augusta and Tarraco stage provincial capitals as mini-Romes. Military and mining landscapes add utilitarian aesthetics of empire.
mapLayers.ideas: Provincial integration after centuries of conquest produces early emperors of Spanish origin in the next century’s horizon and a dense Latin municipal culture. Iberian and Celtic languages retreat under Latin prestige while Basque-line speech survives in the north. Civic ambition is measured in charters and monuments.
mapLayers.philosophy: Seneca the Younger (Corduba origin) is the grounded philosophical celebrity linking Hispania to Roman Stoicism—ethics of inner freedom under autocracy. Provincial elites consume Greek-Latin moral philosophy; rural cult keeps older sacred logics.
mapLayers.science: Silver and other mining (notably Iberian ranges) drive imperial metal science and forced labour logistics. Aqueducts (Segovia’s later fame sits in a long hydraulic tradition), roads, and garum production show applied chemistry and engineering. Army medics and land surveyors are the everyday scientists.

mapLayers.label: Britannia
mapLayers.art: Britannia’s Roman art is frontier-provincial: mosaic floors, bath suites, military diplomas, Mithraea reliefs, and hybrid deities (Sulis Minerva at Bath). Town houses and forts import Mediterranean visual grammar into timber-and-stone hybrids. Native metalwork traditions persist at the edges.
mapLayers.ideas: Client kings, then provincial government after AD 43, overlay tribal geography with roads and civitas capitals. Romanitas is urban and military; rural Brittonic life continues. Hadrian’s Wall (early 2nd c. sequel to this era’s conquest) later fossilises the frontier idea already born under the Julio-Claudians and Flavians.
mapLayers.philosophy: No British philosophical school. Intellectual life is army religion, imperial cult, and sparse literate administration. Syncretic shrine theology—local goddess plus Minerva—carries worldview more than Stoic lecture halls.
mapLayers.science: Military engineering (forts, roads, bridges), lead/silver mining, and hypocaust heating are flagship technologies. Medical kits from forts show practical army medicine. Agricultural villas experiment with Mediterranean crops at climate’s edge.

mapLayers.label: Germania Superior / Raetia etc.
mapLayers.art: Upper German and Raetian provinces display fort architecture, Jupiter columns, Mithraic reliefs, and inscribed altars along the limes. Art is military-civic: parade armour, tombstones of auxiliaries, and small classical temples. Beyond the Rhine, different visual rules apply.
mapLayers.ideas: Frontier provinces exist to tax, recruit, and buffer. Roman law towns face Germanic societies practising different kinship and feud logics. Diplomatic gifts and hostage education (Arminius’s background) are tools of soft conquest that can reverse.
mapLayers.philosophy: Camp religion and imperial cult dominate; philosophical schools are rare on the limes. Ethical life for soldiers is oath (sacramentum), unit loyalty, and mystery initiations (Mithras). Native cosmologies continue outside the forts.
mapLayers.science: Limes surveying, fort standardisation, Rhine bridge logistics, and alpine road engineering (Raetia) are applied sciences of occupation. Metallurgy and supply-chain granaries keep armies alive—logistics as science.

mapLayers.label: Moesia / Thracia / Illyricum
mapLayers.art: Danubian and Balkan provinces mix legionary tombstones, Thracian rider reliefs, Greek coastal marble, and imperial cult temples. Military diplomas and Mithraea mark army taste; local tumulus habits linger. Goldworking memory from Thracian elites feeds hybrid prestige arts.
mapLayers.ideas: Strategic provinces guard the Danube against Sarmatians and later pressures while supplying soldiers to the wider empire. Urbanisation is uneven—Greek cities and new coloniae beside tribal residuals. Latin and Greek administrative zones meet here.
mapLayers.philosophy: Greek philosophical culture persists in coastal cities; inland cult (Thracian rider, local theonyms) carries non-school worldview. Army mystery religions add initiatory ethics. No single Balkan school—plural sacred logics under empire.
mapLayers.science: Danube fleet logistics, mining, road cuts through mountains, and fort medicine. Greek technical literacy on the coasts meets Latin military engineering inland.

mapLayers.label: Achaea / Macedonia
mapLayers.art: Roman Greece lives among Classical masterpieces: temples reused, statues collected for Italian villas, Hadrianic philhellenic building still ahead but Republican/early Imperial elites already treat Greece as museum and school. Local production continues in sculpture workshops and ceramic industries. Architecture layers Roman odeia onto Greek theatres.
mapLayers.ideas: Greece under Rome keeps cultural prestige while losing geopolitical autonomy after 146 BC. Second Sophistic roots and pilgrimage to old sanctuaries redefine Hellenic identity as paideia. Macedonian and Achaean landscapes become provinces and memory stages.
mapLayers.philosophy: Athens remains a philosophy brand: Academy, Lyceum remnants, Stoic and Epicurean teaching continue under Roman patronage. Plutarch (slightly later) exemplifies Greek moral essay under empire. Roman students come to Greece for credentials.
mapLayers.science: Mathematical and medical traditions continue in Greek; libraries and teachers transmit Hellenistic science to Roman elites. Engineering projects are often Roman-funded on Greek soil. Astronomy and geography still speak Greek as their prestige tongue.

mapLayers.label: Asia Minor (Roman)
mapLayers.art: Roman Asia Minor dazzles with marble cities—Ephesus, Pergamon’s afterlife, Aphrodisias sculpture schools—fusing Hellenistic baroque with imperial cult temples. Theatre façades, baths, and stoas make urban theatre of stone. Portraiture and myth sarcophagi export polish westward.
mapLayers.ideas: The province of Asia is a fiscal jewel and cultural broker between Italy and the Near East. Greek civic life under Roman law produces benefactors, festivals, and koina. Early Christian communities emerge in this denser urban fabric within the wider 1st-century horizon.
mapLayers.philosophy: Hellenistic schools thrive: Stoic and Academic teachers, Second Sophistic rhetoric, and Jewish–Greek philosophical crossings (Philo’s Alexandria is nearby in the same eastern intellectual sea). City elites fund chairs and declamation. Thought is Greek-speaking under Roman peace.
mapLayers.science: Hellenistic mathematical and medical inheritance (Galen’s Pergamene origin slightly later) sits in Asian cities. Aqueducts, harbours, and road links show Roman engineering funding Greek urban science. Astronomy and geography continue Alexandrian-style scholarly traditions regionally.

mapLayers.label: Dacia
mapLayers.art: In the Classical atlas window Dacia is still largely outside lasting Roman provincial art; Trajanic conquest (early 2nd c.) lies just after. Pre-conquest Dacian metalwork, fortresses (Sarmizegetusa system), and figurative gold speak an inland mountain aesthetic. Roman propaganda will later invent the visual conquest on Trajan’s Column.
mapLayers.ideas: Dacian kingship under Burebista and Decebalus (flanking this era) organises a formidable Carpathian polity facing Rome across the Danube. Gold and military threat make Dacia an imperial obsession. Tribal-religious structures (including exclusive sacred centres reported by ancients) stiffen resistance identity.
mapLayers.philosophy: Ancient authors credit Dacian/Getae circles with Zalmoxis teachings on immortality—Greek-mediated and debated, but the rare named spiritual figure tied to this zone. Treat as ethnographic theology, not a reconstructed Academy. Ethics of fortress loyalty and sacred mountain centre dominate.
mapLayers.science: Mountain fortress architecture, gold mining knowledge, and iron weapon production are Dacian technical strengths. Agricultural storage and highland logistics support armies. Roman siege science will later meet these fortresses as engineering adversaries.

mapLayers.label: Magna Germania
mapLayers.art: Beyond the Rhine, art is weapon burial, fibulae, bog offerings, and selective Roman import bling—not fora and marble. Elite graves with Roman silver (Hoby cups farther north) show taste for southern drinking theatre. Visual identity is portable and martial.
mapLayers.ideas: Tacitus’s later Germania freezes an ethnographic mirror: freedom, feud, and assembly versus Roman luxury. Post-Teutoburg (AD 9), Rome largely manages the Rhine as limit rather than province. Tribal politics and confederation remain the software of power.
mapLayers.philosophy: No philosophical schools. Sacred groves, sacrifice, and oath (as Romans report) structure cosmology—filtered ethnography. Arminius’s revolt implies a political ethic of autonomy against provincial taxation, not a treatise.
mapLayers.science: Iron weapon smithing, forest-marsh warfare tactics, and agrarian clearances are local sciences. Roman imports teach Mediterranean drinking and weighing without installing aqueduct culture. Knowledge of Roman army habits (via auxiliaries) becomes counter-intelligence.

mapLayers.label: Roman Iron Age Scandinavia
mapLayers.art: Roman Iron Age Scandinavia brightens after the quieter Pre-Roman centuries: richly furnished graves, Roman glass and bronze imports, weapon offerings, and renewed elite display. Gold and silver from southern contact become northern prestige art. Ship and horse gear keep a maritime-warrior aesthetic.
mapLayers.ideas: Chieftains mediate Roman-world goods into northern prestige hierarchies without conquest. Status is feast, gift, and weapon burial—not citizenship. Networks across the Baltic and North Sea anticipate later Germanic political flowering.
mapLayers.philosophy: Bog and weapon deposits continue a sacrificial worldview. No runic philosophy corpus yet (early runes begin to appear on the wider early-century horizon). Cosmology remains oral and place-based; later Eddic systems are not to be back-read wholesale.
mapLayers.science: Boatbuilding, bog-iron, and selective adoption of Roman metal/glass technologies. Agricultural expansion in warmer Roman-period climates (as pollen studies often show) underwrites elites. Long-distance trade literacy matters more than Latin book learning.

mapLayers.label: Hibernia (unconquered)
mapLayers.art: Unconquered Ireland keeps Iron Age metalwork trajectories and ceremonial landscapes without Roman urban art. La Tène-derived ornament and bog deposits continue; Roman objects arrive as rarities through trade, not legions. Visual politics stay royal-site and portable.
mapLayers.ideas: Outside the Empire by choice and logistics, Hibernia becomes Rome’s ethnographic edge (Tacitus notes Agricola’s glance). Indigenous kingship and clientship develop without coloniae. Later Christian conversion will be the real institutional revolution—still ahead.
mapLayers.philosophy: Sacral kingship and deposit ritual—not Roman philosophy schools. No Hibernian Plato; worldview is local, oral, and landscape-bound. Druidic intellectual roles are reported from Britain/Gaul; Irish evidence for this exact century is archaeological inference.
mapLayers.science: Atlantic seafaring, mixed farming, and fine metal casting continue. Absence of Roman roads means indigenous trackway and coastal logistics remain the transport science. Technological change is incremental, not imperial.

mapLayers.label: Sarmatian
mapLayers.art: Sarmatian polychrome gold, tamga signs, long swords, and horse gear define steppe prestige north of the Black Sea in the early Imperial centuries. Greek and Roman imports appear in elite graves as drinking and display kits. Art is mobile heraldry for confederations facing the Danube limes.
mapLayers.ideas: Sarmatian groups (Iazyges, Roxolani, and peers in Roman sources) pressure and bargain with Moesia and Dacia frontiers. Alliance, raid, and settlement deals are the diplomacy of the steppe edge. Identity is Iranian-speaking nomad aristocracy over mixed followers.
mapLayers.philosophy: No school texts. Kurgan and weapon rites continue steppe funerary cosmology. Roman historians supply ethnography; native ethics centre on horse, oath, and confederation loyalty.
mapLayers.science: Cataphract-style heavy cavalry experiments, bow technology, and wagon logistics. Ecological management of Pontic grasslands remains the base science. Frontier trade teaches Roman weights and coins selectively.

ITA.name: Roman Italy / early Empire
ITA.summary: Imperial core under Augustus and successors.
ITA.conflicts: Civil wars behind; frontier wars in Germania, Balkans, East.
ITA.literature: Rome’s voice: Virgil’s imperial nostalgia, Ovid’s metamorphoses, Catullus’s insults, Livy’s moral republic. Latin becomes the software of European memory for fifteen centuries. In the streets, Oscan and Greek still murmur — empire is multilingual under the toga’s brand.
ITA.art: Augustan classicism, Pompeian interiors, historical relief, and concrete monumentalism make Italy the empire’s style capital. Elite villas curate Greek art; streets stage imperial portraits. Military equipment design is standardised beauty.

ITA.religion: Roman civic polytheism: Jupiter–Juno–Minerva and household Lares/Penates; blood sacrifice, augury, and calendrical festivals. Rising imperial cult, plus mystery religions (Isis, Mithras) in the army and cities.
ITA.ideas: Principate ideology—restoration, peace, father of the country—repackages monarchy as republican continuity. Law, citizenship, and Latin letters organise Italian and imperial belonging. Patronage networks are the real constitution.
ITA.philosophy: Cicero’s philosophical dialogues; Lucretius’s De rerum natura; Roman Stoic moralism rising toward Seneca. Greek teachers in Italian households make philosophy a status education. Politics and ethics remain entangled.
ITA.science: Vitruvius, aqueduct commissioners, gromatic surveyors, and military engineers. Medical practice mixes Greek professionals with Roman household knowledge. Italy exports technical standards with the legions.

FRA.name: Roman Gaul
FRA.conflicts: Pacification of tribes; later limes pressure from Germanic groups.
FRA.literature: Full literary blaze: Greek epic and drama already classic; Latin poetry and history rising (Virgil, Livy, Cicero). In the provinces, local languages persist under Latin/Greek prestige. This is the first period where clickable states can quote real verses, not only artifacts. French courts and vernaculars repeatedly set continental fashions of word and dress.
FRA.art: Theatres, amphitheatres, mosaic houses, and Gallo-Roman temple forms (fanum hybrids) romanise the landscape. Local bronze workshops keep Celtic hands inside classical commissions. Imperial cult sculpture anchors city centres.

FRA.religion: Roman Gaul: interpretatio Romana of Celtic gods, imperial cult centers (Lugdunum), and Gallo-Roman temples. Native deposition rites continue beside Roman sacrifice and priesthoods.
FRA.ideas: From Caesar’s conquest to the early Empire, Gaul becomes the model of provincial Latinisation. Elite careers run through Roman offices; tribal names become civitas brands. Roads and rivers rewrite economic geography.
FRA.philosophy: City schools teach rhetoric and imported moral philosophy; druidic public roles fade under Roman suspicion. Syncretic cult theology does everyday metaphysical work. Massalia’s Greek intellectual residue still matters on the coast.
FRA.science: Cadastre, viticulture science, road engineering, and ceramic industries. Army and city doctors carry Greek-Roman medicine inland. Water management remakes oppida landscapes into municipia.

ESP.name: Roman Hispania
ESP.conflicts: Cantabrian wars earlier; integration into empire.
ESP.literature: Full literary blaze: Greek epic and drama already classic; Latin poetry and history rising (Virgil, Livy, Cicero). In the provinces, local languages persist under Latin/Greek prestige. This is the first period where clickable states can quote real verses, not only artifacts. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: Provincial capitals raise theatres, walls, and imperial statues; mosaics floor elite houses; rural sanctuaries keep Iberian votive accents. Mining districts produce a harsher visual world of camps and shafts. Hispania learns to look Roman in marble and brick.

ESP.religion: Roman Hispania: imperial and civic cults, Iberian/Celtiberian survivals in rural sanctuaries, and mystery cults in towns. Sacrifice, vows (ex-votos), and emperor worship structure public religion.
ESP.ideas: Municipal competition and early full provincial integration create dense Latin civic culture. Linguistic shift toward Latin reshapes Iberia while Basque-line speech holds in the north. Veterans and coloniae seed Italian legal habits.
ESP.philosophy: Seneca of Corduba is the emblematic Stoic voice with Hispanic roots—virtue under Nero as philosophical drama. Broader elites share Mediterranean school philosophy; countryside keeps cult practice as wisdom.
ESP.science: Mining metallurgy and labour organisation; aqueducts and bridges; garum and oil agro-industry. Surveyors and army engineers are the province’s technical class.

GBR.name: Roman Britannia
GBR.conflicts: Conquest of tribes; Caledonian resistance; Irish unconquered.
GBR.literature: Full literary blaze: Greek epic and drama already classic; Latin poetry and history rising (Virgil, Livy, Cicero). In the provinces, local languages persist under Latin/Greek prestige. This is the first period where clickable states can quote real verses, not only artifacts. Insular voices and North Sea contact give this place a distinctive accent in the wider European chorus.
GBR.art: Fortress towns, bathhouses, mosaics, and syncretic cult reliefs (Sulis Minerva; Mithras) define Romano-British art. Native fine metalwork continues beyond the soft frontier. Visual romanitas is strongest along roads and in the south/east.

GBR.religion: Roman Britannia: classical temples and imperial cult in towns; Mithraea on the frontier; local deities syncretized (e.g. Sulis Minerva). Rural shrines and votive deposits persist.
GBR.ideas: Claudian conquest installs provincehood; resistance (later Boudica) and cooperation both shape settlement. Tribal civitates become administrative units. Roman identity is layered onto Brittonic substrates, not a settler replacement of the countryside.
GBR.philosophy: Philosophical schools are virtually absent; army oaths, imperial cult, and local-shrine syncretism carry values. Literate administration is thin but real. Wisdom is practical and cultic.
GBR.science: Military engineering dominates: forts, roads, lead mines, hypocausts. Agricultural villas test Mediterranean techniques. Craft glass and pottery industries follow the army.

DEU.name: Roman frontier / Magna Germania
DEU.literature: Full literary blaze: Greek epic and drama already classic; Latin poetry and history rising (Virgil, Livy, Cicero). In the provinces, local languages persist under Latin/Greek prestige. This is the first period where clickable states can quote real verses, not only artifacts. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.
DEU.art: On the Roman bank: limes forts, Jupiter columns, tombstones; beyond: weapon graves and import drinking sets. Teutoburg’s aftermath freezes a split aesthetic—province versus free Germania. Art advertises which side of the Rhine you drink on.

DEU.religion: Limes religion: Roman camps host Jupiter, standards-cult, and Mithras; Magna Germania beyond the Rhine keeps Germanic votive and funerary rites outside imperial liturgy.
DEU.ideas: AD 9 teaches Rome the cost of hasty provincialisation. Diplomacy, trade, and punitive raids replace annexation east of the Rhine. Germanic group politics evolve in the empire’s shadow.
DEU.philosophy: Roman camps import mystery ethics (Mithras) and imperial theology; Magna Germania keeps grove-and-oath cosmology per ethnographers. No local philosophical university—two ritual systems face each other across a river.
DEU.science: Roman surveying and fort modules versus Germanic iron smithing and terrain warfare. Bridgeheads and fleets on the Rhine are laboratories of military science.

GRC.name: Roman Greece
GRC.literature: Homer already antique; tragedy and philosophy still the curriculum of being Greek under Rome. Plutarch teaches parallel lives; Pausanias walks sanctuaries into prose. The eastern Mediterranean is a library with a navy.
GRC.art: Living among Classical monuments, Greeks under Rome still carve, build odeia, and sell heritage. Roman collectors empty sanctuaries even as philhellenic emperors later restore them. Art is memory industry plus local workshop continuity.

GRC.religion: Roman Greece: classical temples and festivals continue under Roman rule; imperial cult joins civic polytheism. Philosophical schools debate gods while sacrifice still defines public piety.
GRC.ideas: Paideia replaces power: being Greek becomes education and language under Roman rule. Cities compete for imperial favour and tourist-pilgrim traffic. Macedonian and Achaean pasts are curated narratives.
GRC.philosophy: Athens remains the classroom of the Mediterranean—Platonic, Aristotelian, Stoic, Epicurean teaching lines continue. Greek philosophy is now an imperial commodity. Moral essay and rhetoric overshadow new metaphysical revolutions.
GRC.science: Greek mathematical and medical literacy still set the curriculum Romans study. Local engineering serves Roman patronage. Libraries and teachers are the infrastructure of science.

TUR.name: Roman Asia Minor
TUR.literature: Full literary blaze: Greek epic and drama already classic; Latin poetry and history rising (Virgil, Livy, Cicero). In the provinces, local languages persist under Latin/Greek prestige. This is the first period where clickable states can quote real verses, not only artifacts. Ottoman and Anatolian layers make this edge of the map a second classical continuum for Europe to face.
TUR.art: Marble urbanism—Ephesus library façades (slightly later peak), theatres, baths, imperial cult temples—makes Asia the showcase of eastern Roman art. Aphrodisias sculptors export myth bodies empire-wide. Greek visual eloquence under Roman funding.

TUR.religion: Roman Asia Minor: dense temple cities, imperial cult, Greek civic gods, and mystery/healing sanctuaries (e.g. Asclepius). Processions and benefactor religion animate urban life.
TUR.ideas: Civic benefaction, koinon politics, and emperor worship organise Greek cities into the Roman fiscal order. Religious pluralism (civic gods, imperial cult, Jewish communities, emerging Christians) densifies the ideascape. Asia is wealthy, wordy, and watched.
TUR.philosophy: Continuing Hellenistic schools and rhetorical philosophy; Jewish-Greek philosophical hybridity in the wider East. City elites fund teachers; debate is public performance. Named Stoic and Platonic teachers circulate in these networks.
TUR.science: Harbour engineering, urban water, and Hellenistic scientific inheritance. Medical and astronomical scholarship remain Greek-speaking strengths. Roman roads amplify older Anatolian route science.

ROU.name: Dacia (contested)
ROU.summary: Trajanic conquest later in the century.
ROU.literature: Full literary blaze: Greek epic and drama already classic; Latin poetry and history rising (Virgil, Livy, Cicero). In the provinces, local languages persist under Latin/Greek prestige. This is the first period where clickable states can quote real verses, not only artifacts. Romanian lands keep Latin memory in a Slavic-Orthodox sea — language as archaeological survival.
ROU.art: Pre-provincial Dacian gold, fortresses, and figurative metal define the Carpathian visual challenge to Rome; Roman Danube camps opposite show legionary art. Full Roman Dacian monumentality awaits Trajan—just beyond this map’s core window. Two aesthetics glare across the river.

ROU.religion: Dacia contested: Geto-Dacian sacral kingship and sanctuary traditions meet Roman military cult after conquest — imperial religion imposed on a resistant ritual landscape.
ROU.ideas: Dacian kingdomhood threatens Moesia and tempts Rome’s gold hunger. Client deals and wars alternate. Contested status is the political idea: independence under pressure.
ROU.philosophy: Zalmoxis immortality teachings (Greek-mediated) are the rare named spiritual marker; otherwise royal-sacred fortress ideology. Roman side brings camp religion. No shared school—collision of cosmologies.
ROU.science: Dacian mountain forts and mining knowledge versus Roman siegecraft and Danube logistics. Both sides practise sophisticated military engineering in mutual study.

IRL.name: Hibernia
IRL.literature: Full literary blaze: Greek epic and drama already classic; Latin poetry and history rising (Virgil, Livy, Cicero). In the provinces, local languages persist under Latin/Greek prestige. This is the first period where clickable states can quote real verses, not only artifacts. Irish monastic and later Gaelic learned traditions punch above demographic weight in Europe’s imagination.
IRL.art: Ireland outside Rome continues Iron Age ornamental metal and ceremonial landscapes; Roman objects are exotic imports, not street furniture. No fora, no mosaics—art stays indigenous and portable. Royal sites remain the monumental idea.

IRL.religion: Hibernia outside the Empire: Iron Age–style royal sites, bog deposits, and local gods. No Roman civic cult; later Christian conversion still centuries away.
IRL.ideas: Unconquered status becomes part of Ireland’s later historical self-story. Indigenous politics develop beside a Roman Britain trading neighbour. Ideas of kingship and clientship evolve without provincial law.
IRL.philosophy: Oral sacral and legal thought—no classical philosophy faculties. Cosmology is landscape ritual and social obligation. Literacy’s big bang awaits Christian mission centuries later.
IRL.science: Atlantic craft, farming, and metalworking continue on local trajectories. Selective Roman goods imply trade awareness without technical romanisation of infrastructure.

UKR.name: Sarmatian steppe
UKR.conflicts: Pressure on Danube provinces; Black Sea politics.
UKR.literature: Full literary blaze: Greek epic and drama already classic; Latin poetry and history rising (Virgil, Livy, Cicero). In the provinces, local languages persist under Latin/Greek prestige. This is the first period where clickable states can quote real verses, not only artifacts. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: Sarmatian gold polychromy, horse gear, and long swords; Greek city ruins and Roman trade goods on the coasts. Kurgan elites keep animal-style vocabulary into the early Empire. Visual power is mounted and portable.
