UKR.religion: Sarmatian steppe: kurgan burial, horse gear, and nomadic cult practice. Greek cities of the coast keep Hellenic temples at the edge of the pastoral world.
UKR.ideas: Steppe confederations bargain with Rome’s Danube provinces—raid, alliance, subsidy. Nomad aristocracy over mixed populations continues the Scythian-era political logic under new ethnonyms. Cities on the littoral live differently from the grass ocean.
UKR.philosophy: Funerary and martial cosmology; no philosophical schools on the steppe. Coastal Greek remnants keep literate ethics in pockets. Worldview is confederation oath and horse wealth.
UKR.science: Cavalry equipment evolution, bowels of steppe ecology, and frontier trade metrology. Technical innovation is military-pastoral, not aqueductal.

periods.label: Migration Period
periods.narrative: Western Roman order fragments. Wielbark culture in Poland is the archaeological horizon standardly linked to early Gothic traditions before south-east movements. Hunnic pressure, Gothic kingdoms, Frankish growth, and Anglo-Saxon settlement in Britain remake politics. Genetics show real mobility (e.g. North Sea influx in eastern England) without Beaker-scale pan-European replacement; elite Germanic layers often sit on Roman provincial majorities.
periods.culturesNote: Wielbark, Chernyakhov, Hunnic horizon, Visigoths/Ostrogoths, early Franks, Anglo-Saxons, early Byzantium — migration-era polities.

iberia.description: Visigothic kings rule a Romanized peninsula from Toledo after earlier Vandal/Alani passage. Arian then Catholic confession politics; harshening Jewish policy. Genetics: Hispano-Roman continua with Gothic elite overlays — the kingdom Islam will shatter in 711.
iberia.ancestryNote: Hispano-Roman continuity dominates; Gothic genetic input limited relative to political power.
iberia.languages: Early Hispano-Romance; Gothic (elite, receding); Latin literacy
iberia.linguisticNote: Gothic language fades; Romance and Latin win — classic elite dominance without language replacement permanence.

britain.description: Post-Roman Britain fragments into Brittonic kingdoms and incoming Anglo-Saxon polities of the east and south. Archaeology shows new burial rites and material culture; genetics and isotopes argue for substantial but regionally variable migration — neither empty-land replacement nor pure elite fashion. Christianity survives in the west; pagan English convert around the turn of the 7th century. The Arthurian legend later romanticizes this collapse-and-making.
britain.ancestryNote: Higher “continental NW” in east; west/north more Romano-British/Celtic continuity. Still WHG–EEF–steppe structured.
britain.languages: Old English forming; Brittonic (west/north); Latin residual
britain.linguisticNote: Language shift to Old English in much of what becomes England; Celtic continues in Wales/Scotland/west.

france.description: Clovis’s Franks conquer rival kingdoms and choose Catholic baptism, aligning with Gallo-Roman bishops. Merovingian rule overlays Roman cities and law with warrior kingship. Ancestry: late Roman Gallic mix plus northern Frankish input — political transformation with demographic layers.
france.linguisticNote: Ethnogenesis of France: Germanic ethnonym, Romance language.
france.ancestryNote: Gallo-Roman substrate + Germanic elite mobility — not Beaker-scale replacement.

central.description: East of the Rhine and along the upper Danube: Alamanni, Bavarians, Thuringians, and other peoples enter Frankish hegemony in pulses. Pagan belts remain. Genetics: northern/central European Iron Age–late antique continua under Migration-era mobility.
central.ancestryNote: Plausible east-central IA–early medieval European mix (BA ternary + mobility). Not a unique “Wielbark genetic component.”
central.languages: Gothic (in standard Wielbark↔Gothic narrative); other Germanic; residual local
central.linguisticNote: Gothic is attested (Wulfila Bible) further along the migration path; Wielbark itself is archaeological, not a text corpus.

scandinavia.description: Germanic Iron Age Scandinavia — the world that will export Vikings — with bog offerings, weapon graves, and proto-kingships. Not yet Christian states. Genetics: deep Nordic continuity from earlier BA/IA.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Proto-Norse attested in Elder Futhark inscriptions; Scandinavia exports people and speech into the migration-era world.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Iron Age Nordic continuity; export of people/culture more than import replacement.

italy.description: Odovacer and then Theodoric’s Ostrogoths rule Italy with Roman administration; Justinian’s Gothic War devastates the peninsula. Lombards take the north (568). Ancestry: late antique Italian continua under successive military elites.
italy.languages: Late Latin/early Romance; Gothic; Byzantine Greek
italy.linguisticNote: Gothic rule temporary; Romance and Latin continuity prevail.
italy.ancestryNote: Rebalancing from imperial eastern Med enrichment; Germanic layers present but not majority-defining.

balkans.description: Eastern Rome holds Constantinople and fights Goths, Huns, Avars, and Slavic settlement. Balkan provinces transform demographically with Slavicization uneven by valley. Genetics: late Roman + Slavic-associated mobility — debated proportions, real cultural change.
balkans.ancestryNote: “Other” elevated to capture Slavic/steppe/diverse inputs; avoid false precision.
balkans.languages: Byzantine Greek; early South Slavic; residual Latin/Romance; steppe languages
balkans.linguisticNote: Major linguistic turnover (Slavic) with incomplete genetic replacement — languages ≠ genes.

eastern.description: Hunnic empire then collapse; Gothic and other peoples move; steppe politics dominate the Pontic edge. Chernyakhov and related horizons. Genetics: steppe–farmer mixes under extreme elite mobility.
eastern.languageFamily: Obscure steppe + Iranian remnants + early Slavic
eastern.languages: Hunnic (obscure); Iranian remnants; early Slavic expanding
eastern.linguisticNote: Do not invent a Hunnic grammar from graves.
eastern.ancestryNote: Highly variable; East Eurasian “other” can be high in some elite burials.

periods.linguistics: East Germanic (Gothic), West Germanic (Frankish, Old English forming), North Germanic (Proto-Norse), Romance emerging from Latin, Greek in the East, early Slavic expansions beginning, Hunnic poorly attested.

mapLayers.label: Wielbark
mapLayers.art: Wielbark cemeteries favour bi-ritual burial—cremation and inhumation—typically without weapons, with paired shoulder fibulae and distinctive female dress sets. Amber, Roman imports, and carefully composed grave assemblages mark status more than monumental architecture. The eponymous cemetery near Malbork anchors a Baltic–Vistula visual language later echoed south-east.
mapLayers.ideas: Community identity is read archaeologically through costume and burial rule rather than royal chronicles. Southward expansion along the Vistula–Bug during and after the Marcomannic Wars suggests kinship groups negotiating Roman-frontier trade, climate stress, and competition with Przeworsk neighbours—mobility as strategy, not a single royal exodus.
mapLayers.philosophy: No native philosophical corpus survives; worldview is inferred from funerary restraint (weaponless graves), gendered dress codes, and selective Roman goods. Prestige seems invested in bodily adornment and cemetery continuity more than in temple architecture—an ethic of portable honour suited to a mobile elite.
mapLayers.science: Craft knowledge centres on amber working, iron and non-ferrous metalwork, and ceramic traditions continuous with local Pomeranian roots. Roman imports imply calendrical and market awareness along amber routes; settlement archaeology tracks field systems and riverine logistics rather than written medicine or astronomy.

mapLayers.label: Chernyakhov
mapLayers.art: Chernyakhov (Sântana de Mureș) material culture mixes Wielbark-style fibulae and weapon-poor burials with Sarmatian and local Pontic tastes: wheel-made grey pottery, glass vessels, bone combs, and open village plans. Elite display is portable—dress and drinking sets—across a huge Danube–Don horizon rather than stone capitals.
mapLayers.ideas: Literary Goths (Ermanaric, later Danubian kingdoms) sit atop a multiethnic archaeological reality. Political attention focused on Gothic leadership in Roman sources, while archaeology shows farmers, herders, and craftsmen sharing a cultural package—domination as hierarchy within mixture, not ethnic purity.
mapLayers.philosophy: Early Gothic Christianity under Wulfila later produces the Gothic Bible—the first major Germanic literary theology—but Chernyakhov itself straddles pagan and converting horizons. Customary law and kinship loyalty, later refracted in Jordanes’ Getica, structure obligation more than school philosophy.
mapLayers.science: High-quality wheel-thrown ceramics, iron tools, and glass consumption show specialised craft and Black Sea trade literacy. Agricultural villages imply crop–livestock systems adapted to steppe-edge climates; Roman diplomatic and market contact transmitted weights, coins, and technical goods without a local scientific literature.

mapLayers.label: Ostrogothic Italy
mapLayers.art: Ravenna under Theodoric fuses Gothic patronage with late Roman building: the Arian Baptistery, Sant’Apollinare Nuovo’s processional mosaics, and the mausoleum’s limestone dome. Court dress and mosaic programs stage a Gothic king ruling a still-Roman city of marble, gold tesserae, and imperial memory.
mapLayers.ideas: Theodoric’s regime keeps Roman civil administration, Senate prestige, and legal dualism—Goths as army, Romans as civilians—under an Ostrogothic Amal kingship blessed by Constantinople. The Edictum Theodorici and Cassiodorus’ Variae advertise civilitas: barbarian kingship justified as guardian of Roman order.
mapLayers.philosophy: Boethius’ Consolation of Philosophy (c. 524), written in Theodoric’s prison, is the era’s philosophical masterpiece: Neoplatonic–Stoic arguments for providence and the goods of the soul amid political ruin. Arian Gothic Christianity and Nicene Roman theology coexist uneasily until Justinian’s wars shatter the experiment.
mapLayers.science: Cassiodorus later founds Vivarium’s copying programme; in Italy, late Roman surveying, aqueduct maintenance, and medical handbooks persist under Gothic rule. Ravenna’s brick and mosaic workshops preserve engineering and material science of the late empire more than invent new theory.

mapLayers.label: Visigothic Hispania
mapLayers.art: Visigothic metalwork peaks in the Treasure of Guarrazar—suspended votive crowns (Recceswinth) with sapphires and pendilia letters offered to church altars. Churches at San Juan de Baños and later Toledo-centred patronage blend Germanic jewellery techniques with Hispano-Roman and Byzantine models.
mapLayers.ideas: After Arian beginnings, Reccared’s conversion (Third Council of Toledo, 589) binds Gothic kingship to Nicene orthodoxy and episcopal councils. The Liber Iudiciorum (Recceswinth) aims at a territorial law for Goths and Romans alike—unity through Catholic monarchy and written code.
mapLayers.philosophy: Isidore of Seville’s Etymologies and historical works organise Christian encyclopaedic knowledge for a post-Roman West: language, nature, and sacred history as one didactic order. Conciliar theology at Toledo defines orthodoxy and royal duty more than speculative metaphysics.
mapLayers.science: Isidore’s compilations transmit classical fragments on cosmology, medicine, and computus to medieval Latin Europe. Iberian agricultural continuity, minting, and church building keep practical Roman techniques alive; scholarly science is clerical compilation rather than new experiment.

mapLayers.label: Vandal corridor (N. Africa off-map)
mapLayers.art: In Africa (off this map’s core), Vandal Carthage patronises Arian churches and late antique mosaics; in Iberian transit zones, archaeology is thinner—corridor more than settled kingdom. Portable wealth, shipborne power, and Mediterranean dress mark a seaborne Germanic elite.
mapLayers.ideas: Geiseric’s 429 crossing and 455 sack of Rome advertise naval kingdom as theological and political challenge to Catholic Rome. Arian court identity versus Nicene majority becomes the ideological fault line until Byzantine reconquest (533–34).
mapLayers.philosophy: Victor of Vita’s persecuted-Catholic narrative frames Vandal rule as heretical tyranny; little Vandal philosophical writing survives. The debate is ecclesiological—who owns orthodoxy—more than abstract ethics.
mapLayers.science: Vandal naval logistics, North African grain routes, and late Roman urban infrastructure (still used under their rule) are the practical sciences of the kingdom. Cartographic Europe sees them as a fringe corridor because their centre of gravity was Carthage, not Iberia.

mapLayers.label: Early Franks
mapLayers.art: Childeric’s grave at Tournai (bees, weapons, gold) and early Merovingian cloisonné garnet jewellery define Frankish bling. Baptisteries and saint cults after Clovis’s conversion pull Gallo-Roman church art into royal service; weapon burial and belt sets signal warrior status.
mapLayers.ideas: Clovis’s victory over Syagrius and Nicene baptism align Frankish kingship with Gallo-Roman bishops against Arian rivals. Salic legal traditions and royal antrustiones build a Christian warrior kingdom claiming Roman Gaul’s mantle without restoring the empire.
mapLayers.philosophy: Gregory of Tours later moralises Merovingian history as divine judgment on kings; early Frankish thought is catechetical and legal. Orthodoxy versus Arianism, and the sacral aura of baptismal kingship, dominate intellectual life over school philosophy.
mapLayers.science: Late Roman road and estate systems, plus Frankish military organisation, structure knowledge of landscape. Monastic and episcopal centres begin to keep computus and basic medicine; technical innovation is incremental within Gallo-Roman craft survivals.

mapLayers.label: Alamanni
mapLayers.art: Row-grave cemeteries with weapons, brooches, and belt fittings map Alamannic presence east of the Rhine and into Alsace–Switzerland. Fine metalwork and occasional Roman reuse (spolia, coins) show frontier taste without a court capital’s monumental art.
mapLayers.ideas: A confederation name (‘all men’) more than a single dynasty: pressure on Roman Germania superior, then coexistence and conflict with Franks. Identity is military and regional—pagus loyalties—before full Merovingian absorption.
mapLayers.philosophy: Pagan cult continuities inferred from burial and place-names gradually yield to Frankish-sponsored Christianisation. Worldview centres on honour, feud, and local sacral landscapes rather than written theology until episcopal networks thicken.
mapLayers.science: Iron weapon manufacture, agrarian clearance in upland valleys, and knowledge of Rhine crossings are the applied sciences of a frontier people. Roman fort ruins become quarries and landmarks in a reused technical landscape.

mapLayers.label: Anglo-Saxon England
mapLayers.art: Sutton Hoo’s ship burial (early 7th c. horizon of the wider migration story) shows gold-and-garnet regalia, patterned helmets, and Byzantine silver—Beowulf’s hall world made material. Earlier furnished inhumations, square-headed brooches, and later manuscript painting grow from this North Sea aesthetic.
mapLayers.ideas: Adventus myths (Hengest and Horsa), heptarchy kingship, and conversion via Rome and Iona remake Britain as English-speaking Christian realms. Law codes (Æthelberht onward) and land books turn conquest into governance.
mapLayers.philosophy: Heroic ethics of loyalty, gift-giving, and fame in poetry sit beside Augustinian missionary theology after 597. Conscience and kingship are taught through saints’ lives and penitentials more than through treatises—yet the tension between feud honour and Christian humility is pervasive.
mapLayers.science: Shipbuilding, textile and garnet cloisonné craft, and open-field beginnings show sophisticated practical knowledge. Monastic schools later add computus and Latin learning; early centuries privilege craft and navigation over natural philosophy.

mapLayers.label: Brittonic west
mapLayers.art: Ogham and Latin-inscribed stones, imported Mediterranean pottery in western bays, and evolving Celtic Christian sculpture mark post-Roman Brittonic zones. Illuminated gospel traditions (later flowering in Insular art) and monastic metalwork keep a distinct visual Christianity beside Anglo-Saxon east.
mapLayers.ideas: Sub-Roman kingdoms (Gwynedd, Dumnonia, and peers) claim Roman and Trojan genealogies while losing the lowland east. Saints’ cults, monastic federations, and bardic memory preserve Brittonic political identity under pressure.
mapLayers.philosophy: Pelagian controversies linger in British Christian memory; monastic ascetic ideals (from Martinic and Irish models) shape ethics. Wisdom is pastoral and poetic—triads, praise poetry—more than Aristotelian schoolcraft.
mapLayers.science: Atlantic seafaring, tin and livestock economies, and monastic computus (Easter debates) are core knowledges. Medical and legal learning travels in Latin and vernacular clerical milieux along western seaways.

mapLayers.label: Hunnic horizon
mapLayers.art: Polychrome cloisonné, mirrored ornaments, and steppe-prestige gold signal Hunnic-period elites from the Carpathian Basin outward. Cauldrons, horse gear, and artificially deformed skulls in some cemeteries visualise a multiethnic imperial confederation more than a single ‘Hun’ style.
mapLayers.ideas: Attila’s court diplomacy—tribute, marriage alliances, terror—organises Goths, Gepids, and others as vassals. The Catalaunian Plains (451) and Attila’s death (453) show how quickly steppe hegemony can assemble and fracture.
mapLayers.philosophy: Roman ethnographers cast Huns as eschatological scourge; within the confederation, ideology is charismatic kingship and plunder redistribution. Little internal philosophical writing survives—power spoke through ceremony and fear.
mapLayers.science: Composite bows, horse logistics, and siege borrowing from Roman engineers underwrite Hunnic warfare. Genetic and isotopic studies now track mobility; contemporary ‘science’ was military and pastoral expertise on the move.

mapLayers.label: Eastern Roman / early Byzantine
mapLayers.art: Constantinople’s churches, ivory diptychs, and the slow birth of icon programmes define early Byzantine visual theology. Ravenna’s Byzantine-facing mosaics and Justinianic rebuilding (Hagia Sophia’s later sixth-century climax just after this slice) radiate imperial Christian aesthetics.
mapLayers.ideas: Roman law (Theodosian Code; Justinian’s later Corpus) and imperial orthodoxy claim universal order while losing the Latin West. Diplomacy, subsidy, and foederati management try to domesticate Migration-Period neighbours.
mapLayers.philosophy: Neoplatonism (Proclus) and Cappadocian theological synthesis still frame elite education; Christianity debates nature(s) of Christ (Ephesus, Chalcedon) as the central metaphysical quarrel. Philosophy serves theology and imperial ideology.
mapLayers.science: Greek medical and mathematical handbooks continue in urban schools; military manuals and fortification engineering defend the Danube and East. Administrative numeracy and grain logistics keep an empire running amid demographic shocks.

mapLayers.label: Early Slavic expansion
mapLayers.art: Early Slavic horizons favour simple handmade pottery, sunken-floored buildings, and relatively modest grave assemblages compared with Germanic furnished burials. Wooden cult sites and later hillforts matter more than stone sculpture in the first expansion phases.
mapLayers.ideas: Ethnogenesis narratives place Slavs spreading through emptied or mixed landscapes of east-central Europe after Germanic departures. Kin-based farming communities, not literate kingdoms, carry the expansion until later state formations.
mapLayers.philosophy: Pre-Christian Slavic cosmology—reconstructed cautiously from later folklore and medieval critiques—centres on household, ancestors, and nature spirits. Written philosophy arrives with Christianisation centuries later.
mapLayers.science: Slash-and-burn and mixed farming, riverine settlement siting, and iron smelting in forest zones are the practical sciences of expansion. Linguistic palaeontology and archaeology jointly track mobility better than any native technical treatise.

mapLayers.label: Germanic Iron Age Scandinavia
mapLayers.art: Weapon graves, gold bracteates with mythical motifs, and bog deposits (including earlier weapon sacrifices’ long memory) define Scandinavian visual religion. Animal-style ornament on brooches and scabbards sets tastes that later Viking art will transform.
mapLayers.ideas: Chieftain halls, petty kingdoms, and mythic genealogies to gods structure power before Viking Age monarchies. Contact with Rome—via gifts, mercenaries, and imports—feeds prestige economies without provincial annexation.
mapLayers.philosophy: Eddic myth in later recording preserves older ideas of fate (wyrd/urðr), honour, and reciprocal gift debt. Wisdom is gnomic and poetic; no seminary philosophy, but a coherent ethic of reputation and courage.
mapLayers.science: Boatbuilding, iron production (including Danish bog ore traditions), and navigational familiarity with skerry coasts underpin later Viking reach. Runic literacy begins as craft-mark and memorial technology, not full literature.

POL.name: Wielbark culture
POL.conflicts: Movements toward Black Sea (Chernyakhov); pressure from and on neighbors.
POL.leaders: Archaeological cultures more than named kings (Wielbark).
POL.religion: Wielbark communities practice cremation and inhumation with Scandinavian links; gods unnamed in texts. Christianity is still a distant Roman/Byzantine horizon, not a local church yet.
POL.culture: Wielbark burial rite changes; amber and trade.
POL.story: Wielbark’s link to Gothic migrations is archaeology’s great detective story — cemeteries hinting at peoples later famous on the Black Sea and in Italy.
POL.literature: Latin letters continue in bishops’ cities; Gothic and other tongues carry oral epic. Later Beowulf and continental hero legends preserve a Migration-Age mood of hall, feud, and gold — composed afterward, remembering this world of warbands. Polish–Lithuanian and later Polish culture specializes in noble liberty myths and romantic survival art.
POL.art: Wielbark cemeteries—bi-ritual, often weaponless, with paired fibulae and amber—dominate the Polish Migration-Period visual record. Settlement fades mid-5th century as the archaeological landscape empties before early Slavic horizons; portable dress, not stone capitals, carries style.

POL.ideas: Gothic-linked Wielbark communities organised prestige through burial rule and amber–Roman exchange along the Vistula. Political ideas survive as practice: costume codes, cemetery continuity, and eventual south-east mobility rather than a written Polish state ideology.
POL.philosophy: No native philosophical schools; worldview is funerary ethics—restraint in weapon deposition, gendered dress, care for cemetery place. Later Slavic incomers bring different household rites into the same riverscape.
POL.science: Amber working, iron and bronze craft, and river logistics are the technical backbone. Roman imports imply weight and market literacy; after Wielbark collapse, new agrarian systems recolonise cleared and abandoned zones.

UKR.name: Chernyakhov / Gothic steppe edge
UKR.conflicts: Hunnic shock; collapse and westward Gothic migrations.
UKR.leaders: Gothic and steppe elites in Chernyakhov horizons; Hunnic overlords.
UKR.religion: Chernyakhov / Gothic steppe edge mixes Germanic, Sarmatian, and local rites — kurgans, weapon graves, and limited Christian contact. Steppe cults and household offerings outrank organized churches.
UKR.culture: Multi-ethnic Chernyakhov villages; Hunnic shock mobility.
UKR.story: The Hunnic storm empties and remakes the Pontic edge — Attila’s Europe begins in these grasslands.
UKR.literature: Latin letters continue in bishops’ cities; Gothic and other tongues carry oral epic. Later Beowulf and continental hero legends preserve a Migration-Age mood of hall, feud, and gold — composed afterward, remembering this world of warbands. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: Chernyakhov open villages yield wheel-made grey wares, glass cups, bone combs, and Wielbark-style fibulae across the forest-steppe. Aesthetic power sits in ceramic standardisation and dress sets, not cities; Hunnic-period gold later overlays the same corridors.

UKR.ideas: Multiethnic Gothic-centred hierarchies manage agriculture and diplomacy on Rome’s Pontic doorstep. Ideas of kingship (Ermanaric in legend) float above mixed Sarmatian, Germanic, and local farming populations sharing one material package.
UKR.philosophy: Conversion-era Gothic Christianity (Wulfila’s Bible belongs to the wider Gothic story) meets older pagan custom; philosophy is customary law and sacral kingship remembered in Getica more than in local treatises.
UKR.science: Specialised pottery kilns, iron tools, and Black Sea trade goods show craft intensity. Steppe-edge farming and stockbreeding tune crops to continental seasons; Roman diplomatic contact transmits coin and measure.

ITA.name: Ostrogothic Italy
ITA.leaders: Odoacer; Theodoric the Great; Justinian’s generals (Belisarius, Narses).
ITA.religion: Arian Gothic elites over Catholic Romans; Byzantine Orthodoxy in reconquest.
ITA.culture: Senatorial Roman continuity under Gothic rule; Ravenna mosaics.
ITA.story: Theodoric’s long peace and the Gothic War’s devastation bookend Italy’s transformation from Western Empire to early medieval patchwork.
ITA.literature: Cassiodorus and Boethius try to keep Latin thought alive under Gothic kings; the Consolation of Philosophy is a prison lamp. Ostrogothic Ravenna speaks in mosaic as much as in edict.
ITA.art: Ostrogothic Ravenna paints Arian and court mosaics onto late Roman brick—Sant’Apollinare Nuovo, the Arian Baptistery, Theodoric’s mausoleum. Italy remains a mosaic-and-marble civilisation under Gothic military dress.

ITA.ideas: Theodoric’s civilitas: Goths as army, Romans as civil society, Amal kingship under Eastern imperial grant. Cassiodorus’ letters advertise continuity of Roman administration after 476’s symbolic end.
ITA.philosophy: Boethius’ Consolation fuses Neoplatonism and prison ethics at Theodoric’s court; Arian–Nicene tension is the public metaphysics. Philosophy is still Greek-Latin school inheritance, now under Gothic kings.
ITA.science: Aqueducts, surveying, medical handbooks, and mosaic workshops keep late antique technology alive. Ravenna’s engineers and copyists preserve more than they invent until Justinian’s wars disrupt the system.

ESP.name: Visigothic Hispania
ESP.conflicts: Wars with Suebi, Byzantines in south; internal faction.
ESP.leaders: Visigothic kings at Toledo; earlier Vandal passage memory.
ESP.religion: Visigothic Arianism then conversion to Catholicism (Reccared); Jewish policy harshening.
ESP.culture: Toledo councils; fusion law codes; Roman infrastructure reuse.
ESP.story: Visigothic Spain’s unity-under-Toledo is later remembered as the Christian kingdom Islam will overrun in 711 — an origin told backward from al-Andalus.
ESP.literature: Latin letters continue in bishops’ cities; Gothic and other tongues carry oral epic. Later Beowulf and continental hero legends preserve a Migration-Age mood of hall, feud, and gold — composed afterward, remembering this world of warbands. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: Visigothic goldsmithing—Guarrazar votive crowns with sapphires and lettered pendilia—and compact churches mark Hispania’s Christian-Germanic aesthetic. Vandal passage leaves thinner Iberian traces; the lasting style is Toledo-centred royal piety in metal.

ESP.ideas: From Arian foederati kingdom to Reccared’s Catholic conversion (589) and territorial law (Liber Iudiciorum). Unity of Goth and Roman under one faith and code becomes the political idea of Visigothic Spain.
ESP.philosophy: Isidore of Seville’s Etymologies organise Christian encyclopaedism—language, nature, sacred history—for a post-Roman West. Conciliar Toledo defines orthodoxy as royal-philosophical duty.
ESP.science: Isidore transmits classical fragments of cosmology and medicine; mints, irrigation survivals, and church building keep Roman practical arts. Clerical computus, not laboratories, structures learned time.

FRA.name: Frankish Gaul
FRA.leaders: Clovis; Merovingian kings; early mayors of the palace.
FRA.religion: Clovis’s Catholic baptism allies Franks with Gallo-Roman bishops against Arian rivals.
FRA.culture: Lex Salica; warrior retinues; Gallo-Roman villa afterlives.
FRA.story: Clovis’s baptism is France’s oldest royal conversion story — a pagan warlord choosing Catholic Rome’s prestige.
FRA.literature: Latin letters continue in bishops’ cities; Gothic and other tongues carry oral epic. Later Beowulf and continental hero legends preserve a Migration-Age mood of hall, feud, and gold — composed afterward, remembering this world of warbands. French courts and vernaculars repeatedly set continental fashions of word and dress.
FRA.art: Childeric’s Tournai treasure and Merovingian garnet cloisonné set Frankish bling against Gallo-Roman saint cults and baptisteries after Clovis. Weapon graves and belt suites visualise a warrior aristocracy in Roman Gaul’s ruins.

FRA.ideas: Clovis’s Nicene baptism and conquest of Syagrius invent Catholic Frankish legitimacy against Arian rivals. Salic custom and royal retinues rebuild Gaul as a Christian kingdom claiming Roman inheritance.
FRA.philosophy: Early Merovingian thought is episcopal and legal—orthodoxy, baptismal kingship, saintly patronage—later moralised by Gregory of Tours. School philosophy waits on monastic libraries.
FRA.science: Late Roman roads and villas reused; Frankish military organisation and estate agriculture dominate technique. Episcopal centres keep basic computus and care of bodies.

GBR.name: Anglo-Saxon kingdoms forming
GBR.conflicts: Conflict with Brittonic west; North Sea migration politics.
GBR.leaders: Traditional heptarchy kings; later narrative figures (Vortigern, Arthur as legend — not documentary).
GBR.religion: British Christianity in the west; incoming Anglo-Saxon paganism then conversion (Augustine 597 still near this horizon).
GBR.culture: Post-Roman material simplicity; epic memory forming; Irish missions.
GBR.story: The Adventus Saxonum — migration, war, and settlement — becomes England’s origin debate: invasion myth vs gradual cultural change.
GBR.literature: Latin survives in British clergy; Old English poetry will later remember this age’s mood — halls, feud, sea-roads — in Beowulf and elegy. Oral formulaic verse is the period’s true press.
GBR.art: Anglo-Saxon furnished burials and, at the period’s long edge, Sutton Hoo’s gold-and-garnet ship funeral rewrite ‘Dark Age’ Britain as a dazzling North Sea art world. Brittonic west answers with inscribed stones and Atlantic Christian carving.

GBR.ideas: Adventus myths, heptarchy kingship, and conversion from Rome and Iona remake lowland Britain as English-speaking Christian realms while Brittonic kingdoms hold the west. Law codes begin to turn conquest into order.
GBR.philosophy: Heroic loyalty and gift ethics in poetry meet Augustinian missionary theology. Penitentials and saints’ lives teach conscience; feud honour and Christian humility remain in tension.
GBR.science: Shipbuilding, cloisonné craft, and textile wealth show high artisanal science; monastic schools later add Latin computus. Brittonic Atlantic seafaring keeps older maritime literacy.

HUN.name: Sarmatian / early Magyar prelude zone
HUN.summary: Carpathian basin peoples before the later Magyar conquest of the 9th–10th centuries.
HUN.conflicts: Hunnic then Gepid/Avar-era upheavals in the wider Middle Danube memory.
HUN.leaders: Named kings scarce; Avar khagans dominate the wider basin’s politics in this era.
HUN.religion: Sarmatian and early steppe groups keep horse-and-kurgan funerary religion; Roman Christian missions are peripheral. Local cult practice, not dioceses, structures the sacred.
HUN.story: The basin is a highway of peoples — the stage on which Magyars will later found Hungary.
HUN.literature: Latin letters continue in bishops’ cities; Gothic and other tongues carry oral epic. Later Beowulf and continental hero legends preserve a Migration-Age mood of hall, feud, and gold — composed afterward, remembering this world of warbands. Hungarian culture keeps a steppe-origin memory inside a Latin-Christian and later Habsburg frame.
HUN.art: Hunnic-period Carpathian Basin assemblages flash polychrome cloisonné, horse gear, and cauldrons—an imperial confederation’s prestige kit worn by many peoples. Monumental stone is scarce; gold and horses are the media.

HUN.ideas: Attila’s tribute diplomacy and multiethnic vassalage organise the middle Danube until 453. Ideas of empire here are charismatic, extractive, and short-lived compared with Rome’s paperwork.
HUN.philosophy: Roman writers cast the Hun as scourge; inside the confederation, ideology is loyalty to the qaghan-like king and redistribution of plunder. Written philosophy is external ethnography.
HUN.science: Composite bow, cavalry logistics, and borrowed Roman siege craft are Hunnic applied sciences. Isotopes and aDNA now track the mobility their horsemen practised.

TUR.name: Eastern Roman Anatolia (edge)
TUR.summary: Anatolian heartland of the Eastern Roman Empire beyond the Balkan focus of this map tick.
TUR.conflicts: Persian wars on the eastern front; Balkan crises pulling imperial attention.
TUR.leaders: Eastern Roman emperors (Arcadius to Justinian’s eve).
TUR.religion: Imperial Christianity of the Eastern Roman world: episcopal cities, liturgy, relics, and Christological debate. Monasteries and pilgrimage already shape Anatolian sacred geography.
TUR.culture: Greek Roman cities of Asia Minor.
TUR.story: While Europe’s west fragments, Anatolia taxes and prays for an empire that still calls itself Roman.
TUR.literature: Latin letters continue in bishops’ cities; Gothic and other tongues carry oral epic. Later Beowulf and continental hero legends preserve a Migration-Age mood of hall, feud, and gold — composed afterward, remembering this world of warbands. Ottoman and Anatolian layers make this edge of the map a second classical continuum for Europe to face.
TUR.art: Constantinople’s early Byzantine ivories, silks, and church programmes radiate imperial Christian aesthetics toward a fracturing West. Cross-in-square experiments and court dress define the look of surviving Rome.

TUR.philosophy: Neoplatonism and Chalcedonian Christology dominate elite metaphysics; philosophy serves theology and the emperor’s sacred office. Schools in the capital still teach Greek logic.
TUR.science: Greek medicine, mathematics, fortification, and grain logistics keep an empire running. Administrative numeracy is a survival technology amid Migration-Period shocks.

DEU.name: Alamanni / frontier Germans
DEU.conflicts: Conflict with Franks; shifting Rhine politics.
DEU.leaders: Merovingian frontier kings; Alamannic and Bavarian dukes; Thuringian rulers.
DEU.religion: Pagan districts beside Christian Frankish power; Irish/Anglo-Saxon missions coming.
DEU.culture: Row-grave horizons; warrior burials; forest-agrarian society.
DEU.story: East of the Rhine is not ‘Germany’ yet — a mosaic of peoples being pulled into Frankish Christianity.
DEU.literature: Latin letters continue in bishops’ cities; Gothic and other tongues carry oral epic. Later Beowulf and continental hero legends preserve a Migration-Age mood of hall, feud, and gold — composed afterward, remembering this world of warbands. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.
DEU.art: Alamannic and early Frankish row-grave zones east of the Rhine fill with weapons, brooches, and belt fittings; Roman spolia reuse marks the frontier aesthetic. No single capital’s mosaic programme—status is worn and buried.

DEU.ideas: Confederate Alamanni and expanding Franks renegotiate the old limes world. Political ideas are pagi, war-bands, and gradual Merovingian overlordship rather than a German nation.
DEU.philosophy: Pagan sacral landscapes yield piecemeal to Frankish-sponsored Christianisation. Honour, feud, and local cult structure right conduct before cathedral schools exist.
DEU.science: Iron weapon production, upland clearance, and Rhine crossing knowledge are frontier sciences. Roman fort stone becomes quarry and mnemonic for a reused technical landscape.

periods.label: Frankish & Early Medieval
periods.narrative: Charlemagne’s Frankish/Carolingian Empire (c. 800) politically unites much of Western and Central Europe under Christian Latin literacy, then divides (Verdun 843). Concurrently: Viking diaspora, Al-Andalus, Byzantium, First Bulgarian Empire, early Rus’. Demographically this is elite and institutional change on early medieval ancestries — not a new Paleolithic component.
periods.culturesNote: Carolingian Frankish Empire, Anglo-Saxon/Viking Britain, Al-Andalus, East Francia–Slavic frontier, Byzantium & Bulgaria, Kievan Rus’ beginnings.

iberia.description: Asturias–León and other northern Christian polities resist and raid south; Al-Andalus under the Emirate/Caliphate of Córdoba is western Europe’s richest court culture — Arabic letters, science, and agriculture. Jews and Mozarabs mediate. Genetics: Iberian early medieval mixes with North African gene flow in the south.
iberia.ancestryNote: Regional contrast: Andalusian samples can show elevated “other”; Christian north more continuous. Avoid a single Spain number.
iberia.languages: Arabic; Mozarabic; early Castilian/Catalan/Portuguese lines; Basque
iberia.linguisticNote: Arabic prestige south; Romance consolidation north — bilingual and multi-faith for centuries.

britain.description: Heptarchy consolidation under Wessex meets the Viking Great Army: Danelaw settlement, Alfred’s burhs and learning program, then Æthelstan’s brief wide kingship. Norse-Gaelic Dublin and Scottish/Pictish politics frame the islands. Old English ± Old Norse contact reshapes speech. Genetics: Anglo-Saxon–Brittonic base with Scandinavian admixture in the east and north — a real migration pulse on a smaller scale than Beaker, not a Mesolithic reset.
britain.linguisticNote: Heavy Old Norse lexical impact on English in contact zones.
britain.ancestryNote: North Sea Germanic base + Norse input in Danelaw/isles; regional Celtic continuity.

france.description: Carolingian West Francia after Verdun becomes a landscape of great principalities under a weakening king; Viking Seine and Loire raids force fortification and eventually Normandy’s grant (911). Monasteries keep Latin learning; Romance speech diverges from Latin. Ancestry: late antique Gallo-Roman–Frankish continua under elite and raider mobility.
france.ancestryNote: Continuity with Merovingian-era Gaul + elite circulation across the empire.
france.languages: Old French forming; Latin (church/chancery); Germanic dialects in east
france.linguisticNote: Imperial lingua franca is Latin; vernaculars are Romance/Germanic — bilingual elite world.

central.description: East Francia and the stem duchies face Viking, Magyar, and Slavic frontiers; Carolingian structures give way to ducal power that Ottonians will later reforge into empire. Missionaries move east. Genetics: central European early medieval continua.
central.languages: Old High German; West Slavic languages; Latin literacy
central.linguisticNote: Enduring German–Slavic linguistic frontier begins here.
central.ancestryNote: BA/IA base + early medieval Slavic-related admixture in parts of the east-central zone.

scandinavia.description: Late Iron Age societies launch the Viking diaspora: trade, raid, and settlement from Newfoundland’s fringe to the Caspian routes. Kings begin to centralize as conversion politics appear. Material culture: ships, silver hoards, proto-towns (Hedeby, Birka, Kaupang). Genetics: Nordic Iron Age continuity with mobility outward more than replacement inward.
scandinavia.linguisticNote: Old Norse relatively unified yet dialectally spreading overseas.
scandinavia.ancestryNote: Nordic IA continuity; diaspora admixed abroad more than at home.

italy.description: Carolingian and late Lombard north; papal Rome; Byzantine south; Muslim conquest of Sicily (9th c.). A peninsula of three civilizations. Ancestry: late antique Italian continua with Mediterranean mobility.
italy.languages: Italian vernaculars; Latin; Greek; Arabic in Sicily
italy.linguisticNote: Long-lasting north/south linguistic and cultural split.
italy.ancestryNote: North–south contrast; Mediterranean “other” higher in south/ports.

balkans.description: Byzantium survives and reforms; First Bulgarian Empire Christianizes in Slavic Orthodoxy; Avars fade. The Balkans remain imperial and Slavicizing. Genetics: early medieval Balkan mixes.
balkans.ancestryNote: High uncertainty by valley/coast; schematic elevated “other.”
balkans.languages: Old Church Slavonic/South Slavic; Byzantine Greek; Bulgar Turkic elite layer (receding)
balkans.linguisticNote: Slavic language establishment with complex elite ethnogenesis.

eastern.description: Khazar sphere, Magyars moving west, and Scandinavian–Slavic networks forming early Rus’ along the river roads. Steppe–forest exchange defines the age. Genetics: eastern continua with Turkic and Norse elite layers.
eastern.languages: Old East Slavic; Old Norse (Varangians); Turkic steppe languages
eastern.linguisticNote: Rus’ name and elite links Norse; language of the land becomes East Slavic.
eastern.ancestryNote: Forest-steppe mix; Norse signal limited relative to Slavic majority demography in most models.

periods.linguistics: Old French/Gallo-Romance under Latin clergy; Old High German; Old Norse; Old English ± Old Norse; Arabic in Al-Andalus; Greek; South Slavic + Bulgar elite layer; Old East Slavic with Varangian Norse.

mapLayers.label: Carolingian heartland
mapLayers.art: Aachen’s Palatine Chapel, illuminated Gospel books (Ada, Coronation Gospels), and revived monumental architecture advertise a Roman–Christian imperial aesthetic. Ivory carving, liturgical plate, and monastery plans (St Gall ideal) standardise sacred visual order across the heartland.
mapLayers.ideas: Charlemagne’s correctio—reform of liturgy, law, and learning—casts the king as guardian of orthodoxy. Capitularies, missi dominici, and the imperial coronation of 800 articulate a Western empire in dialogue and rivalry with Byzantium.
mapLayers.philosophy: Alcuin, Theodulf, and the court school revive the liberal arts; debates on images (Libri Carolini) and the filioque show theological philosophy in Latin. Boethius and Augustine are curricular bedrock for an ethic of Christian rulership.
mapLayers.science: Computus reform, Carolingian minuscule as information technology, estate surveys (polyptychs), and bridge/road logistics are the sciences of governance. Medical and astronomical excerpts circulate in monastery libraries without a research university.

mapLayers.label: East Francia
mapLayers.art: After Verdun (843), East Frankish churches and royal palaces continue Carolingian forms while local schools (Fulda, St Emmeram) illuminate manuscripts. Ottonian splendour is just beyond this horizon; here the art is monastic and royal-chapel Carolingian.
mapLayers.ideas: Louis the German’s realm and the Strasbourg Oaths (842) show East Francia as a German-speaking political community inside partitioned empire. Frontier policy toward Slavs and Danes defines kingship as much as Italian dreams.
mapLayers.philosophy: Hrabanus Maurus and Fulda exegesis dominate intellectual life: biblical commentary as philosophy of history and morals. Vernacular beginnings (Hildebrandslied, baptismal vows) encode ethic in German tongue.
mapLayers.science: Monastic computus, herbals, and agricultural polyptych knowledge persist; mining and forest clearance on eastern marches are applied environmental science. Latin school grammar is the gateway technology for clergy.

mapLayers.label: Carolingian / Lombard Italy
mapLayers.art: Lombard eight-century stone carving (Cividale, Tempietto) and goldsmith work meet Frankish conquest patronage after 774. Italian cities keep late antique churches alive; illuminated law books and charters visualise hybrid rule.
mapLayers.ideas: The Lombard kingdom’s defeat folds northern Italy into Carolingian structures while local aristocracies and papal Rome pursue autonomy. Legal pluralism—Roman, Lombard, Frankish—frames property and status.
mapLayers.philosophy: Paul the Deacon’s History of the Lombards and grammar teaching at court connect Italian letters to Carolingian reform. Monasteries debate Benedictine observance; speculative philosophy remains patristic.
mapLayers.science: Urban artisan continuity (stone, glass, metal), irrigation in Po agriculture, and notarial literacy are Italian strengths. Medical recipes and Roman agronomy survive in manuscript more densely than north of the Alps.

mapLayers.label: Asturias / Christian north
mapLayers.art: Asturian pre-Romanesque churches (San Julián de los Prados, Santa María del Naranco) invent a compact royal sacred architecture in the northern mountains. Cross of the Angels and Victory Cross goldwork proclaim Visigothic heirship after 711.
mapLayers.ideas: Pelagius’s resistance myth and Alfonso II’s court cast Asturias as refuge of Christian Spain. Ideology of reconquest and Visigothic legal memory legitimise a small kingdom against al-Andalus.
mapLayers.philosophy: Mozarabic liturgy and monastic rules shape northern Christian thought; Beatus of Liébana’s Commentary on the Apocalypse (late 8th c.) offers a vivid theology of history against adoptionist controversy and Muslim power.
mapLayers.science: Mountain agrarian systems, fortification of passes, and manuscript computus in tight scriptoria constitute local knowledge. Technical splendour is concentrated in goldsmithing and masonry rather than abstract science.

mapLayers.label: Al-Andalus
mapLayers.art: Córdoba’s Great Mosque (hypostyle hall, horseshoe arches, later maqsura splendour) defines Umayyad visual power. Ivory pyxides, silks, and city palaces make Andalusi art a Mediterranean high style unmatched in contemporary Christian north.
mapLayers.ideas: Umayyad emirate then caliphate claims Hispanic-Islamic sovereignty distinct from Abbasid Baghdad. Arabic literacy, court ceremonial, and dhimma arrangements structure a plural society of Muslims, Christians, and Jews.
mapLayers.philosophy: Andalusi letters later flower with Ibn Masarra and, further on, Ibn Rushd—but already in the emirate–caliphate era, Arabic falsafa, kalām, and legal schools (Mālikī dominance) frame reason and revelation. Jewish and Christian scholars work inside Arabic intellectual space.
mapLayers.science: Irrigation engineering (norias, qanats adaptations), agronomy, astronomy, and medicine travel with Arabic libraries. Córdoba’s book culture makes al-Andalus Europe’s densest scientific information network in this era.

mapLayers.label: Wessex / Anglo-Saxon England
mapLayers.art: Alfredian and later West Saxon patronage rebuilds churches after Viking wars; Insular-descended manuscript art and metalwork continue. Burh earthworks and stone towers are the visual politics of defence.
mapLayers.ideas: Alfred’s law-book preface and programme of vernacular translation cast the king as teacher-ruler. English identity hardens against the Danelaw while learning is framed as spiritual and political necessity.
mapLayers.philosophy: Translations of Gregory, Boethius, and Augustine into Old English make philosophy pastoral and royal. Wisdom literature and penitential discipline teach ordered souls for an ordered realm.
mapLayers.science: Alfred’s burh system, shipbuilding, and candle-clock anecdote tradition show practical measurement; monastic schools restore Latin computus and medicine after disruption. Technology is defensive and didactic.

mapLayers.label: Danelaw / Norse zones
mapLayers.art: Hybrid Anglo-Scandinavian sculpture (hogbacks, cross shafts with Jelling-style beasts) and furnished warrior graves mark Norse presence. Place-name landscapes are an invisible art of settlement memory.
mapLayers.ideas: Danelaw treaties and the idea of ‘Danish’ law create a plural legal England. Army settlements become farming communities under kings who bargain with Wessex.
mapLayers.philosophy: Norse honour culture and Christian conversion pressures coexist; oath, feud, and lordship ethics meet English penitential norms. Worldviews collide in shared market towns more than in academies.
mapLayers.science: Open-boat and knarr know-how, urban crafts at York (Jorvik), and agricultural colonisation of taken land are applied sciences. Weight-based silver economies reintroduce calculation into daily exchange.

mapLayers.label: Norse Ireland
mapLayers.art: Dublin’s urban archaeology—house plans, comb-making, Insular-Norse metalwork—shows a fortified longphort become town. High crosses in the Irish hinterland continue native sacred art beside the port’s hybrid gear.
mapLayers.ideas: Norse-Gaelic dynasties broker trade, slaves, and alliances among Irish overkings. Dublin is a node in an Irish Sea world linking York, Isle of Man, and Norway.
mapLayers.philosophy: Irish monastic learning and Norse warrior ethics meet in conversion-era elites; filid poetic grades keep a native intellectual order outside the town walls. Moral thought is still more monastic than scholastic.
mapLayers.science: Ship maintenance, urban craft specialisation, and silver economies are Dublin’s technical core. Irish computus and Latin learning remain strongest in older monastic centres, not the longphort.

mapLayers.label: Danish kingdom
mapLayers.art: Jelling stones (just after the strict Carolingian century, but in the kingdom’s arc) and earlier elite burials show royal monumental claims. Animal ornament and hall complexes visualise emerging monarchy.
mapLayers.ideas: Danish kings negotiate raid, trade, and Frankish border politics (Danevirke). Conversion becomes a royal tool for international recognition as much as faith.
mapLayers.philosophy: Pre-Christian mythic kingship yields to missionary Christianity; ethics of ring-giver generosity persist under new baptismal names. Written philosophy arrives with churchmen.
mapLayers.science: Danevirke earthwork engineering, harbour sites, and agricultural intensification underpin royal power. Seafaring remains the master technology.

mapLayers.label: Norwegian kingdom
mapLayers.art: Ship burials and richly carved objects (Oseberg horizon straddles this era’s end) display textile, wood, and animal-style mastery. Coastal chieftain seats are the galleries of power.
mapLayers.ideas: Petty kings and earls compete until Harald Fairhair traditions claim unification; west-over-sea migration to Isles and Iceland exports Norwegian political forms.
mapLayers.philosophy: Fate, reputation, and law-assembly (thing) customs structure right conduct. Eddic wisdom in later texts preserves older maxims against reckless pride.
mapLayers.science: Clinker ship technology, navigation by coast and stars, and ironworking in fjord farms are Norway’s sciences of survival and expansion.

mapLayers.label: Swedish kingdom
mapLayers.art: Vendel and Valsgärde boat graves, helmets, and shield fittings show Uppland elite art linked to earlier Migration styles. Eastern silver and Islamic coins in hoards become part of the visual economy.
mapLayers.ideas: Svear kings and Birka’s trade entangle Sweden with Frankish missions (Ansgar) and eastern routes toward the Rus’. Kingship grows through control of nodes, not continuous territory.
mapLayers.philosophy: Cult at Uppsala (as later remembered) and hall religion organise cosmic kingship; Christianity enters as court option and conflict. Moral life is honour before creed.
mapLayers.science: River–Baltic transport, fur and slave trade logistics, and specialised smithing at central places constitute applied knowledge. Runes mark ownership and memory.

mapLayers.label: Byzantine Empire
mapLayers.art: Post-iconoclast Macedonian beginnings restore monumental icons and mosaic splendour; Constantinopolitan court dress and silk define imperial taste. Missionary art later travels to Moravia and the Rus’ with the cross.
mapLayers.ideas: Byzantium claims Roman continuity against Carolingian upstarts; Photian controversies and Balkan diplomacy manage Bulgaria and the Slavs. Orthodoxy plus law equal civilisation.
mapLayers.philosophy: Photios’ erudition and Aristotelian–patristic school traditions keep Greek philosophy alive. Theology of images after 843 (Triumph of Orthodoxy) is the public metaphysics of the age.
mapLayers.science: Greek medical and mathematical texts, military manuals (taktika), and fire-projected naval weapons sustain technical edge. Administrative archives and surveying support tax and theme armies.

mapLayers.label: First Bulgarian Empire
mapLayers.art: Pliska and Preslav’s palatial and church architecture, proto-Bulgarian metalwork, and after conversion an explosion of Slavonic manuscript culture define khan-to-tsar visual power. Stone inscriptions proclaim rulership in Greek and later Slavic.
mapLayers.ideas: Krum to Boris I: from steppe-tinged khanate to Christian tsardom balancing Byzantium. The decision for Byzantine Christianity (c. 864–70) is geopolitical philosophy in action.
mapLayers.philosophy: Conversion imports Byzantine theology; Cyril and Methodius’s disciples bring Slavonic liturgy and a literary language capable of scripture and law. Intellectual life becomes monastic-Slavic almost overnight.
mapLayers.science: Fortified capitals, military organisation against Byzantium, and adoption of writing systems (Glagolitic/Cyrillic lineages) are state sciences. Agrarian surplus feeds both army and new Christian institutions.

mapLayers.label: Great Moravia
mapLayers.art: Great Moravian church foundations, Latin and Byzantine-influenced liturgical gear, and stronghold architecture at Mikulčice and related sites show a Slavic polity choosing Christian monumental forms. Metalwork mixes Avar-era echoes with Frankish imports.
mapLayers.ideas: Rastislav’s invitation to Byzantine missionaries (863) seeks ecclesiastical independence from East Frankish bishops—language politics as sovereignty. Svatopluk’s expansion makes Moravia a brief central-European power.
mapLayers.philosophy: Cyril and Methodius introduce a philosophy of vernacular sacred speech: liturgy in Slavonic as worthy as Latin or Greek. Latin clergy contest that claim; the quarrel is about who mediates truth.
mapLayers.science: Fortification engineering, long-distance trade (including Byzantine and Frankish goods), and the technology of writing (Glagolitic) are Moravia’s knowledge revolutions. Statecraft outruns its short political life.

mapLayers.label: Kievan Rus’
mapLayers.art: Early Rus’ elite taste is readable in dirham hoards, Scandinavian-style jewellery, and river-port crafts before full Christian monumentalism. Later eleventh-century churches stand on ninth–tenth-century commercial foundations forming in this era.
mapLayers.ideas: Varangian-led polities along the Dnieper organise tribute (poliudie) and trade toward Byzantium. Primary Chronicle traditions (written later) mythologise calling-of-the-Varangians as origin of ordered rule.
mapLayers.philosophy: Pagan cult and oath practices precede Vladimir’s later conversion; in the frankish-era slice, ideology is still warrior-merchant reciprocity and steppe diplomacy. Written philosophy waits on baptism and Church Slavonic.
mapLayers.science: River navigation, portage logistics, fur/slave/silver trade accounting, and ship types adapted from Scandinavian models are Rus’ sciences. Urbanising Kiev and Novgorod begin as technical nodes on a water road.

mapLayers.label: Khazar steppe
mapLayers.art: Khazar material culture mixes steppe mobile prestige with urban Sarkel-style fortification; religious plurality leaves a thinner iconic programme than Christian or Islamic neighbours. Trade silver and belt sets speak louder than churches.
mapLayers.ideas: The Khazar Qaghanate manages Silk Road–Volga trade and buffers Byzantium, Arabs, and steppe rivals. Elite conversion to Judaism (debated in detail, attested in sources) is a striking third-way identity between cross and crescent.
mapLayers.philosophy: Correspondence traditions (Khazar Correspondence) dramatise philosophical-religious choice among faiths—whether fully historical or literary, they stage reason-of-state as confession. Plural subject populations practise multiple rites under Turkic overlordship.
mapLayers.science: Steppe cavalry logistics, fortress building on the Don, and customs knowledge of caravan tariffs are Khazar technical strengths. Geographic position makes them information brokers between forest and caliphate.

mapLayers.label: Early Croatian polity
mapLayers.art: Early Croatian churches (ninth-century foundations along the Dalmatian hinterland) and Latin epigraphy show a Slavic elite adopting Adriatic Christian architecture. Interlace stone sculpture links local carving to wider Insular–Italian ornamental habits.
mapLayers.ideas: Dukes negotiating with Franks, Byzantium, and the papacy build a recognised Christian principality. Baptism and Benedictine monasticism are tools of international legitimacy.
mapLayers.philosophy: Latin Christianity supplies moral and political vocabulary; native Slavic social ethics persist in kinship and customary law. Intellectual life is episcopal and monastic, oriented to Rome more than Constantinople.
mapLayers.science: Adriatic maritime contact, hillfort-to-church settlement shifts, and literacy in Latin charters are the knowledge base. Agricultural hinterlands feed coastal exchange more than abstract science.

FRA.name: Carolingian Frankish core
FRA.conflicts: Saxon wars; Lombard Italy; Muslim Spain marches; civil wars after 843.
FRA.leaders: Charlemagne; Louis the Pious; later Charles the Bald (West Francia).
FRA.religion: Latin Christian empire; forced Saxon conversion; alliance and tension with the papacy.
FRA.culture: Carolingian Renaissance — palace school, minuscule script, liturgical reform.
FRA.story: The imperial crowning at Rome (800) and the Saxon Wars define Carolingian power: sacred empire built with the sword. Verdun (843) then splits the dream among grandsons.
FRA.literature: Einhard’s Charlemagne, capitularies as prose of power, monastic histories. The vernacular is gathering strength offstage for later chansons de geste that will reinvent this age as epic.
FRA.art: Aachen’s chapel memory, Gospel books in gold covers, and monastery plans broadcast Carolingian sacred design from the Frankish heartland. Ivory, liturgy, and minuscule pages are the empire’s visual software.

images.caption: Shrine of Charlemagne — medieval Christian reliquary

FRA.ideas: Charlemagne’s correctio and the 800 imperial coronation cast the Frankish king as Western emperor and reformer of Christendom. Capitularies and missi try to make ideology administrable.
FRA.philosophy: Alcuin’s liberal arts, image debates (Libri Carolini), and Augustinian–Boethian curricula train clerks in Christian rulership theory. Philosophy is palace-school theology.
FRA.science: Computus reform, polyptych estate accounting, and Carolingian minuscule as information tech are sciences of governance. Bridges, roads, and military levies apply geometry to power.

DEU.name: East Francia
DEU.conflicts: Slavic frontier wars; Viking raids on coasts/rivers.
DEU.leaders: Louis the German; Arnulf; early stem-duke politics after Verdun.
DEU.religion: Latin Christianity with royal and episcopal sponsorship; baptism, Mass, and saints’ cults structure public life. Missionary pushes east plant churches among Saxons and neighbors, often with political force.
DEU.culture: East Frankish lordship; monastic centers; frontier marches.
DEU.story: East Francia becomes the kernel of the later Holy Roman Empire — a kingdom born from treaty lines at Verdun.
DEU.literature: Carolingian Latin renewal (Alcuin, Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne), vernacular beginnings, and in the isles the flowering of Old English and Insular Latin. Annals invent yearly time; hagiography invents holy celebrities. German lands often host the workshop — print, metal, and later industrial form — for Europe’s ideas.
DEU.art: East Frankish monasteries (Fulda and peers) illuminate manuscripts in Carolingian styles while royal churches hold the eastern realm’s sacred art after Verdun. Stone and script, not yet Ottonian gold, dominate.

ITA.name: Carolingian / Lombard Italy
ITA.summary: Frankish rule in north; Byzantine south.
ITA.leaders: Charlemagne as Lombard king; popes; Byzantine officials in the south.
ITA.religion: Rome’s Latin papacy, Greek Orthodoxy in the south, and rising Islam in Sicily create a three-way ritual map — Mass, Byzantine liturgy, and congregational prayer on one peninsula.
ITA.culture: Lombard law memory; Roman ceremonial; Mediterranean trade seeds.
ITA.story: The Donation ideology and papal–Frankish alliance remake Italy into the empire’s sacred theater.
ITA.literature: Carolingian Latin renewal (Alcuin, Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne), vernacular beginnings, and in the isles the flowering of Old English and Insular Latin. Annals invent yearly time; hagiography invents holy celebrities. Italian cities teach prestige: from Roman monumentality to Renaissance brand management of beauty.
ITA.art: Lombard stone carving and goldsmith work meet Frankish conquest patronage after 774; Italian cities keep late antique churches in continuous use. Hybrid ornament marks Carolingian Italy.

ITA.ideas: Lombard legal identity persists under Frankish structures while popes and local dukes pursue autonomy. Plural law—Roman, Lombard, Frankish—frames status.
ITA.philosophy: Paul the Deacon and Italian grammarians feed Carolingian letters; Benedictine debates shape monastic ethics. Speculative philosophy stays patristic.
ITA.science: Urban crafts, Po Valley agriculture, and notarial literacy are Italian technical strengths. Medical and agronomic manuscripts circulate denser than in the north.

ESP.name: Asturias vs Al-Andalus
ESP.leaders: Emirs/caliphs of Córdoba; Alfonso II of Asturias; counts of Barcelona.
ESP.religion: Al-Andalus: Islamic prayer, Qur’anic law, and mosque life; northern Christian kingdoms keep Mass and saints; Jewish communities maintain synagogue and law. Three ritual civilizations in one peninsula.
ESP.culture: Córdoba’s libraries and mosques; Asturian churches; frontier raid culture (razzias).
ESP.story: Almanzor’s raids (late 10th c. still ahead of this tick’s heart) haunt Christian memory — Córdoba as both civilization and threat.
ESP.literature: Carolingian Latin renewal (Alcuin, Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne), vernacular beginnings, and in the isles the flowering of Old English and Insular Latin. Annals invent yearly time; hagiography invents holy celebrities. Iberia’s art of contact — Christian, Jewish, Islamic — keeps Europe from pretending it was ever only Latin.
ESP.art: Split visual world: Asturian pre-Romanesque churches and Victory gold crosses in the Christian north versus Córdoba’s Great Mosque and ivories in al-Andalus—Europe’s sharpest art frontier.

ESP.philosophy: Beatus apocalypse commentary in the north; Arabic falsafa, Mālikī law, and Jewish thought in the south. Reason-and-revelation debates are denser in Andalusi libraries.
ESP.science: Andalusi irrigation, astronomy, and medicine outpace northern computus; Asturian masonry and manuscript craft hold the mountain refuge’s tech. Knowledge follows confession and court.

GBR.name: Wessex vs Danelaw
GBR.conflicts: Viking wars; reconquest of the Danelaw.
GBR.leaders: Alfred the Great; Edward the Elder; Æthelstan; Norse kings in York/Dublin orbit.
GBR.religion: Latin Christian Anglo-Saxon kingdoms; pagan Norse arrivals converting unevenly.
GBR.culture: Alfredian translation program; burhs; epic and chronicle (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle).
GBR.story: Alfred’s refuge in the marshes and reconquest become England’s founding resistance story against the Great Heathen Army.
GBR.literature: Alfred’s translation program — Pastoral Care, Boethius, Psalms — invents English as a language of state thought. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle pins years like nails. Riddles and elegies glitter in Exeter’s book.
GBR.art: Alfredian rebuilds, burh earthworks, and Insular-descended books define West Saxon visual politics; Danelaw zones add hogbacks and Anglo-Scandinavian beast styles.

GBR.science: Burhs, ships, and restored monastic computus are defensive and didactic sciences; York’s crafts show Norse urban technique inside the island economy.

IRL.name: Irish kingdoms & Norse-Gaelic beginnings
IRL.summary: Gaelic over-kingships with early Viking bases appearing on coasts late in the century.
IRL.conflicts: Inter-dynastic cattle politics; first Norse raids (from 795 in annals).
IRL.leaders: Uí Néill over-kings; Munster rivals; early Norse chieftains in camps.
IRL.religion: Christian monastic Ireland (Mass, reliquaries, high crosses) meets pagan Norse newcomers whose gods and ship-burial rites convert unevenly in the towns.
IRL.culture: High-cross monastic art; learning that exports missionaries.
IRL.story: The Annals’ first Viking raid notices begin Ireland’s long Norse chapter — monasteries as both treasure and target.
IRL.literature: Carolingian Latin renewal (Alcuin, Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne), vernacular beginnings, and in the isles the flowering of Old English and Insular Latin. Annals invent yearly time; hagiography invents holy celebrities. Irish monastic and later Gaelic learned traditions punch above demographic weight in Europe’s imagination.
IRL.art: Dublin’s longphort-to-town archaeology—combs, weights, hybrid metalwork—meets high crosses and monastic art in the Gaelic hinterland. Two aesthetics share the Irish Sea.

IRL.philosophy: Monastic Latin learning and native poetic grades carry ethics; Norse warrior values convert unevenly. Philosophy is still monastic more than scholastic.
IRL.science: Ship maintenance, silver economies, and urban crafts in Dublin; Irish computus and medicine remain strongest in older monasteries.

DNK.name: Danish kingdom
DNK.leaders: Early historically foggy kings culminating toward Bluetooth’s line.
DNK.religion: Norse pagan sacrifice and hall cult dominate; Ansgar-style missions plant fragile churches. Baptism is still a royal/port phenomenon, not a finished conversion.
DNK.story: Denmark sits at the mouth of Baltic–North Sea violence and trade — the workshop of the Viking Age.
DNK.literature: Carolingian Latin renewal (Alcuin, Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne), vernacular beginnings, and in the isles the flowering of Old English and Insular Latin. Annals invent yearly time; hagiography invents holy celebrities. Danish gatekeeping of the Baltic Sound makes culture a toll-booth as well as a stage.
DNK.art: Elite halls, animal ornament, and defensive earthworks (Danevirke) visualise an emerging Danish monarchy facing the Frankish world. Monumental runestones crescendo just after this slice.

DNK.philosophy: Ring-giver ethics and pagan cult yield to missionary Christianity at court pace. Written philosophy arrives with churchmen.
DNK.science: Harbour engineering, Danevirke logistics, and agricultural intensification underpin royal power; seafaring is master technology.

NOR.name: Norwegian kingdom forming
NOR.leaders: Sea-kings and local petty kings before Harald Fairhair’s unification traditions.
NOR.religion: Norse paganism — blót, burial mounds, and sacred groves — remains dominant. Christian contact arrives via trade and raid; forced conversion is still ahead.
NOR.culture: Shipburial elite display; skaldic praise; thing assemblies.
NOR.story: The Viking launch from fjords toward Ireland, Francia, and beyond begins Norway’s global hour.
NOR.literature: Carolingian Latin renewal (Alcuin, Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne), vernacular beginnings, and in the isles the flowering of Old English and Insular Latin. Annals invent yearly time; hagiography invents holy celebrities. Norwegian arts remember ships first — keel as national metaphor from Oseberg to oil platforms.
NOR.art: Ship-burial horizons and carved animal-style wood/metal display chieftain wealth along the fjords—portable splendour before stone cathedrals.

NOR.science: Clinker-built ships, coastal navigation by skerry and star, and ironworking in fjord farms are survival sciences that enable overseas expansion.

SWE.name: Swedish / Varangian world
SWE.leaders: Uppsala kings in later tradition; Rus’ expedition leaders.
SWE.religion: Uppsala-centered pagan cult memory, local blót, and mound burial persist while Varangian routes bring Byzantine and Latin Christian contact religions east and west.
SWE.story: Swedish Vikings as ‘Rus’’ in eastern sources link the Mälaren to the Black Sea.
SWE.literature: Carolingian Latin renewal (Alcuin, Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne), vernacular beginnings, and in the isles the flowering of Old English and Insular Latin. Annals invent yearly time; hagiography invents holy celebrities. Swedish culture often exports northern clarity — from rock art to modern design temperaments.
SWE.art: Vendel/Valsgärde boat graves and Uppland helmets continue Migration-style elite art; eastern silver dirhams enter the visual economy of hoards.

SWE.science: Baltic–river transport, fur/slave logistics, and specialist smithing at central places; runes mark ownership and memory.

TUR.name: Byzantine Anatolia
TUR.summary: Themes of Asia Minor as the empire’s military reservoir.
TUR.conflicts: Arab frontier warfare; iconoclasm politics earlier/around the era.
TUR.leaders: Byzantine emperors (Irene, Nikephoros, later Macedonians still ahead).
TUR.religion: Greek Orthodoxy: Divine Liturgy, icons, and monasticism under iconoclast/iconophile controversy. Imperial church and holy images are political as well as sacred.
TUR.story: Anatolia’s soldiers keep Byzantium alive while the west invents new kingdoms.
TUR.literature: Carolingian Latin renewal (Alcuin, Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne), vernacular beginnings, and in the isles the flowering of Old English and Insular Latin. Annals invent yearly time; hagiography invents holy celebrities. Ottoman and Anatolian layers make this edge of the map a second classical continuum for Europe to face.
TUR.art: Post-iconoclast Constantinople restores icons and mosaic splendour; silk and court ceremonial define Byzantine taste for Frankish-era Europe.

TUR.philosophy: Photios’ erudition and the theology of images (Triumph of Orthodoxy, 843) are public metaphysics. Greek patristic–Aristotelian schooling continues.
TUR.science: Medical and mathematical Greek texts, taktika, and naval weaponry sustain technical edge; themes and tax archives are administrative science.

BGR.name: First Bulgarian Empire
BGR.summary: Khan then Christian rulers south of the Danube balancing Byzantium.
BGR.conflicts: Byzantine wars; conversion politics under Boris I (later 9th c.).
BGR.leaders: Krum (memory); Boris I; early Bulgarian khans/princes.
BGR.religion: Bulgar elite paganism gives way to Slavic Orthodoxy after conversion: baptism, liturgy in Slavic, and a new patriarchal church tying rule to rite.
BGR.story: Boris’s conversion is the Balkans’ state-baptism parallel to northern Europe’s royal conversions.
BGR.literature: Carolingian Latin renewal (Alcuin, Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne), vernacular beginnings, and in the isles the flowering of Old English and Insular Latin. Annals invent yearly time; hagiography invents holy celebrities. Bulgarian letters pioneer Slavic Christian literacy — a soft empire of books south of the Danube.
BGR.art: Pliska and Preslav’s palatial and church architecture mark the First Bulgarian Empire’s shift from steppe-tinged khanate to Christian monumental capital; stone inscriptions proclaim rulers.

BGR.philosophy: Slavonic liturgy via Cyril and Methodius’s disciples creates a philosophy of vernacular sacred speech. Intellectual life becomes monastic-Slavic with startling speed.
BGR.science: Fortified capitals, military organisation, and adoption of Glagolitic/Cyrillic writing systems are state sciences; agrarian surplus feeds army and church.

UKR.name: Early Rus’ river road
UKR.summary: Scandinavian–Slavic networks forming along the Dnieper before Vladimir’s baptism.
UKR.conflicts: Khazar tribute politics; steppe raiders; Byzantine trade diplomacy.
UKR.leaders: Semi-legendary Varangian princes of the Primary Chronicle tradition.
UKR.religion: Rus’ river road remains largely pagan (Perun and related cults in later memory) while Byzantine and missionary Christianity arrive along trade — baptism still episodic.
UKR.story: Askold, Dir, and Oleg in chronicle memory — the origin tales of a polity that will choose Orthodoxy.
UKR.literature: Carolingian Latin renewal (Alcuin, Einhard’s Life of Charlemagne), vernacular beginnings, and in the isles the flowering of Old English and Insular Latin. Annals invent yearly time; hagiography invents holy celebrities. Borderland creativity — Cossack, Ruthenian, and European currents braided under dangerous skies.
UKR.art: Early Rus’ river-port crafts, Scandinavian-style jewellery, and dirham silver precede later church monumentality—trade aesthetics on the Dnieper road. Khazar steppe gear fringes the east.
